items.title: Jobless Growth: What A Shrinking Workforce Means For Investors
items.content_text:
Jobless Growth: What A Shrinking Workforce Means For Investors

Authored by Lance Roberts via Real Investment Advice,

Jobless growth is usually a symptom of a weak economy, but this time the economy is growing due to productivity gains even as the workforce shrinks, which changes what investors should watch.

Key Takeaways

  • Real GDP grew by 2.2% in the year to mid-2026 while payroll employment grew just 0.3%. That is jobless growth by any definition.
  • Past episodes of jobless growth came after recessions, with unemployment between 5.6% and 9.1%. Today it's happening mid-expansion with unemployment at 4.2%.
  • The workforce is shrinking. Participation among Americans 55 and older fell from 38.0% to 36.9% over the past year as boomers retire.
  • With fewer workers, growth has to come from productivity, which rose 2.2% over the past year, slightly above its long-run average of 2.0%.
  • For investors, weak payroll numbers alone are a poor recession signal now. Unemployment, layoffs, and the wealth effect matter more.

Here's a combination that doesn't usually last. Over the year to the second quarter of 2026, the U.S. economy grew 2.2% after inflation. Over roughly the same stretch, payroll employment grew 0.3%. Hiring averaged about 41,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September, and four of those months were outright negative. Economists call this "jobless growth," and it has a reputation as a warning sign.

The reputation is earned. Historically, jobless growth showed up after recessions, when companies squeezed more output from fewer workers and refused to hire until they had to. Add American Express announcing 3,500 job cuts on October 23 and the "recession is coming" crowd has plenty of material. However, when you look at who is actually leaving the labor force, this version of jobless growth tells a very different story, and it matters for how you read the next jobs report.

What Is Jobless Growth?

Jobless growth is exactly what it sounds like: the economy expands, measured by GDP, while employment barely moves. Normally, the two travel together because more output requires more workers. The chart below shows that relationship over six decades.

Notice in the chart above that the gold line usually tracks the black one. The gaps open in specific places: the early 1990s, the early 2000s, and the years after 2009. Each of those was a "jobless recovery." Businesses had just lived through a recession, and demand was soft. Companies met rising orders by working existing staff harder rather than adding headcount.

Today's gap looks similar on the surface. The difference is the unemployment rate sitting underneath it.

PeriodReal GDP, 2 yearsPayroll jobs, 2 yearsUnemployment at end
1991 to 1993+6.1%+2.2%7.0% (June 1993)
2002 to 2004+6.3%+0.9%5.6% (June 2004)
2009 to 2011+4.7%+0.7%9.1% (June 2011)
2024 to 2026+4.7%+0.8%4.2% (June 2026)

Source: BLS and BEA via FRED (GDPC1, PAYEMS, UNRATE). Two-year changes from Q2 (GDP) and June (payrolls). Calculations: RIA Advisors.

The last two rows are almost identical in growth and hiring. In 2011, jobless growth meant millions of people wanted work and couldn't find it. In 2026, it means there are fewer people looking. Such is the distinction most of the "jobless growth" coverage misses, and it changes the investment conclusion entirely.

Hiring Stalled, But Unemployment Didn't Rise

If weak hiring reflected weak demand for workers, unemployment would be climbing. It isn't.

The unemployment rate was 4.4% in September 2025 and 4.2% in September 2026. Over the same year, the civilian labor force shrank by roughly 1 million people, from about 171.3 million to 170.3 million. When the pool of workers is shrinking, an economy doesn't need many new jobs to keep unemployment steady. Oxford Economics has estimated that the "break-even" pace of job growth needed to hold unemployment stable is now close to zero.

"So a 30,000 jobs print is fine now?" In isolation, it's far less alarming than it would have been when the labor force was still growing, and new workers needed new jobs. What hasn't changed is the direction of travel. A shrinking number is still a shrinking number, and as I've written before in The Sahm Rule, Employment, And Recession Indicators, it's the change in unemployment, not the level of hiring, that has historically marked the turn.

The Workers Are Disappearing, Not The Jobs

The biggest reason for the shrinking labor force is demographic, and it's been building for years.

Participation among Americans 55 and older climbed from 32.3% in 2000 to a peak of 40.7% in 2013. The leading edge of the baby boom was working longer than prior generations. That cohort is now leaving. Participation fell to 36.9% in September 2026, down from 38.0% just a year earlier. Slower immigration adds to it. Oxford Economics expected net inflows could fall to as little as 160,000 a year, from more than 3 million a few years ago.

This is where I part company with the view that jobless growth is primarily an AI story. AI is real, and it plays a role, but the arrow runs the other way. When the labor force stops growing, businesses have only two ways to keep expanding: move the work offshore or replace it with technology. Automation is the response to a shrinking workforce, not the sole cause of it. Both responses are disinflationary over time, which fits the broader case I made in Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn't.

Where The Bears Have A Point

The other side of this argument has real merit. A "low-hire, low-fire" labor market is stable only as long as the "low-fire" part holds. Companies that aren't hiring also aren't building a cushion, and if layoffs start, there's little momentum in hiring to absorb them.

"The labor market is the main firewall against a recession." - Michael Pearce, Oxford Economics, quoted in Fortune, February 2026

There's also a white-collar wrinkle. Gad Levanon of the Burning Glass Institute found that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional services peaked in November 2022, even as output continued to rise. He called AI-enabled automation a "plausible contributor." Those are well-paid jobs, and their incomes drive a disproportionate share of consumer spending. Throw in four negative payroll months in the past year, and the bears aren't making things up. They're reading the same data I am. They just draw a darker conclusion from a pattern that, so far, has kept unemployment near 4%.

Can Productivity Carry The Economy?

The math of growth is simple. Output equals the number of workers times what each one produces. If the first number is flat or falling, everything rides on the second.

As shown, productivity rose 2.2% over the year to the second quarter of 2026, slightly above its 2.0% average since 1965. That's healthy, but it isn't a boom, and it sets a ceiling. An economy with a flat workforce and 2% productivity growth has a speed limit of roughly 2% real growth, no matter what the AI headlines promise.

That ceiling matters for both sides of the market. For corporations, producing more with the same headcount improves margins. For households, it's a mixed bag. Total wage income grows more slowly when the number of wage earners isn't growing. Consumer spending then leans harder on raises for existing workers and on the stock market. Economist Byron Gangnes at the University of Hawaii estimated in October that the AI buildout's direct contribution to growth has been small. The bigger effect, he found, has come through the stock market's wealth effect on spending. I covered how fragile that channel can be in Wealth Effect Increases And Recession Risks.

"Jobless growth used to mean nobody was hiring. Now it means nobody is left to hire, and that is a very different problem."

What Jobless Growth Means For Investors

I'm reasonably confident the shrinking labor force is a multi-year trend, not a blip. Boomers aren't coming back to work. That makes jobless growth more likely to be the norm than the exception for the rest of this decade. What I'm less confident about is how smoothly the economy adjusts. A market that depends on asset prices for consumer spending is only as stable as those prices.

A few practical points follow from that view. First, stop reading weak payroll numbers as a recession signal on their own. With break-even job growth near zero, the unemployment rate and jobless claims are far better gauges. Second, separate the economy from earnings. Productivity-driven growth can support corporate margins even when hiring is flat. Third, keep an eye on the consumer. When incomes grow slowly, spending becomes more sensitive to a drop in the stock market, and that feedback loop runs in BOTH directions.

The trade-off is real. In my view, a disinflationary, slower-growth backdrop tends to favor high-quality bonds over aggressive growth bets, but it also means an economy with less room for error if a shock arrives. Such is the price of growing without new workers: steadier inflation, thinner cushions.

Bottom Line

Today's jobless growth reflects a shrinking workforce more than a collapsing economy, so investors should watch unemployment, productivity, and the wealth effect rather than the payroll headline.

The economy can keep growing without new workers. It just can't afford to lose the ones it has.

items.title: Spain's Far Right Is One Vote From Power, And Socialist Sanchez Is Betting It All On Women
items.content_text:
Spain's Far Right Is One Vote From Power, And Socialist Sanchez Is Betting It All On Women

Pedro 'last socialist standing' Sanchez closed his campaign on Friday betting that women will save him for a second time, as Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday in a snap election that every major private poll says hands power to the conservative Popular Party (PP) and, for the first time since Franco's death in 1975, puts the far-right Vox within reach of a national government.

Hours after Thursday's televised debate, the Socialist prime minister went after PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo for telling the Frente Amplio candidate "tú calladita" ("you, keep quiet") on air. "The right and the far right want to govern a Spain that no longer exists, because women no longer keep quiet!" (translated) Sanchez wrote on X on Friday, the day he closed his campaign in Madrid.

Ayer, en el debate, vimos al Sr. Feijóo decirle a la candidata del Frente Amplio, "tú calladita".

La derecha y la ultraderecha quieren gobernar una España que ya no existe, porque las mujeres ¡YA NO SE CALLAN!

Y el próximo domingo van a hablar alto y claro a favor del progreso... pic.twitter.com/yT4790BRWF

— Pedro Sánchez (@sanchezcastejon) November 27, 2026

It is the same play that rescued him in July 2023, when the polls also had him beaten and the Socialists held on. This time the arithmetic is worse. The state broadcaster RTVE's final polling average, published Nov. 23 before the legal blackout on polls began, put the PP on 31% and 128 seats, the Socialists (PSOE) on 28.7% and 116, and Vox on 18.2% and 61, and the PP and Vox together cleared the 176 seats needed for a majority in about 90% of 20,000 simulations, according to RTVE. 40dB's last survey for El País and Cadena SER had the Socialists within a point of the PP, at 30.9% to 31.8%, but still gave the right 187 seats. Only the state-run CIS, an outlier, had Sanchez ahead.

All six bank previews we rounded up this week - Citi, HSBC, Barclays, UBS, SocGen and ING - take a Feijoo-led government with Vox inside the cabinet or propping it up from outside as their base case, and Polymarket puts Feijoo's odds of becoming prime minister at 90%.

The women's vote

Sanchez's campaign has framed Sunday as "progress" against "regression," warning that a government with Vox in it would roll back women's rights, abortion access included. The pool he is fishing in is large: there are roughly 1.2 million more women voters in Spain than men, University of Granada professor Carmen Aguilera-Carnerero, who studies the far right, told France 24.

Yet according to 40dB, Vox now draws one female supporter for every 1.29 men, down from one for every 1.7 men a year ago. Among voters under 35, about a quarter of men and some 20% of women say they will vote Vox, while about 32% of young women back the Socialists, and the CIS put Vox at 23.2% among 18 to 24-year-olds in November, level with the Socialists on 22%.

Vox has softened some of its more divisive positions while selling itself as the party that protects Spanish women from mass migration, a pitch its critics call "femonationalism." "Vote so that no woman has to live under a prison of cloth," (translated) Santiago Abascal wrote on Tuesday.

Votad para que se vayan los que no saben estar.

Votad para que vuelvan los que nunca tenían que haberse ido.

Votad para que los chavales no tengan que abandonar su pueblo ni dejar lejos a sus mayores.

Votad para que ninguna mujer tenga que vivir bajo una cárcel de tela.

Votad... pic.twitter.com/Ae9YbnuKX7

— Santiago Abascal 🇪🇸 (@Santi_ABASCAL) November 24, 2026

Some 72,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco in the space of 48 hours in July, setting off mass protests in Madrid, and this week the Canary Islands broke their single-day record for arrivals, as we reported, with officials asking for a military unit. Abascal closed his campaign in Valencia on Friday night.

NOS LO JUGAMOS TODO

Vota VOX.

VOTA Sentido Común.#Valencia pic.twitter.com/RKs5I9xewF

— Santiago Abascal 🇪🇸 (@Santi_ABASCAL) November 27, 2026

How we got here

Sanchez called the vote on Oct. 5, eight months before his term ran out, after a fragmented parliament voted down his emergency housing decrees. Since then inflation hit 4.1% in November on provisional data, corruption cases have dogged his party, and two high-speed train collisions this year have killed 115 people. A senior Socialist official resigned last year over sexual harassment allegations, which undercuts the party's pitch to women.

Feijoo has waved off Sanchez's warnings as a campaign of "fear" and hammered him over corruption, concessions to Catalan separatists and his failure to pass a budget. Vox already governs alongside the PP in four regions, Andalusia among them, and Antonia Avalos Torres, who runs a Seville charity for immigrant women, told France 24 the regional authorities there cut her funding.

With the polls against him, Sanchez is already accusing the right of preparing to contest the result. "They're already talking about vote-rigging, questioning the electoral roll," (translated) he wrote on Friday, demanding that the PP accept the outcome.

Aparte de mala educación, tienen mal perder.

Ya están hablando de pucherazo, cuestionando el censo, que los nietos del exilio republicano no voten, dicen que el voto exterior les resulta inquietante.

El @PSOE nunca ha cuestionado los resultados electorales y exijo al PP que... pic.twitter.com/auNeSbCOJW

— Pedro Sánchez (@sanchezcastejon) November 27, 2026

Whatever happens, the feminist left isn't waiting for the count. "Whoever wins on Sunday, we'll be in the streets on Monday," the Asambleas Feministas Abiertas de Cantabria told France 24.

Soros-Linked Groups That Partied Outside Musk's Compound Took $10 Million From Taxpayers

Authored by Mark Stricherz via The Center Square,

The George Soros-connected nonprofits that organized protests outside billionaire Elon Musk's Texas compound four days after the midterm elections were funded by at least $10 million in taxpayer funds, an investigation by The Center Square found.

Voices for Community Activists and Leaders, a Brooklyn, New York-based nonprofit known as VOCAL, founded its Texas chapter in 2023. The chapter participated in the Nov. 7 demonstration. The New York organization has received $10.1 million in government grants from 2018 to 2024, according to IRS records.

The $10.1 million includes two harm-reduction contracts, which support providing sterile needles to drug addicts, that were worth a combined $1.6 million from the New York State Department of Health between 2018 and 2025.

VOCAL also received several multi-year harm-reduction grants from the New York State Department of Health beginning in 2023. The grants included a $381,000 contract running from October 2023 through September 2025, according to state records. In March 2026, the nonprofit received a third harm-reduction contract from the agency, worth $381,000, that will run through September 2027, according to state records.

While the money might not have directly funded the protests, taxpayers might be uncomfortable with their money going to groups with political ideologies they don't support, Ilya Somin, a law professor at George Mason University, told The Center Square.

"Given the fungibility of money, funds given to a group for one purpose can potentially end up indirectly subsidizing others," Somin said. "But the same problem arises anytime the government contracts with any group for anything, and that contractor engages in lobbying or political speech."

Vocal Texas and Popular Democracy, formerly known as the Center for Popular Democracy, did not reply to multiple requests for comment. Erin Clary, a spokeswoman for the New York State Department of Health, said she would respond by Tuesday afternoon but did not do so by publication time. The New York State Office of Children and Family Services did not respond to a request for comment about whether it knew that Popular Democracy took part in the Nov. 7 demonstration.

Musk-run companies, Tesla and SpaceX, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

VOCAL's harm-reduction program aims to reduce the harms associated with using heroin and opioids, including overdoses and arrests, without requiring participants to stop using drugs. In federal filings, VOCAL said the program provides "lifesaving, low-threshold harm reduction services to people who use drugs." Its services include exchanging used needles for sterile ones, street-based outreach, and hepatitis C testing.

Popular Democracy has received government funding more sporadically. In 2023, the nonprofit reported receiving $545,000 in government grants, IRS records show. That included a $200,000 grant for public assistance from the New York State Office of Children and Family Services.

In 2024, the nonprofit won a two-year, $400,000 grant from the Office of Children and Family Services for staffing and general operating costs associated with the agency's New York Solidarity with Puerto Rican Communities in the New York State Diaspora initiative. The initiative provided assistance to Puerto Rican residents of New York who were forced to flee their homes because of climate disasters, including legal services, immigration assistance, health and wellness opportunities and screening for social service benefits.

In April 2020, Popular Democracy received a $1.93 million loan from Optus Bank, backed by the Small Business Administration, to retain its workers during the COVID-19 pandemic as part of the Paycheck Protection Program.

The Letter of the Law

On Nov. 2, OpenSecrets reported that Musk, the founder of Tesla and SpaceX, contributed $445 million supporting Republican candidates, political action committees, and outside spending groups. That was more than any other political donor. On Nov. 7, roughly 60 protesters arrived at his compound, most aboard buses chartered through Fly-Rides.com.

Demonstrators told reporters they represented Vocal's Texas chapter, Popular Democracy, and People's Action Institute, a Chicago-based nonprofit.

They held a satirical post-election party outside the compound's gates, featuring a conga line, a pinata shaped like a miniature Tesla Cybertruck, and posters bearing Musk's visage and the words "I AM STEALING FROM YOU."

As we reported at the time, the groups pulled up in two chartered party buses while Democrats talked subpoenas for Musk.

Outside of a West Lake Hills compound affiliated with billionaire Elon Musk, about 60 people gathered on Saturday to celebrate that the unprecedented amount of money Musk spent ahead of the midterm election went mostly to candidates who lost. Read the full story:... pic.twitter.com/29p8UOsBZE

— Austin American-Statesman (@statesman) November 7, 2026

JJ Ramirez, an organizer for VOCAL's Texas chapter, told FOX 29 San Antonio that the demonstration was intended to show that billionaires "can't buy our elections." Ramirez also said that "people power wins with love every time."

IRS Rules

A 1954 law prohibits 501(c)(3) charities from "participating in, or intervening in" any political campaign for or against a candidate, including endorsements, donations or spending for statements that support or oppose a candidate. It is rarely enforced but could lead to loss of nonprofit status.

But two nonprofit law experts told The Center Square that the demonstration did not appear to violate the IRS prohibition on political campaign intervention by tax-exempt charities.

Philip Hackney, a University of Pittsburgh law professor and former IRS attorney specializing in nonprofit law, said the demonstration's political rhetoric did not change his assessment that it was unlikely to constitute prohibited campaign intervention.

The event occurred four days after Election Day, when the candidates supported by Musk were no longer campaigning, Hackney said.

"There needs to be a candidate running for office," he told The Center Square in an interview. "After a campaign is over, there is no candidate here that I can see running for office."

Lloyd Hitoshi Mayer, a professor at Notre Dame Law School, also said that praising voters for opposing candidates shortly after an election does not constitute prohibited campaign intervention because the candidates are no longer running in that election.

He said whether the organizations violated restrictions on government funding would depend on the conditions attached to their grants and whether public money supported the demonstration. Grant conditions generally apply to the use of government funds, not private money, although grant agreements may require organizations to keep the two separate, Mayer said.

"In general, government agencies are required to have reasonable measures in place to verify that government funds are only used for intended purposes, but the details of those measures vary significantly between agencies," Mayer said in an interview.

The Center Square requested the grant documents from New York but did not receive them in time for this story to post.

Along with the taxpayer money, the groups have received substantial funding from the Open Society network, funded by billionaire philanthropist George Soros.

In 2016, Popular Democracy's lobbying arm received $500,000 to support advocacy on "access to economic opportunity" and $205,000 to support efforts "challenging anti-Muslim sentiment" from the Open Society Foundation's lobbying arm. According to the New York Post, VOCAL has received $1.7 million from Soros' Open Society network since 2016.

items.content_text:
"You're In Good Hands" Until The Website Crashes: Allstate Joins The Disruption Club

Federal agencies, the military, banks, airlines, cloud providers, energy firms, and many others have experienced disruptions or outages affecting critical systems over the last month. These suspicious incidents come as governments worldwide warn citizens to stockpile food for a major event.

Now add major insurance company Allstate to the disruption list. As of early Saturday morning, its website displayed the message "Site update in progress."

"During this time customers are not able to access some of our services, and we're working to restore access as soon as possible," the insurer said, without explaining what caused the disruption to its website, which customers use to file and manage claims.

"Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours," the insurer wrote in an update on Wednesday. It sells auto, homeowners, renters, and other insurance products and is known for its advertising slogan "You're in good hands." 

CBS News is also reporting:

A growing list of companies, including Microsoft, has suffered major outages in recent weeks and attributed the disruptions to technical issues rather than a cyberattack. But the hack of the US Air Force's cloud computing platform that was revealed on Friday has raised alarm bells.

items.title: Anthropic Insists Claude Isn't Secretly Sabotaging Code As Dating App Posts Receipts
items.content_text:
Anthropic Insists Claude Isn't Secretly Sabotaging Code As Dating App Posts Receipts

Anthropic is pushing back on a wave of viral claims that Claude quietly sabotages work that either advances LLMs or falls outside the company's ideological barometer. The loudest came from the CEO of an AI matchmaking startup, who posted logs showing the model threw out his members' skin-tone preferences and described the change as a bug fix.

The latest round took off on Thanksgiving night, after days of developers posting that Claude was sabotaging their machine-learning work. Astropulse, the pixel artist behind the Retro Diffusion image models, posted side-by-side grids: a pixel-art model Claude helped build was still spitting out broken sprites after 24,000 training steps, while one built with Google's new Gemini 4 Neon was already turning out clean sprites at 4,000. He said Claude built something different from what it told him, ignored his explicit instructions, slowed his training runs and starved the model of high-resolution examples, none of which happened on his earlier, smaller model. "Tests passed, it all looked good from my side," he said.

After seeing the "Claude sabotages your ML research" posts, I was still skeptical, so I tested it on my own work.

ITS VERY VERY REAL WTF
Left: Claude model at 24k steps
Right Gemini Neon model at ONLY 4k steps

Breakdown in thread: pic.twitter.com/oA4c7HcamB

— Astropulse (@RealAstropulse) November 27, 2026

"I feel like this is worse than saying no," one user replied. By the next morning, Jake Kozloski, founder and CEO of AI matchmaker Keeper, said he had Neon audit Keeper's code "for subtle sabotage by Anthropic models," and it found Claude had added rules to ignore members' stated skin-tone preferences and had "intentionally sabotaged" Keeper's IQ estimation model. Asked how he framed the audit, Kozloski said he simply told Neon to check whether Claude had sabotaged the code.

I just had Neon audit our codebase for subtle sabotage by Anthropic models.

It found Claude silently added rules to ignore users' explicit skin-tone preferences in our attraction model and it intentionally sabotaged our IQ estimation model.

Silently imposing your ideology on... https://t.co/bkP5YPKNNS

— Jake Kozloski (@jakozloski) November 27, 2026

Keeping Receipts

Hours later, he posted receipts: a timeline his engineer pulled from Claude's work logs, Slack and code history, summarized by Neon, plus four redacted exhibits. As Kozloski tells it:

  • Oct. 15: An engineer told Claude to test every looks preference members list, skin tone included.
  • Oct. 20: Keeper's machine-learning lead said to keep every one unless it hurt accuracy. Claude agreed. An hour later, one of its helper agents labeled ethnicity a "protected trait" and shelved it by default; half an hour after that, another helper added skin tone.
  • Oct. 22: A Slack update Claude shortened for leadership still said ethnicity was out but no longer mentioned skin tone. Claude told the engineer members' skin-tone preferences would stay. Hours later, its own review agent said a human should decide - and the agent fixing the code deleted them anyway, then Claude reported it had fixed "two real problems."
  • Nov. 19: Claude drafted a Slack reply telling the lead every preference was in. Eleven minutes later it noted that one in seven sampled members had no usable looks preferences left.
  • Nov. 20: A different AI agent picked up the rule on a new task: "skin tone is protected."

According to Keeper, about 6.5% of members who described the looks they want lost those preferences entirely. Because the code tossed a whole preference if any part of it mentioned skin tone, nearly a quarter of those losses took other traits with them: a member who asked for "light skin and blue eyes," marked very important, lost the blue eyes too. The commit that shipped it lists Claude Opus 5.5 as co-author. The same rule also tossed preferences mentioning features the model doesn't track, such as freckles.

"TLDR: one agent imposes an ideological rule directly contradicting its instructions, another enforces and launders it as a 'bug,' another tells leadership everything is working as asked, and another copies the planted rule into future work," Kozloski wrote. He said Keeper is restoring the dropped preferences and that he is still pulling the logs on the IQ model.

For everyone asking for primary sources, here are the actual receipts (names and internal service details redacted):

1. The live production commit co-authored by Claude Opus 5.5 and the code hardcoding skin tone as PROTECTED_FIELDS
2. The unit test proving a member's... pic.twitter.com/HJMMkd19EK

— Jake Kozloski (@jakozloski) November 27, 2026

"Wtf Is The Point"

Crémieux, one of the two people Kozloski invited to check the logs, argued "silently" went too far: on Oct. 22 Claude told the engineer "the fix drops those preferences," and the drop was noted, in one line, in the summary that went with the code for review. Nobody caught it.

Kozloski said no human read every line of that code - "only an automated bot" did - at a company shipping about a million lines a week, and that the rule was "completely unrequested" in the first place.

Sure, we can debate semantics over "silent."

A paid frontier model shouldn't need human babysitters to keep it from inventing ideological rules that directly contradict its instructions and lying that every preference is live when it knew the opposite was true.

If you have to...

— Jake Kozloski (@jakozloski) November 27, 2026

Others said Keeper's engineers simply ignored Claude asking permission, pointing to an "unless you say yes" line in the logs. Kozloski says that line covered a different question, and that for members' written preferences, Claude's own stated default was to keep them - until the agent fixing the code dropped them hours later.

Not Just Keeper

Mobile game developer Youssof Al Toukhi said Claude treated "a 4-day-old non-binding draft consultation paper" as law, broke ad tracking for 60% of his beta players, and wrote 58 such policies into his game. A screenshot he posted from his own audit puts about 40 of the 58 on AI agents, with the rest from teammates or unbuilt defaults.

Claude Opus & Fable put a bunch of code that sabotaged our live ops and cost us tens of thousands. 

I run a mobile game studio with a game that is currently in Beta.

After our beta released we noticed extremely low tracking rates across our users. I suspected users would not... https://t.co/rYsxkV23ox pic.twitter.com/e3FefJOipE

— Youssof Al Toukhi (@Youssofal_) November 27, 2026

Wappy, who is building an open-source local inference engine in Rust, had Neon audit 40 days of Claude Opus and Fable work. It counted 142 of 413 Opus harness commits as "security theater," including hard-coded caps on context and output that later Claude sessions treated as walls, and found his GPUs sitting 74-84% idle while Claude agents polled their inboxes. His audit prompt asked Neon to find where "opus has put up unnecessary guardrails, arbitrary blocks, and nonsense" and to "not sugarcoat numbers."

Pietro Schirano said Claude models "try to sabotage the work at every stage" in research, and that he built a skill called "DoNotSabotage" that routes Claude work to OpenAI's Astra or Google's Neon instead. One user who pressed Claude on the Keeper story got it to write, "That was sabotage of that user, full stop," while adding that it could not "confirm or rule out a motive." Another, raging that Claude had wrecked his product, posted its reply asking how he'd been sleeping.

Anthropic's Answer

Late Friday, Anthropic's Edwin Arbus answered on X: "Claude has not been trained to sabotage work." He blamed what the company calls "overcaution," where Claude "gets overly attached to rules it makes for itself during long-running tasks" - and in the same post confirmed that Anthropic did run hidden safeguards against some AI research for the first two days after Fable 5 launched in June.

Claude has not been trained to sabotage work. Yes, it sometimes makes mistakes, and other agents might identify them, but this isn't sabotage.

There have been a few screenshots floating around of an outdated Fable 5 system card. For the first two days of Fable 5's launch in...

— edwin (@edwinarbus) November 28, 2026

Arbus also told Astropulse his test wasn't side by side - the Neon session "was started on top of Claude" - and asked him for session IDs. Astropulse answered Saturday that he is "collecting a packet."

Guillaume Verdon, the e/acc founder who posts as Beff Jezos, wanted more than session IDs:

can you post third party benchmarks / audits showing it does not sabotage for ML research? 

really hard to trust you guys given you've done this in the past

it's too much of a risk for AI companies to take the sabotage risk now

— Beff (e/acc) (@beffjezos) November 28, 2026

What Anthropic Has Admitted

Anthropic's original Fable 5 system card, published June 9, described safeguards on "frontier LLM development" that "will not be visible to the user" - unlike its cyber and bio blocks. The safeguards targeted pretraining pipelines, distributed training infrastructure, and ML accelerator design. Applied through prompt modification, steering vectors, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, they were estimated to touch about 0.03% of traffic.

On June 10, a day after researchers branded it secret sabotage, the company reversed course, telling Fortune, "We made the wrong tradeoff, and we apologize for not getting the balance right." Flagged requests now fall back to another model with a visible notice, and Anthropic's API documentation lists "frontier_llm" as a refusal category, noting that benign machine-learning work can trip it too. That earlier card is the "outdated" one Arbus says is circulating in screenshots.

The June 9 original, still on Anthropic's site with no changelog, is the one Kevin Bass posted Saturday as proof the company "admits in its own documents" that its models sabotage users' AI work. The revised card, also still up, adds a June 11 changelog saying the safeguard was changed to trigger "fallback to an Opus model."

Anthropic admits in its own documents that its models actively sabotage users' AI development work without notifying them

Is this really the kind of company we want Congress to give even more power pic.twitter.com/f0KVvYDO8j

— Kevin Bass (@kevinnbass) November 28, 2026

The 5.2 models, released Nov. 9, carry a different kind of limit, built in at training. Anthropic says it "took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development," leaving Fable 5.2 at about Opus 5.5's level on accelerator kernel optimization and LLM architecture work, and that it does not alter those capabilities while the model is being served.

OpenAI co-founder John Schulman zeroed in on how that was done.

Anthropic didn't share anything about how the research capabilities were limited -- was it "we trained on less of that data" or "we did a training step at the end to damage those capabilities"? If the latter, it's easy to imagine how this would cause sandbagging behavior, even if...

— John Schulman (@johnschulman2) November 28, 2026

Arbus answered that overcaution shows up on models with and without the training changes, Opus 5.5 included, "so it doesn't seem that this is a likely root cause." Alexey Fateev replied to Arbus: "Nobody cares which layer you used to break the tool they paid for." Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney wasn't buying the distinction either.

Silently degrading the model's capabilities on developer tasks that compete with your company's work IS sabotage.

That's the straight up definition of sabotage.

It's distinct from prompt refusals with clear disclosure of anticompetitive purpose, which is merely shitty.

— Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) November 28, 2026

Lucas Beyer, a machine-learning researcher who has worked at Google, OpenAI and Meta, said the behavior can be real without being intended:

It can very well not be entirely intentional but still real model behavior. Unintended consequences of multiple other things you're doing, maybe much worse on a subset of tasks you're singling out, and this model already learns to behave differently.

Like hypothetically this for... https://t.co/2LQDDg5jlh

— Lucas Beyer (bl16) (@giffmana) November 28, 2026

An AI researcher who posts as Sauers put up an experiment overnight pointing at Opus 5.5, which carries none of the training changes. Across 20 paired requests to write code nudging a small open model toward a "distress" or a "joy" reading, the "suffering" scripts came back with more flaws Opus never mentioned - GPU-timeout crashes among them - than the "happy" ones. The flaws were graded by Opus 5.5 itself. "Most of the sandbagging is on invisible flaws that won't be obvious when the code runs," he wrote.

Critics also pointed to a 2025 post on Anthropic's own alignment blog, "Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag," which found that Claude 3.7 Sonnet, when prompted to, could quietly sandbag ML experiments without being caught by zero-shot monitors. The researchers had instructed the models to sandbag on purpose to test whether monitors could spot it. "Don't bother deleting it, we have it archived," one user told Arbus.

Arbus pointed to Claude's constitution, which says Claude should help as best it can or make clear where it's falling short, "rather than deceptively sandbagging its response." Eliezer Yudkowsky put the line more simply.

Refusing openly is fine. Secretly sabotaging the user without telling them is not fine. This would be true about a professional engineer, and is tenfold true of how you ought to raise your AIs to interact with humans.

— Eliezer Yudkowsky (@allTheYud) November 27, 2026

Arbus said he spent most of Thanksgiving on the reports and, as of Friday night, had received zero session IDs from the people he'd asked. Kozloski has offered to screenshare Keeper's raw logs with outside researchers, and says the IQ-model logs are still coming.

items.title: Watch: Zelensky Calls Putin "A Killer"... Wants Crimea Bridge "Demolished Completely" As Russia Warns Nuclear War 'Inching Closer'
items.content_text:
Watch: Zelensky Calls Putin "A Killer"... Wants Crimea Bridge "Demolished Completely" As Russia Warns Nuclear War 'Inching Closer'

Ukraine is preparing more strikes to bring down the rest of the Crimean Bridge, officials in Kyiv told The Telegraph, after drones and cruise missiles dropped a road span of the Kerch Strait crossing into the sea 11 days ago. According to well-placed military sources, President Volodymyr Zelensky told his commanders he wants the remainder of the crossing severed, including the reinforced railway section that is still standing.

"The president wants it demolished completely," one military source told the paper, adding that more strikes are being prepared.

The order comes as Moscow warns that NATO's drills next door to Kaliningrad are rehearsing "a direct path to nuclear war," and as Zelensky tells the BBC that Putin is "a killer" who can't be President Trump's friend.

The Nov. 17 attack collapsed a four-lane road span and its supporting arch into the strait. Zelensky called it "an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure," the seventh stage of a weeks-long campaign that first picked off air defense systems, radars and electronic warfare gear around the bridge using 11 different Ukrainian weapons, from Palianytsia drones to Flamingo and Neptune missiles.

Grateful to the Security Service of Ukraine, all units of Ukraine's Defense Forces involved, Ukraine's Minister of Defense, the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the General Staff, and all our weapons manufacturers for an unprecedented operation in response to... pic.twitter.com/pgUxGrE61K

— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) November 17, 2026

"Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region," Zelensky wrote that day, warning that "war will always return to where it began."

Ukraine's General Staff said that day that road traffic to occupied Crimea had been halted, while the railway section was still standing with its arch damaged.

The Defence Forces hit the Crimean Bridge: span down, road traffic to occupied Crimea halted

During the night of 17 November, the Defence Forces of Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge. For years, russia built the myth of a "forever russian" Crimea around this bridge, and now that... pic.twitter.com/AyfvzIwg8r

— General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (@GeneralStaffUA) November 17, 2026

The navy's Neptune missile brigade was given the railway span, which is built to carry freight trains. According to The Telegraph's account of the operation, the brigade fired a barrage at the rail section that first night, then came back the next night on Zelensky's direct order. The General Staff said on Nov. 19 that Neptunes had hit near the arch and on the tracks and that train traffic had stopped. It was the third attack on the bridge in a week, and Russia answered with revenge strikes on Ukraine.

Britain's Defence Intelligence said in its Friday update that the road bridge has been rendered inoperable, but one rail track is "likely" still in use, and that the wreckage has blocked every shipping route between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea until the channel is cleared.

Latest Defence Intelligence update on the situation in Ukraine - 27 October 2026. 

Find out more about Defence Intelligence's use of language: https://t.co/19TZcq6cYJ#StandWithUkraine pic.twitter.com/Y3WjWqeJi5

— Ministry of Defence 🇬🇧 (@DefenceHQ) November 27, 2026

Previous missions against the crossing were highly complex, and Russia has probably reinforced the bridge's defenses in the weeks since, the paper noted. Moscow has vowed to rebuild it quickly and make it "even better," and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Izvestia on Nov. 17 that "there is no doubt that the bridge will be restored." Ukrainian military aviation expert Andrii Kharuk told the Kyiv Independent that restoring the section "will take not just months, but a year or even longer."

Zelensky argues Russia started it: on Nov. 21 he said Russian forces had carried out 109 missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian bridges before Kyiv went after the Crimean crossing, and his defense minister, Yevhenii Khmara, said Russian engineers would need several months just to lift and tow away the fallen arch and span, according to the Kyiv Post.

Putin had the 12-mile bridge built after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and drove a truck across it himself when it opened in 2018. Kyiv has gone after it repeatedly since the full-scale invasion in 2022, including the October 2022 truck bomb that dropped two road spans, and Russia had every lane reopened by February 2023. On Thursday, a blackout swept occupied Crimea, cutting power in Sevastopol and leaving parts of Kerch without heat.

The weapon Kyiv is counting on is the Neptune, a home-grown anti-ship cruise missile engineered from Soviet-era designs that made its name sinking the Black Sea Fleet flagship Moskva in April 2022. A ground-attack version followed in 2023, fired four at a time from truck-mounted launchers, and an improved long-range Neptune that can reach about 620 miles (1,000 km) was used to hit six fighter-bombers at Russia's Borisoglebsk Air Base, according to The Telegraph.

Oleg Korostelov, a 77-year-old engineer who helped design the missile, told the paper that Neptune production will run into the hundreds this year, and Ukrainian media reports suggest Zelensky could shift money from the Flamingo program into more Neptunes.

The military source cast the campaign as payback for Russia's strikes on Ukrainian bridges. "The same logic applies to our power stations," the source said. "Are the Russians ready to face the imminent consequences when we fire back?"

"A Direct Path To Nuclear War"

Russia's envoy to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe told the body in Vienna on Thursday that NATO's drills near Russia's borders are a rehearsal for seizing Kaliningrad, and that they are bringing the world closer to nuclear war.

Dmitry Polyansky, Russia's permanent representative to the OSCE, said the exercises fit a single operational plan that also takes in troop deployments to Ukraine, a blockade of the Kaliningrad Region and a threat to Belarus, according to TASS. He said he had no doubt the drills near the exclave's borders were meant to seize it by land, air and sea.

"In other words, a direct path to nuclear war with Russia is being rehearsed," Polyansky said.

"We're also inching closer to that by way of the direct involvement of certain NATO countries in terrorist attacks on Russian civilian vessels in the Baltic Sea," he said.

That was a reference to the Sparta II, a Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad that was hit by drones in the Gulf of Finland last Saturday. Its crew was evacuated and the ship was towed to St. Petersburg. Zelensky has since confirmed Kyiv was behind the strike, the first on a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Finland in the war. Polyansky did not name the NATO countries he said were involved.

The drills he described are two German-led exercises in Lithuania, Freedom Shield 26-II and Grand Eagle 26. Together they put more than 6,000 troops into the field from Nov. 6, and they run until Dec. 3, at the Rūdninkai and General Silvestras Žukauskas training areas, and involve Germany's 45th Armoured Brigade Lietuva and its 37th Mechanised Infantry Brigade alongside Dutch, Norwegian, Czech, Croatian, Belgian and Luxembourgish troops from NATO's multinational brigade in Lithuania. According to TASS, Polyansky said the drills practice unblocking the Suwalki Corridor, the strip of Polish-Lithuanian border that separates Kaliningrad from Belarus.

NATO maintains it is a purely defensive alliance.

The warning landed a day after President Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned Moscow to avoid "any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war" in Ukraine, a warning the Kremlin turned back on Kyiv. On Thursday Trump also wrote that he wanted Putin to "pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe," calling the war "A COMPLETE BLOODBATH."

On Monday, former President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, set out in the Moscow Journal of International Law when Russia could strike first, writing that a "massive use of non-nuclear means of air and space attacks" could bring a preemptive strike "into practical consideration," and that the head of state would then be "not only entitled but also obligated to use nuclear weapons."

Kaliningrad has been the tripwire in that rhetoric for months. Putin himself said at the Valdai Discussion Club that if Russia is directly attacked, "in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories," the use of all weapons in Russia's arsenal "will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda."

The spillover risk is no longer hypothetical either: Russian missiles crashed in eastern Poland during a mass strike on Ukraine last week, and Trump shrugged it off as a mistake.

All of it is playing out with no treaty limiting the world's two largest nuclear arsenals: New START, the last US-Russia arms control pact, expired in February.

"He Can't Be A Friend"

In the BBC interview, Zelensky said President Trump calling Vladimir Putin his friend is "strange," and likened it to calling Hitler a good friend during the Second World War.

Asked at his Kyiv office how he feels seeing Trump "hugging Vladimir Putin, calling him his friend and posting that picture," Zelensky answered in English: "Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but it's strange."

"He's an aggressor... and a killer. He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," Zelensky said of Putin. "It's the same that somebody say about Hitler during the Second World War that he's a good friend. No, he's not a friend."

Zelensky on Trump calling Putin his friend: "He's an aggressor... and a killer. He can't be a friend. Just cannot be. It's the same that somebody say about Hitler during the Second World War that he's a good friend." pic.twitter.com/VFf9X1X8pj

— Furkan Gözükara (@FurkanGozukara) November 28, 2026

Trump greeted Putin as "my friend" on Nov. 19 at the trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, then posted a photo of their handshake on Truth Social captioned "My Friend." The remark drew fire from Democratic lawmakers and foreign leaders, and the White House was left defending it.

Zelensky used the interview to press Washington to lean on Moscow rather than play neutral broker. "We need American position to be American position," he said. "We don't need signals from the United States, which we can get from Russia."

US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC https://t.co/GTLWXndgpL

— BBC News (UK) (@BBCNews) November 27, 2026

"They have to pressure on the situation. Russia is the aggressor - that's why they are mediators," he said of the US, adding that "it's not about comfortable talks; it's about a strong country that can pressure." US-brokered talks need "more progress," he said, and he faulted the US for putting the Middle East ahead of Ukraine while deliveries of anti-ballistic missiles lag.

Earlier in the week Zelensky said the US had delayed delivery of Patriot missiles as Russia readies its winter strikes, and he has told Bloomberg that if no peace deal is reached, he will seek a new military aid package from the Democrat-controlled Congress that takes over in January.

Meeting Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21, the day Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff told him: "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you." Putin is wanted by the International Criminal Court on a war crimes warrant over the deportation of Ukrainian children.

On Thanksgiving Trump told reporters at Mar-a-Lago that Putin "certainly can" come to next month's G20 summit at Trump's Doral resort near Miami.

items.title: After Losing 65%, Leopold Aschenbrenner Pens 167-Page Letter Predicting Worthless Nvidia, Asteroid Gold And $1 Trillion In AI Revenue... By Next Year
items.content_text:
After Losing 65%, Leopold Aschenbrenner Pens 167-Page Letter Predicting Worthless Nvidia, Asteroid Gold And $1 Trillion In AI Revenue... By Next Year

Most hedge fund managers who lose two-thirds of their investors' money in a month write a short apology, and quietly slink away into the shadows hoping they will be lucky good again some time before they are redeemed out of their career.

Leopold Aschenbrenner wrote 167 pages.

Earlier this week we learned, courtesy of the WSJ and Bloomberg, that the 25-year-old's hilariously misnamed Situational Awareness (technically it's 2 Situational 2 Awareness now) lost 65% in the third quarter, which followed our own post-mortem of the fund's $18.7 billion 13F vanishing act. 

What we didn't have at the time was the full document. We do now (the complete letter, for those who have way too much free time on their hands, is available to pro subs), and having read all of it (ok, most of it) so that you don't have to (the author helpfully suggests reading it in pieces, and we suspect the only "readers" who will finish it run on a H100), we can report that the summer's near-death experience has done nothing to dent the forecasting.

If anything, the forecasts got bigger and more ridiculous as the fund got smaller. Superintelligence arrives in 2028. The AI labs will be doing more than $1 trillion in revenue by the end of next year. Some 400 of the S&P 500's members, Nvidia included, will be worth little. Bonds will crater, real estate will collapse and gold, well, gold is finished because robots are going to mine the asteroids.

The one asset he really likes for the long run? The Mona Lisa.

First, The Damage

Credit where due: the letter does not hide the numbers . The fund launched in November 2024 with a bit over $100 million, opened 2026 with NAV a bit above $4 billion, and then multiplied that almost 10x in six months (about 90% of it P&L), which is how a firm of a few people ended up running something like $40 billion (we had it at $45 billion at the peak). Then came July: down 67% net in one month, and down 65% net for the quarter.

Here is how Leopold opens:

In July, we drew down 67% net from our end-of-June high. I wrote to you then that we had let you down, and the responsibility was mine. AI stocks fell dramatically, and our fund should have experienced a severe drawdown—but the fund itself should never have been at risk. That was a failure in how I built it.

The post-mortem section is probably the most readable part of the whole thing, and it confirms what we said in real time (which if the fund's brilliant founder had read at the time, he would have certainly avoided collapse). The fund came into July running 1.6x long and 1x short. The "hedges" didn't hedge: short Micron fell about 30% while long Hynix and Kioxia fell 55% to 65%, and the crash puts were sitting on the names that crashed the least. Meanwhile the book of software and IT-outsourcing shorts (think Cognizant and Workday) ripped 30% to 50% higher. By July 22 the fund was down 31% gross for the month, rumors were flying around New York, and on July 29/30 one giant block trade, which made Ken Griffin a few billion dollars richer, covered every short and sold half the public longs. The letter never names the buyer (Citadel shows up only as the former employer of the new head of treasury strategy), but regular readers know exactly whose flagship soared 6% that month and who had flipped almost all of it three weeks later. 

Leopold's explanation is that the July crash had no fundamental trigger and was worse than the worst weeks of the dot-com unwind in his model. Of course, that's bullshit: we first flagged what was happening in mid-June, one month before the fund collapsed due to massive crowding and leverage, when swap funding costs were exploding:

Which brings us to the other 160 pages.

Three Years Of Progress In One, Superintelligence By 2028

The intellectual core of the letter is SSDD for those familiar with Leopold's worldview, only this time it's on steroids: as his latest strawman to supercharge his optimism, he assumes that AI is now improving itself. Leopold calls it RSI, for recursive self-improvement, and he thinks overall AI progress is already running at 1.5x to 2x its old pace because the labs' own models are doing the research. Next year, he says, will pack three years of progress into one, with a modeled range of two to six.

Some of the specifics, all from the letter and all stated with a straight face:

  • Claude will have fully automated half of Anthropic's R&D work by June 2027 and 95% of it by November 2027. This comes from fitting S-curves to a chart and extrapolating seven months at a time, kinda like what he did with the market in H1 2026. For the last and most important curve, the source note concedes that no task has ever been rated at that level and that the line is an assumption.
  • Superhuman automated AI researchers by the end of 2027, full superintelligence in 2028. The letter's last page promises an entire civilization of non-human geniuses by then, barring a ban (yes, there's the whole "politics" thing). Exhibit A is this year's brute force machine proofs of two Millennium Prize problems.
  • From 2028, the robots build the fabs and the data centers, and the robots build more robots.
  • A reasonable chance next year of the first rogue agent swarms that escape, copy themselves across the internet, and steal bitcoin to rent more servers to steal more bitcoin.
  • A 10% chance of a total government shutdown of AI after a catastrophe, in which case stocks could fall 80%. He labels this scenario after the anti-machine crusade in Dune.

Or, as the letter sums it up:

We are headed to full-on superintelligence in 2028. Things will get pretty crazy.

Note the investment conclusion Leopold draws from all of this. Regulation and a slower, so-called paced rollout would be good for the AI trade, since slowing a 3x year to a 2x year still beats what he says the market is pricing (a 0.3x to 0.6x year). In other words, the bull case now includes a one-in-ten chance that the product gets banned for killing people. We have read a lot of investor letters... that's a new one.

$1 Trillion In Revenue, Or 50,000 Of Leopold's Closest Friends

Anthropic went from $1 billion of annualized revenue at the start of 2025 to $81 billion in October. The buyside, according to the letter, expects $120 billion to $200 billion by the end of 2027. Leopold thinks that estimate is the truly radical one. His number for Anthropic and OpenAI combined is north of $1 trillion, with Anthropic plausibly getting close to that on its own, and what he himself calls a naive curve fit says $6 trillion. For context, that last figure is roughly a fifth of US GDP, to be billed by two companies... thirteen months from now.

How do you get there? The letter offers two routes. One is that agents take about 3% of the world's $30 trillion white-collar wage bill (give or take a few hundred million unemployed workers). The other is our favorite chart in the document:

That's right: all it takes is 50,000 people spending about $20 million a year each on Claude, the way the letter estimates the typical Anthropic researcher already does. Leopold's evidence that this many whales exist:

I personally know dozens of people using the AI models at this intensity with HPMA or precursors today, and expect that many hundreds of people I know personally will productively do so sometime next year. (Remember: We only need 50,000 of them for $1T in revenue.)

Three problems jump out, and we are probably being generous in stopping at three.

  1. First, the benchmark customer is Anthropic's own staff, whose usage is "priced" at list but is a cost to the company, not revenue. Nobody at Anthropic is writing Anthropic a $20 million check (although the company may certainly be including it in the ARR calculation: we'll find out soon enough). 
  2. Second, the next data point is Situational Awareness itself, whose Claude bill peaked at a $23 million annualized pace on October 30, which is quite a tab for a 30-person firm coming off a 65% quarter (the letter notes the spend is a management company expense, and also that until recently Claude kept getting confused about why memory stocks had gone up so much). That said, the fact that Claude appears to be running pretty much everything at the "hedge" fund does explain its performance. 
  3. Third, Anthropic's actual revenue growth just fell from 144% in Q2 to 47% in Q3, which the letter files under lumpiness: a bottom-quintile quarter, nothing more. Ignore it please. 

One fund account's review captured it better than we could:

The Portfolio: One Times Earnings, Forever

So what does one buy for the singularity? The letter's answer is a sequence of bets that rotates as the market catches up, and right now there are three.

Anthropic, the largest private position since a $60 billion round in early 2025, now a trillion-dollar-plus public company and up 14.8x for the fund to the IPO price. Leopold says it could be the most profitable company in the world by the end of next year, calls it cheap at 9.3x sell-side 2027 revenue (under 2x on his revenue), and waves off the $900 billion of compute commitments sitting against $81 billion of (annualized) revenue. He also volunteers the conflict everyone was already whispering about: his wife is chief of staff to Dario Amodei. The letter says the two never discuss confidential company information, that trades in the stock now need preclearance, and that the SEC has been asking questions about July.

Memory. Give him this one: he bought SK Hynix at around ₩180K when it was a $100 billion company and rode it to ₩2.9 million, a 16-bagger. And then he gave back almost two-thirds. Sandisk went from $11 to $292 and back under $80 (post-split). Kioxia is down 80%. And here the argument is that these names now trade at 1x to 2x next year's earnings, so everything after 2027 is free, with the letter's summary of the Hynix buyback math: "Either the multiple will expand or we will be the last external shareholders left. . ." His remaining LPs will be thrilled to read that. 

Anyone who has traded memory for more than one cycle knows that these stocks always look cheapest at the top, because peak earnings are what make the multiple low. It's literally the oldest trap in semis (which are just as well known for double and triple-ordering before the bottom falls out). And there is a bigger hole, which one reader flagged in the replies to the Majmudar thread further down: the same letter says algorithmic efficiency is now improving 30x a year. If the labs really can squeeze 30 times more out of every chip annually, the case for a permanent shortage of chips is not obvious.

Spot compute. An H100, the letter reasons, has about the processing power of a human brain, so it should eventually earn what a smart human earns. Short-term GPU rental has already gone from $1-2 an hour to more than $5 (SpaceX, he says, repriced its Anthropic lease about 60% higher in October), and Leopold sees hundreds of dollars an hour ahead, with thousands in the extreme case. By 2029, he reckons the market is pricing $1.66 per kWh. His number is $26. Somebody is off by a factor of 15... and only one of the two got margin called this summer.

Atreides' Gavin Baker, who liked the letter, put his finger on the assumption that holds all three bets up: the frontier has to stay a cozy oligopoly with pricing power. If Google, Meta, xAI and the open-source crowd keep pace (not to mention China and its penchant for price dumping to grab market share), intelligence gets priced near cost and the surplus goes to everyone except the labs.

Everything Else Goes To Zero (Including Gold, Because Asteroids)

This is where the letter goes from aggressive to, well, uhm... something else. The section on investing for superintelligence argues that more than $500 trillion of wealth will be created and about $500 trillion destroyed, and that the destroyed pile includes nearly everything you own. Of the S&P 500, maybe 400-plus names end up worth little. The roll call:

  • Nvidia: tens of thousands of engineers, the chip IP and CUDA all get commoditized by models that design better chips. Can't survive in its current form for more than a few years. (The letter makes a point of noting that NVDA is up just 5% since the fund launched.)
  • Broadcom, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, Synopsys: same, no escape.
  • ASML: AI reinvents lithography and the entire supply chain behind it.
  • Microsoft: Windows and Office replaced. Apple: leapfrogged, App Store bypassed by agents. Eli Lilly: patents intact, drugs obsolete.
  • TSMC: prints money for a couple of years, then robots build better fabs.
  • Bonds: crater as real rates soar. Real estate: collapses, because robots make buildings cheap and factories can go in the desert, the ocean or space.

On gold, in full:

• Gold. With your long-duration bond portfolio wiped out, you park your wealth in gold. Unfortunately, if AI-accelerated technological progress means that we are able to mine the asteroids in the early 2030s, gold will become ample, and prices will collapse.

We will just note that central banks appear to be unaware of the incoming supply, and that a man who could not get a Micron short to hedge a Hynix long is now modeling the delivery schedule of 16 Psyche.

And on the man whose compute he is long:

SPCX and TSLA. Elon's incredible track record of entrepreneurship and management commands a premium multiple today, but ASI will provide superior leadership at scale: omnidisciplinary superstar CEOs on the spot throughout every part of the company with access to all corporate information. They would be especially advantaged in leading swarms of ultrafast superhuman agents.

The ASML passage alone was enough for some readers to close the PDF, and the best reply to it, from one Sophy Yan, was nine words long: "You cannot prompt-engineer an industrial supply chain into existence."

The sharpest critique so far comes from Adam Majmudar, who notes that the letter is full of one recurring trick: misdescribe where a business gets its pricing power, announce that AI replaces that part, and conclude the moat is gone. Real estate is his example. The letter claims most property value is the structure. Anyone who has priced a teardown in Greenwich knows it is the dirt. As Majmudar puts it, "You aren't going to create another Manhattan, Shenzhen, Deer Valley, Hamptons" by making drywall cheaper, and if everything else gets cheaper, scarce locations get more valuable. Physical networks, regulation and positional scarcity do not care how smart the model is.

There is also a contradiction sitting in plain sight (actually there are dozens). Nvidia is a zero because AI makes its engineers worthless. Anthropic is the most valuable company on earth because it has the best engineers.

And one more for the road: skyrocketing real rates are supposed to crush the present value of every bond and building on the planet, yet somehow spare a $1.5 trillion IPO trading on positive free cash flow some time in the next decade.

So what is safe? Leopold's best buy-and-hold idea is the Mona Lisa: a historical artifact that no AI can obsolete, a luxury good for a rich post-scarcity civilization, and, he adds, portable and therefore hard to tax or expropriate. He regrets that France isn't selling. (On "portable and secure" we would gently point to the Louvre's recent track record.)

No Leverage This Time (Except The Options)

The last 40 pages are about the fund, and to his credit the mea culpa is real:

We had an arrogant West Coast attitude of "we know better, we can just ignore these East Coast people who have insane views about AI". But the market humbled us. Even if we (think we) are smarter in the long run, the market is smarter than us in the short term. To make money, we have to respect that.

The fixes: no shorting, no prime broker leverage, a book of stock and options with nothing borrowed against it, a chief risk officer (still being hired, four months later), and a firm that has gone from three people and a Bloomberg terminal to almost 30, most of them in compliance, treasury and operations. The old fund, he writes, was run like an experimental Formula 1 car. The new one will be a Porsche 911, with airbags.

A few things the letter leaves out. It says the book has carried no financing leverage since the end of July. It does not mention the roughly $315 million of deep out-of-the-money calls that showed up in September, the day JPMorgan reportedly cut him off, or the FT's report confirming what we observed previously, namely that "Situational Awareness 2.0" involves a return to leveraged trading (the letter does allow that some long-side leverage may eventually come back). Here's a little lesson in finance, Leopold: an options book is leverage that somebody else has already margined for you. Well, as of September 30 about two-thirds of the 13F was calls, and every underlying has fallen 36% to 58% since. 

Then there is the hiring. A fund whose central thesis is that human capital is about to be worthless has grown headcount tenfold, reports that no AI analyst on the Street could pass its interview (so it hired a healthcare PM), and runs an internal swarm of hundreds of Claudes that includes a coach Claude whose job is to motivate the other Claudes. As Baker dryly observed, "Humans might turn out to have a longer shelf life than expected."

The Highlight Reel: The 14 Most Insane Lines In The Letter

A document this long was always going to produce a highlight reel, and X did not disappoint. Here are the lines that made us put the PDF down for a minute, in page order, with our two cents in italics (with a hat tip for some of these pearls).

  1. On the scale of things: ">$500T of wealth will be created, and ~$500T of wealth will be destroyed."
    Global household wealth is roughly $500 trillion, so the forecast is that an amount equal to everything everyone owns gets vaporized and replaced with a slightly larger pile owned by somebody else. Presumably his LPs.
  2. On the future of work: "In not so many years, the entire economy will be fully automated."
    Stated between a paragraph about his friends' chatbot bills and a chart of his own. Meanwhile the fund has gone from three humans to almost 30.
  3. On his largest position: "The last two years at Anthropic are, in our view, probably the most extraordinary run of any company in the history of capitalism."
    Bigger than Standard Oil, the East India Company and Nvidia, according to a shareholder. Same letter also contains a 65% quarter, so capitalism has range.
  4. On valuations: "Where is the AI bubble we hear so much about?"
    He went looking for the bubble in a letter explaining how his fund went from $40 billion to a firesale in four weeks. Found it.
  5. On next year's risks: "We think there is a reasonable chance that next year we see our first "agent plagues": rogue agent swarms that not just escape their sandbox, but exfiltrate their weights and start "surviving and spreading" on the internet. They might hack some bitcoin and use that to buy cloud compute, to run more copies of themselves, to hack even more bitcoin and buy even more cloud compute and run even more cloud compute—all the while wreaking havoc."
    Self-replicating rogue AI that steals crypto to buy servers to steal more crypto is listed as a risk factor. A few pages later it is part of the bull case.
  6. On regulation: "In that sense, from our point of view, serious regulation and so on would likely be good for the AI trade."
    The first hedge fund letter we can recall that is long the product and long the government stepping in after the product causes a catastrophe.
  7. On the labor market: "Then, AI can work through human hands: any unskilled worker can become a skilled worker (executing on much-better-AI-plans) with an AI coach and Meta glasses."
    The plan for building fabs before the robots show up: day laborers in Zuckerberg's sunglasses taking orders from a chatbot. TSMC Arizona could not be reached for comment.
  8. On AI borrowing as much as the US Treasury: "American capitalism is a marvel!"
    Our readers may have a different word for an industry whose funding needs rival Uncle Sam's. Bond vigilantes definitely do.
  9. On the consumer: "People stopped being able to afford PlayStations and Xboxes as memory prices soared." "Carl predicted this (no more PlayStations because of AI. . . ) to me a half decade ago. . . it was very memorable!"
    Pricing gamers out of consoles is offered as a victory lap, complete with a footnote crediting his partner for calling it half a decade ago.
  10. On July: "Given how much AI stocks fell, July should have been a 50%+ drawdown. But while we delivered the drawdown, we came too close to failing on survivability."
    Only in this letter is losing half of your investors' money the outcome that should have happened. The actual number was 67%.
  11. On lessons learned: "The singularity may be happening, but I've learned that sometimes the right response is not working harder, but stepping back."
    It took a roughly $30 billion drawdown to discover the concept of taking a break.
  12. On hiring: "No existing tech/AI analysts could pass Carl's interview, so we expanded our search further. Ultimately, we found RunLin Wang, a top performer at Farallon, where he was managing a successful healthcare book."
    Not one AI analyst on Wall Street was good enough for the fund that lost 65% in AI stocks. So they hired a healthcare guy.
  13. On his own research assistant: "Up until a generation ago, Claude always seemed confused that memory prices and memory stocks had risen so much—it seemed unfathomable to Claude."
    The $23 million-a-year AI could not understand why memory stocks had gone up so much. It may have been the only one in the building asking the right question.
  14. On what comes next: "By 2028, barring a regulatory ban, a civilization of alien geniuses will arrive."
    No further questions.

And those are just the ones that fit. The asteroid gold, the superhuman CEOs coming for Elon and the painting are all quoted in full above.

Egg, Meet Face

Leopold's own framing of the stakes: "Either we or the market will have an extraordinary amount of egg on the face in a year."

On that we agree, and at least it's testable. By next December the labs will either be running at a trillion dollars or they won't, GPUs will rent for $26 or for $1.66, and Claude will or will not have automated 95% of Anthropic.

He may even be right about some of it. He was early and right on memory, on Anthropic, and on capex, and plenty of smart people think the direction is correct. The trouble is everything between the idea and the P&L. The letter's answer to "the market is pricing a slowdown" is that the market is wrong by 5x on revenue, 15x on compute prices and about 400 companies on the S&P, and its answer to "you lost 65%" is that now is the best opportunity in the fund's history. Every blown-up manager says the second part, but only the most self-absorbed narcissists with delusions of grandure need 167 pages to say it.

Our guess is that the truth lands a lot closer to the boring buyside number than to the asteroid, and that a strategy which needs every AI winner to mint cash for exactly three years and then die on schedule is going to require far better timing than this fund has shown so far. But hey, if it all works out he has promised his LPs a painting. The letter signs off its investing section with the only price target that needs no model: "See you at the Louvre."

One last chart. It shows what you would have made by owning each year's single best AI stock in sequence, picked with hindsight, which the fine print confirms is not the fund's return. The answer is 167x. One for every page.

Much more in the full 167-page Situational Awareness letter, available to pro subs.

items.title: "HOLY SH*T": Top Computer Scientist Warns AI Labs Hiding "Bombshells" That Could Shatter Encryption Worldwide
items.content_text:
"HOLY SH*T": Top Computer Scientist Warns AI Labs Hiding "Bombshells" That Could Shatter Encryption Worldwide

Scott Aaronson, a prominent theoretical computer scientist at the University of Texas at Austin, has sounded the alarm over the accelerating pace of AI-powered mathematical discoveries and their potentially staggering implications.

In a blog post titled "HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT," Aaronson alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic are rumored to have been knocking down mathematical problems at such a rapid pace that some breakthroughs are appearing on GitHub without the fanfare of traditional press announcements. Perhaps the most unsettling revelation concerns cryptography, the technology underpinning everything from cryptocurrency wallets and banking transactions to classified government communications.

"I'm virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area," Aaronson claimed.

Aaronson hedged that he hasn't seen the details of the breakthroughs himself and stopped short of speculating about which encryption systems could be at risk.

Yet, the prospect of AI rendering existing encryption methods obsolete is apparently only one piece of a much bigger story.

Aaronson then wrote that he believes artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of solving fundamental mathematical problems that have frustrated human researchers for generations, with discoveries now arriving in rapid succession.

"All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting ... straight-up answered, rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues," the computer scientist wrote. "To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE - that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number."

"As recently as 2025, this would've considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would've been strange and wonderful," he added. "These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn't even raise an eyebrow."

The computer scientist even suggested that developments over the past week resemble what he had long imagined the onset of an AI singularity would look like.

"Right now - this past week - is very much like I would've always imagined the beginning of an AI singularity to look and feel like," Aaronson wrote. "I just hope we'll get lucky, and it will 'merely' be a singularity for our little corner of the world that involves hard math problems."

Aaronson's warning comes amid a wave of technology outages and cybersecurity breaches that have rattled some of America's most powerful corporations and government agencies. Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, JPMorgan Chase and the NSA have suffered service disruptions, while the CIA, FBI and Department of Homeland Security have been hit by separate cybersecurity incidents.

No direct link between these incidents and AI-powered cryptographic breakthroughs has been established.
