items.title: Milei Just Unplugged Argentina's Money Printer, And Not One Lawmaker Voted No
items.content_text:
Milei Just Unplugged Argentina's Money Printer, And Not One Lawmaker Voted No

Authored by Owen Evans via The Epoch Times,

Argentina's Congress approved legislation on Thursday barring the central bank from printing money to finance government spending, advancing a central pillar of President Javier Milei's economic reform program.

Under the new charter, the central bank's primary objective will be to preserve the value of the Argentine peso, while its ability to finance the Treasury through temporary advances or direct purchases of government debt will be prohibited.

Milei was elected in 2023 on a promise to reduce government size and tame astronomical inflation, backed by a chainsaw-wielding image.

During his election campaign, Milei pledged to shut down Argentina's central bank and replace the Argentine peso with the U.S. dollar as part of a plan to eliminate inflation.

The legislation establishes that the primary mission of the central bank is to preserve the value of the currency, said Milei's office in a statement on Thursday, adding that it removes the economy minister's right to participate in meetings of its board of directors.

The legislation reverses provisions introduced in 2012 under then-President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner that expanded the central bank's ability to finance government spending.

The law puts an end to "91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity, and institutional decay," Milei's office said in a statement on Thursday.

Tenemos nueva Carta Orgánica para el @BancoCentral_AR . Se terminó con más de 90 años de estafa via emisión de dinero para financiar déficit fiscal...
VLLC! pic.twitter.com/PGom0ew3pQ

— Javier Milei (@JMilei) November 26, 2026

The number of businesses with at least one registered employee in Argentina fell by 32,429, or 6.3 percent, between November 2023 and August 2026, according to a Nov. 16 report by Argentine think tank Fundar.

In a Nov. 25 BNP Paribas report, economist François Faure said that the Argentine economy "most likely slipped into a technical recession (two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP) in the spring of 2026."

Argentina's unemployment rate rose from 6 percent at the end of 2023 to 8 percent by mid-2026, while household consumption fell by 1.8 percent in the second quarter of this year, according to the report.

Faure said the debt-to-GDP ratio has fallen by 17 percentage points since the end of 2024. He said that this was "thanks to a return to a balanced budget, as well as i) inflationary erosion (which reduces the debt-to-GDP ratio in pesos) and ii) the real appreciation of the peso against the dollar (which reduces the debt-to-GDP ratio in foreign currency)."

Milei, a Trump ally, is a fierce opponent of communism, socialism, and collectivism.

"The road to socialism is always and everywhere the road to totalitarianism, because the socialist has to use every tool available to deny a reality that proves his ideas are false, harmful, and destructive to any nation," Milei said at then-Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro's election campaign launch in Brazil on July 25.

Argentina's Senate passed a bill on Thursday to suspend the country's primary elections. Milei's La Libertad Avanza party is polling roughly level with the opposition Peronists ahead of Argentina's October 2027 presidential election, according to a November poll by Argentine consultancy Analogías.

If approved, the electoral reform bill would suspend next year's primaries, reduce public financing for political parties and eliminate the mandatory presidential debate before general elections. "We want a system that is more efficient. We want a system that is simpler and more transparent," said Sen. Bruno Olivera of ruling party La Libertad Avanza.

Albania's "Flamingo Revolution" Erupts Into Chaos As Globetrotting Greta Thunberg Finds New Cause

Protesters clashed with police in Albania's capital earlier today during a student-led demonstration demanding the resignation of the country's center-left prime minister, Edi Rama.

items.title: Lacalle: A December Hike Would Be "Stubbornness Disguised As Credibility"
items.content_text:
Lacalle: A December Hike Would Be "Stubbornness Disguised As Credibility"

Authored by Daniel Lacalle,

The Federal Reserve raised rates during an external oil shock. Now commodities, gasoline, and inflation expectations are falling rapidly, and the forward curve remains in deep backwardation, signaling disinflation. However, the cost of tight money will linger long after the spike is gone.

The FOMC minutes of the October meeting show that almost all participants judged that further hikes would likely be appropriate. In fact, two members dissented in favor of an immediate increase, and Governor Christopher Waller mentioned a half-point move in December to "shock people." He defended a rate cut in January despite elevated core PCE and rising inflation expectations, while also discussing a large rate hike as those figures rapidly reversed. However, the market has already moved on.

Commodities are falling fast, inflation expectations are plummeting, and the first alternative-data estimates for November point to a negative monthly CPI print. Once again, central banks are fighting yesterday's war with a tool that does nothing to change its cause.

The cause was never excess demand or an overheated economy. Money velocity remains contained at 1.47, money supply growth comes mostly from government spending, and there are no signs of excess credit-taking or unsustainable demand growth. Rather, the opposite. The 2026 CPI surge came from the war with Iran and the disruption of flows through the Strait of Hormuz, a supply shock imported from the Persian Gulf, with no relation to an overheated American consumer or a spend-price spiral.

In the past month, the shock has been reversing, and fast. Brent has lost about a fifth of its value in November as Middle East supplies recovered to prewar levels. Over the past month, gasoline futures have dropped almost 20 percent and heating oil nearly 21 percent. Copper is down 16 percent, silver 28 percent, wheat 11 percent, and sugar 17 percent, while the CRB index has dropped more than 10 percent and the S&P GSCI almost 13 percent. Furthermore, the average retail price of gasoline has fallen to roughly $3.65 a gallon, down about 15 percent in a month and close to the $3.50 threshold that consumers consider more concerning.

The impact on prices is immediate. The Bloomberg Price Index points to a 0.1 percent monthly decline in November. Energy subtracts more than a quarter of a percentage point, while core goods are basically flat. If confirmed, it would be the first negative monthly print since June. Headline annual inflation still looks high, at 4.2 percent. However, that number is the rearview mirror of the oil spike, and it will fall rapidly as base effects and lower energy prices feed through.

Market participants understand this. One-year USD inflation swaps have collapsed from above 3.5 percent in the spring to below 2 percent, and two-year swaps are near 2.1 percent. More importantly, long-term expectations never de-anchored. The 30-year inflation swap barely moved through the entire Iran geopolitical risk episode, staying within a band of 2.3 percent to 2.5 percent. The single most important variable for the Fed, inflation expectations, showed that investors viewed the shock as temporary. Core PCE expectations also proved more stable than hawkish Fed members suggested.

Core PCE inflation remained at 3.0 percent year on year in June, July, and August and barely rose to 3.1 percent in September, far from the ludicrous concept of a "second-round" inflation burst that hawkish Fed members warned about. Forecasts were clear as well. The Philadelphia Fed's survey left its core PCE projections unchanged at 3.3 percent for 2026 and 2.4 percent for 2027, while cutting its 10-year PCE inflation expectation to 2.20 percent. The Fed's own September projections kept core PCE for 2027 at 2.5 percent, exactly as in the June estimate, with 2026 revised up by just one-tenth of a point. However, the same committee increased its expected federal funds rate for 2027 from 3.6 percent to 4.1 percent. Half a point of additional tightening for an unchanged medium-term inflation outlook shows a policy driven by fear of headlines.

It is incredible to see that central bank rhetoric is the most hawkish in years. J.P. Morgan's NLP Hawk-Dove score for the Fed has climbed above 30, close to the levels of 2022. Monetary authorities are synchronizing their tightening measures at the same time that the commodity impulse is fading.

Hawks will argue that core CPI rose 0.3 percent for three consecutive months and that energy has passed through to core goods and services. However, that pass-through was almost nonexistent, and the individual transport and goods prices that did rise because diesel soared are falling now. Fed officials seem to ignore that prices are determined by demand, not costs.

Monetary policy works with lags of 12 to 18 months. Hiking today to fight a nonexistent second-round effect means the full burden of tighter policy appears when the shock has disappeared, accelerating a Fed-engineered private-sector contraction instead of preventing inflation.

Inflation is always a monetary phenomenon. When the price of oil soars without an excess of money creation, families and businesses spend more on energy and less on everything else. That is a change in relative prices, and it reverses when the supply disruption ends. Raising rates to combat it is like treating a broken leg with chemotherapy. The patient suffers the terrible side effects, and the leg heals on its own anyway.

Rate hikes have made credit more expensive for families and small businesses at the worst time and done nothing to reduce government spending. In fact, rate hikes have inflated the interest expense of a heavily indebted federal government. Even Citigroup warns that U.S. interest rates are "unsustainably high," with falling equity valuations and risks to AI investment threatening growth, and that easing energy prices and tighter financial conditions could eventually push the Fed into an urgent 180-degree move to a dovish stance as the economy weakens and financial risks rise. Citi still expects an interest rate hike in December, followed by a hold, and then cuts later in 2027. That is the classic central bank pattern of hiking into the peak and cutting into the slump.

The Federal Reserve claims to be data dependent. It does not show it. The data are clear. Oil is down a fifth in a month, gasoline is heading below $3.50, commodity indices are in free fall, alternative-data nowcasts point to negative monthly inflation, and market-based expectations are back below the 2 percent target in the short term and stable in the long term.

Hiking in December would be stubbornness disguised as credibility.

The Fed engineered a market sell-off and decided to hurt families and businesses with a misguided rate hike when there was no sign of an overheated economy, just an external energy shock. Now that the damage has been done, it is stubbornly talking about rate hikes.

There is nothing in the job market or core inflation pointing to the need for rate hikes.

Commodity disinflation lowers the Taylor-rule interest-rate estimate, while money supply and velocity do not justify further tightening. The trend in commodities and CPI estimates, which are negative for November, shows that, under the lower-neutral-rate limit, the implied federal funds rate should be below current levels, even supporting a rate cut.

Central banks failed to see the 2021 inflation coming because they ignored the monetary excess they created. In 2026, they are making the opposite mistake, treating an external supply shock affecting individual prices as if it were a monetary problem affecting aggregate prices. 

The result will be the same. Another policy mistake.

Demolishing the private sector and engineering a market crash with unwarranted rate hikes is not a sign of independence but evidence of irresponsibility.

items.title: "They Should Pull Their Fingers Out And Buy My Shares": New Mandelson Files Expose Epstein Pal's Conflicts
items.content_text:
"They Should Pull Their Fingers Out And Buy My Shares": New Mandelson Files Expose Epstein Pal's Conflicts

Peter Mandelson spent more than six months as Britain's ambassador in Washington still holding a large stake in Global Counsel, the lobbying firm he co-founded, while the Foreign Office's top civil servant set up what he called a "light touch" process to watch him for conflicts, according to 32 documents the UK government released on Thursday.

When the Foreign Office press team asked him in July 2025 to clear its answer to a Private Eye query showing his stake was still "substantial," Mandelson replied in one line: "They should pull their fingers out and buy my shares."

The papers are the third volume the government has handed Parliament under a Feb. 4 Commons order for everything on his appointment. Other material is still held back at the Metropolitan Police's request while detectives investigate whether Mandelson passed confidential government information to Jeffrey Epstein while he was a cabinet minister in 2008-2010. He was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, has not been charged and denies wrongdoing.

BREAKING: Govt publishes more documents on disgraced former US ambassador Peter Mandelson.

Sky's Sam Coates takes you through the most important parts.https://t.co/jSzH9GhzTp pic.twitter.com/l8YZs123T9

— Sky News (@SkyNews) November 26, 2026

The Blind Trust That Wasn't

On Jan. 5, 2025, the Foreign Office's outgoing permanent under-secretary, Sir Philip Barton, went through Mandelson's conflict-of-interest form and wrote: "Global Counsel equity - unless this can be sold immediately, I assume it is going in a blind trust. When will this happen by?"

Two days later an official whose name is redacted pushed back: "it is a bit difficult to see how this could be genuinely 'blind'," because Mandelson "would know that he continued to hold the equity" and could "theoretically be (or could be perceived to be) in a position to influence the value of that interest as US Ambassador."

Barton's successor, Sir Oliver Robbins, settled it in a March 6 letter to Mandelson's deputy in Washington, James Roscoe. "The ideal would have been for GC to have bought him out of this position before he took up the appointment," Robbins wrote. "GC has however not made an offer that Lord Mandelson considers commensurate with the fair value."

A blind trust, Robbins went on, would not work "for a large holding in a privately-owned company." Instead Roscoe was told to get a list of Global Counsel's senior clients, take "a monthly forward look" at the ambassador's business engagements and report to Robbins every quarter. Robbins had already sent Mandelson the draft, describing it as a process "that protects you against perceptions of benefitting GC in some way while in public office," to be run "in a light touch way." Mandelson forwarded it to the foreign secretary's chief of staff, Jon Garvie: "Did you see this ?"

"Has Not Divested"

Robbins wrote that Mandelson expected the Messina Group, the firm founded by Democratic strategist Jim Messina, "who took a stake in GC last year," to bid for the whole company, at which point he would "exit his shareholding entirely." On March 28 Robbins told then-Foreign Secretary David Lammy that Global Counsel had made Mandelson an offer, which he had accepted, and that he expected it to be "executed next month."

Four months later, Robbins' office wrote on Aug. 8 that "HMA has not divested the stake" and that Robbins needed to put a new note to the foreign secretary "asap." That note, dated Aug. 26, said the other party "has not been able to execute this transaction" and that Global Counsel was "raising debt" to make an offer in September.

Robbins' office sent that note to Mandelson before it went to Lammy, telling him it would be issued "as soon as I have your edits / go-ahead," and Mandelson filled in the one blank, the date his shares were valued: "April 2024." The final version told Lammy that because the valuation "will not change," Mandelson "has no ongoing economic interest in GC's commercial performance."

"Under The Radar"

In April 2025, Mandelson wrote from his embassy account to an official at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, whose name is redacted, about "alternative options to the WTO" and "how likeminded partners come to terms with China." He proposed a lunch for May 13 so he could bring "a former trade colleague of mine," also redacted, to "lead off." "It would be best to keep this under the radar," he wrote.

The official answered that meeting him had been "a delight" and that "'Prince of Darkness' couldn't be farther from the truth!" When the council's staff came back with dates in June, Mandelson forwarded the email to a Global Counsel employee and asked: "Do you have date preference for trade think in ?" The reply: "June 10/11 look pretty good."

A Speech Edited By The Firm

On Aug. 27, 2025, Mandelson sent a Global Counsel director the draft of his Ditchley lecture and asked whether "the arguments need strengthening at all." The director's edits came back the next morning. The speech's "pure hostility towards China," the director wrote, did not "obviously align with what looks like HMG's considerable effort to achieve a rapprochement with China."

The director had also suggested "toning down some parts of your apologia of the Trump administration," warning that it would be "counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool Aid." Mandelson replied: "I will soften the lecture on China and add tone in the q and a !"

"So We Have Time!"

The files also show how loosely the paperwork moved after then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer named him on Dec. 20, 2024. On Christmas Eve, a Foreign Office official chasing his conflict-of-interest forms was told there was no need to do more until Dec. 30: "His start date on FCDO payroll will be 6 Jan earliest, more likely to be mid-Jan, so we have time!"

His security clearance came through on Jan. 29, 2025, for five years rather than the usual seven. The next day the department's security chief, Ian Collard, wrote that Mandelson had been asked to complete his remaining clearance forms "as an urgent priority," and that "matters pertaining to his overseas contacts" would be reviewed by the authorities that control access to the most sensitive intelligence. Officials reviewing his form in January also asked about a UBS speaking engagement "with Asian clients."

On Sept. 5, 2025, six days before he was fired, Mandelson messaged Starmer's chief of staff, Morgan McSweeney: "Are you taking peter Kyle away....?" and then, "You should solve your Darren issue and put him at DSIT." McSweeney replied that evening: "I think we seized that day quite well."

Mandelson was fired on Sept. 11, 2025, two days after Bloomberg sent him questions about his emails to Epstein, among them a June 2008 note from around the time Epstein pleaded guilty: "I think the world of you and I feel hopeless and furious about what has happened." The scandal engulfed Starmer, who resigned as Labour leader in June and was succeeded by Andy Burnham as prime minister on July 20.

Asked on Thursday whether an appointment like Mandelson's could happen now, Burnham said: "I don't think we have yet seen the change that this system down here needs."

Andy Burnham says he would tackle the "vested interests" which he believes contributed to the Peter Mandelson scandal, ahead of the latest release of documents relating to the former US ambassador.

The prime minister also said his 10-year plan would address the issues with... pic.twitter.com/UQgymRKSXb

— Sky News (@SkyNews) November 26, 2026

As for the shares Global Counsel never bought, the firm itself collapsed into administration in February 2026 after a swathe of clients cut ties over Mandelson's links to Epstein.

Asked whether the strike could cost Kyiv European support, she declined to tie the two together. "I wouldn't link the question of resources. I think we must do our best to keep helping Ukraine defend itself, but we must also defend the security of our borders and our citizens. On this I have been, and intend to keep being, very clear with President Zelensky and with Ukraine" (translated).

Zelensky confirmed on Monday that Ukrainian drones had hit the corvette Merkury, among the newest ships in Russia's navy, along with a Russian cargo vessel off the Libyan coast, and called the operation "exemplary." Two Libyan navy officers have since died of their wounds, and the eastern Libyan army of Russian ally Khalifa Haftar vowed revenge.

Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani went further in the Senate on Thursday. "We are convinced that violating Libya's sovereignty is a mistake and that it does not help Ukraine's cause," he told senators, adding that the Italian government stands with Ukraine but "the war cannot be extended to the Mediterranean" (translated).

Speaking in Baku, Tajani said Rome had no warning: "We were not informed of absolutely anything; we did not provide any kind of support to the Ukrainians." On Tuesday he called Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha to register Italy's concern that the conflict could spread into the Mediterranean and to stress respect for Libya's sovereignty and unity.

Italy has about 200 troops in Libya with its Miasit mission between Tripoli and Misurata, and Rome is weighing stronger protection for them, according to military sources quoted Thursday.

Inside Meloni's coalition, Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini's League has been far blunter. "I wouldn't want someone to be bringing the war to Italy's doorstep, because we're talking about the Mediterranean" (translated), Salvini said Monday.

In a statement Wednesday, the League said the deaths of the two Libyan soldiers made the "act of war" a few hundred kilometers from Italy even more serious, and that conducting military operations on a sovereign country's territory without first consulting Western partners, Italy above all, is "unacceptable" (translated). It warned the strike could deepen the split between Tripolitania and Cyrenaica and undercut the UN's and US envoy Massad Boulos's diplomacy in Libya.

The decree that has let Italy send military supplies to Kyiv every year since 2022 runs out in a little over a month, and Salvini wants the arms shipments stopped in 2027, as Gazzetta del Sud noted.

In March, Moscow blamed a Ukrainian drone boat for blowing up the Russian LNG tanker Arctic Metagaz between Malta and Libya, and on Thursday the Kremlin turned President Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte's warning against expanding the war back on Kyiv. Now Rome, one of Kyiv's steadiest backers since 2022, is telling Zelensky the Mediterranean is off limits.

items.content_text:
Trump Signals Rethink On US Troop Cuts In Europe After Greenland Deal

Authored by Victoria Friedman via The Epoch Times,

President Donald Trump has indicated that a security deal over Greenland has influenced his thinking on possible U.S. troop reductions in Europe.

Trump made the comments on Nov. 26 after participating in Thanksgiving holiday calls to service members.

When a U.S. service member asked about encouraging allies to take greater responsibility for their own defense, Trump said allies were increasing defense spending and buying American military equipment, including F-35 fighter jets.

Taking questions from the press after the event, the president said European NATO allies were not helpful in their initial response to the Iran conflict.

"They weren't very helpful," he told reporters. "But we got Greenland, and we got Greenland. That's three times the size of Texas, and that made me feel a little bit differently, to be honest."

Trump after speaking with Mark Rutte about US troops in Europe: "They weren't very helpful to us on, you know, Iran... But we got Greenland. That's three times the size of Texas." pic.twitter.com/LEE8MMcObe

— Furkan Gözükara (@FurkanGozukara) November 27, 2026

Trump did not specify whether troop reductions in Europe remained under consideration or announce a decision on U.S. force levels.

The president then said that European allies were now involved "and they've been great."

"And Mark Rutte, I have to say, is a great leader. He is a fantastic leader," he said of NATO's secretary-general, with whom he had had a meeting on Nov. 25.

Greenland Deal

Trump made the remarks after Denmark's parliament approved, earlier this month, a security agreement that will allow a larger U.S. military presence in Greenland.

The deal amends the 1951 Defense Agreement signed by the United States and Denmark.

While the 1951 agreement already granted the United States sweeping military rights in Greenland, the new deal strengthens certain access rights and allows the United States to expand its military footprint on the Arctic island, but does not transfer sovereignty over the island to the United States.

Trump told the press on Nov. 26 that he and Rutte had discussed Greenland.

"We made that deal, which everyone said was not makeable," he said. "And I want to thank Denmark, the country of Denmark. They were great, but we made that deal."

.@POTUS on his meeting with @SecGenNATO: "We discussed Iran, and he doesn't want them to have a nuclear weapon... We discussed Greenland... Most of it was focused on Russia-Ukraine." pic.twitter.com/WeMlyEraXm

— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) November 26, 2026

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly said that the United States must purchase or annex Greenland "for the purpose of national security" before Russian or Chinese interests are entrenched in the area.

After negotiations between U.S., Danish, and Greenlandic officials, Trump announced a security deal on Sept. 18 and signed it with Greenland and Danish leaders at a ceremony on Sept. 22 at the U.N. General Assembly in New York City.

Greenland lawmakers then approved it on Nov. 3, and Danish lawmakers backed it on Nov. 19.

NATO Spending

Trump has long advocated that other alliance members take more practical and financial responsibility for collective security.

The press raised NATO spending, and Trump responded that allies were not only spending more on their own defense but also buying U.S. defense equipment, such as F-35 fighter jets.

"I was able to get NATO to go from 2 percent, which they weren't paying, to 5 percent, which they will soon be paying, and everyone thought that was a miracle," the president said, referencing a June 2025 agreement by NATO members to raise defense and security-related spending to 5 percent of gross domestic product by 2035, a proposal backed by Trump.

NATO figures show that European allies and Canada increased their combined defense spending by nearly 20 percent in real terms in 2025 compared with the previous year.

"Because of me, they're becoming more self-sufficient," Trump said of NATO members. "We want them to because you know ... we have the greatest military in the world, and we're protecting a lot of countries that haven't been paying their share, and now they are."

He added that the United States cannot continue protecting every nation in the world, calling it unfair to U.S. taxpayers.

Today's WLFI episode is just another rerun of insider circular lending to cash out, unauthorized insider selling, the illegal freezing of investor assets, and investor fraud.

items.title: "Be Ready": Britons Hoard £700 Million In Cash After Crisis Warning
items.content_text:
"Be Ready": Britons Hoard £700 Million In Cash After Crisis Warning

Authored by Anastasiia Chabaniuk via Traders Union,

UK households are increasing cash holdings after the government urges the public to prepare for potential emergencies under its "Be Ready" campaign. 

Bank of England data indicates as much as £700 million has been hoarded over the past five weeks, highlighting how official preparedness messaging is influencing consumer behavior.

Cash buildup follows emergency guidance

As reported by Bloomberg, citing the Bank of England, the amount of cash in circulation has increased by £1.5 billion since Oct. 22, when the government stepped up its public readiness message.

That increase follows comments from Security Minister Dan Jarvis, who tells people to keep three days' worth of essentials, including bottled water, food, wind-up radios and cash in a mix of coins and notes, to manage through a cyber attack, severe weather or other emergencies.

Preparedness push shapes household behavior

The figures suggest households across the UK are responding directly to official advice by holding more physical money at home, even as digital payments dominate most day-to-day spending.

The scale of the increase, including an estimated £700 million accumulated over the past five weeks, points to a broader public focus on resilience and access to funds during disruptions that could affect power, communications or payment systems.

As we reported earlier, ordinary Europeans are building emergency kits after a month of hacked supermarket freezers, hoax bomb threats and a worldwide email outage - and their governments are telling them to.

items.title: AfD's Weidel Warns Party Ban Is Coming In 2027 'To Save Democracy'
items.content_text:
AfD's Weidel Warns Party Ban Is Coming In 2027 'To Save Democracy'

Authored by Remix News Staff via Remix News,

The German government will try to ban the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in 2027, said AfD co-leader Alice Weidel in a new interview with Welt.

"The party ban procedure, which is now called the review procedure, will come anyway. They will try it next year, 2027," she told the newspaper during a podcast.

Alice Weidel über ihr Coming-Out, die Brandmauer und ihre Kanzlerambitionen https://t.co/0X0k8S33SV pic.twitter.com/yHV4yLX8Vl

— WELT (@welt) November 27, 2026

She noted that the votes for such a ban are already there in the Federal Council. "Yes, because the votes for it are being collected in the Federal Council. The majorities are already there, they are very hardworking," she said.

She warned that state-backed Trojan horses can now be used to manipulate data to frame AfD politicians and members. This material will be used in the ban proceedings, she stated.

"What we are experiencing here is actually the de facto abolition of the rule of law, to be perfectly clear. The worst part is that state Trojans can be planted on data carriers, computers and phones, and the data can be altered - i.e., so-called false-flag operations can be performed....They simply want to get rid of the political competition. We are preparing for it. And we'll see what happens."

She noted these state-backed Trojan horses, which are powerful tools that can hijack phones and computers, giving intelligence unlimited access to keystrokes, chat messages, emails, files, and contacts, were made possible via reforms. Previously, using such tools was illegal.

"This naturally also coincides with the reform of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the Federal Intelligence Service," she said. "Falsifying data is, of course, something where we are abandoning the principles of the rule of law. This reform is absolutely unconstitutional."

It is unclear how much Weidel is drawing on information that is readily available and how much was leaked to her, but she appears relatively certain a ban procedure is coming next year. There are a number of methods by which a ban procedure can be initiated but it would ultimately need to be affirmed by the Constitutional Court.

Such a move would send shockwaves through Germany given that the AfD routinely receives between 28 and 30 percent of support in polling, making it the most popular party in the country.

The comments were made during a long-form interview with Welt, which explored a wide range of topics, including Weidel's experience coming out as a lesbian. She also addressed her party's difficulty in cracking the 30 percent barrier.

"Previously the sound barrier was at 10, then at 15, then at 20, now we are at 30 percent. And we had exceeded 30 at one point. If I were supported by public broadcasting with such continuous election advertising as Ms. Baerbock, on the trampoline, for example - can you imagine that, me on the trampoline on (German state-funded news outlet) Tagesschau? - then we would be beyond 40 percent. This is also due to the media coverage, the defamation campaigns, and of course the fact that public broadcasting is absolutely left-wing and green, supporting clientelism and government policy. And is simply designed to damage the AfD and, in some cases, to launch smear campaigns."

So far, the CDU has been opposed to initiating a ban against the AfD. In the spring of 2025, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that voting on an AfD ban in the Bundestag is not the right path, saying it "smacks too much of the elimination of political rivals."

However, the mood may have changed since then. The AfD has only grown more popular, the German economy is drowning in debt and facing years of stagnation, Merz faces rock-bottom approval ratings on par with Emmanuel Macron, and his CDU party has few options to recover lost support. As Remix News previously wrote, if the CDU moves forward with a ban procedure, it could actually end up proving disastrous for the CDU itself. However, Merz is a man of the establishment, not necessarily the CDU. He may want to cement his legacy with the left by being the man who backed an AfD ban.

Furthermore, with Donald Trump severely weakened at home, the AfD can no longer count on him or his State Department to meaningfully threaten the German government with sanctions if a ban eventually arrives.

It is no doubt a precarious time for the AfD and 2027 may be an inflection point. The establishment no longer knows how to democratically counter the AfD. They may now resort to authoritarian methods to "save democracy."

items.title: "Situation Is Entirely Unsustainable": Single-Day Record Broken After Massive Wave Of Illegal Migrants Lands On Spanish Canary Islands, Military Unit Requested
items.content_text:
"Situation Is Entirely Unsustainable": Single-Day Record Broken After Massive Wave Of Illegal Migrants Lands On Spanish Canary Islands, Military Unit Requested

Authored by Remix News Staff via Remix News,

The remote Spanish island of El Hierro, with just 12,000 inhabitants, has been pushed to the breaking point with the largest single-day arrival of irregular migrants ever recorded on the Atlantic route. On Tuesday, 2,121 people reached the island aboard 15 overcrowded cayucos, according to regional authorities.

Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo declared a level-2 emergency and formally requested the Military Emergencies Unit (UME), Spain's military disaster-relief unit.

Clavijo told Defense Minister Margarita Robles that existing resources could no longer guarantee public health conditions.

"This situation is entirely unsustainable," he stated.

He also directly addressed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on X.

"The Canary Islands can take no more. We are experiencing unprecedented migration pressure in the 32 years of the Atlantic Route. Today I requested an urgent meeting with European Commission President @vonderleyen. I demand an immediate response from the EU. These people are arriving in Europe, and it is not fair for us to respond alone to a crisis of this magnitude," he wrote.

Canarias no puede más. Vivimos una presión migratoria sin precedentes en 32 años de Ruta Atlántica. Hoy he solicitado a la presidenta de la Comisión Europea @vonderleyen una reunión urgente. Reclamo una respuesta inmediata de la UE. Estas personas llegan a Europa y no es justo que respondamos solos a un drama de esta magnitud

— Fernando Clavijo (@FClavijoBatlle) November 25, 2026

The number of migrants arriving in just one day, which included hundreds of women and minors as well as at least one death and a newborn, surpassed previous daily records and left local health and reception systems in collapse.

November alone has brought more than 15,000 arrivals to the island, which exceeds the number of residents on the island, while year-to-date figures for the Canary Islands in total stand near 28,000, according to Spanish newspaper El Nacional. The numbers have risen rapidly in just the last two months.

The crisis comes right before general elections in Spain on Nov. 29. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez recently claimed to Canary residents that the migratory situation was "under control." Vox leader Santiago Abascal replied on X by quoting the claim and stating: "Yes, it's under control. Of course. You're leading the invasion."

Sí, está bajo control. Claro. Tú diriges la invasión.

— Santiago Abascal 🇪🇸 (@Santi_ABASCAL) November 25, 2026

Most come from West African countries including Senegal, Gambia, Mali, and Guinea. While the temporary reception center on El Hierro is designed for just 500 people, it has been overwhelmed by the arrivals, with many housed in makeshift facilities elsewhere on the island before being rapidly redistributed across mainland Spain. Hospitals and emergency services have reported severe strain due to the huge wave of migrants.

Around 120 personnel, including doctors, nurses, and technicians, began arriving Thursday from bases in the Canaries and other locations.

Paula Jover, president of Vox in the Canary Islands parliament, posted about the migrant invasion of the islands, arguing that the Sánchez government has failed to stop the flow and that Spain needs secure borders and deportations.

😡 2.100 inmigrantes en un solo día. 14 cayucos. Un fallecido, 203 mujeres y 127 presuntos menores.

👉 El Hierro bate nuevamente récord histórico de una tragedia que el Gobierno de Sánchez es incapaz de frenar.

😡 Mientras PSOE y sus socios miran hacia otro lado, Canarias... pic.twitter.com/x10HXuNLBE

— Paula Jover (@PaulaJover_) November 26, 2026

Polls so far have the center-right Partido Popular (PP) of Alberto Núñez Feijóo in the lead, with Vox averaging about 18 percent. Combined, the two right-of-center parties are projected to exceed the 176 seats required for a majority in the 350-seat Congress, potentially ending Sánchez's minority government.

items.title: FlyDubai Allowed Back In Tel Aviv, Two Months After Its Co-Pilot Allegedly Tried To Crash A Jet Full Of Israelis
items.content_text:
FlyDubai Allowed Back In Tel Aviv, Two Months After Its Co-Pilot Allegedly Tried To Crash A Jet Full Of Israelis

Flydubai will fly back into Tel Aviv on Thursday, Dec. 3, nearly two months after an Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked his captain and tried to bring down a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight packed with Israelis. The Dubai carrier has reopened ticket sales for the route, and an Israeli source told The Times of Israel that the airline is being let back in "under new security arrangements."

Transportation Minister Miri Regev approved the return on Monday, after a delegation of senior Israeli security officials and ministry staff, led by ministry Director-General Moshe Ben-Zaken, came back from talks with Emirati aviation officials in Dubai. According to the Israeli source, the approval still needs clearance from the Shin Bet, the Mossad and the National Security Council.

The ministry said the delegation "presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident," and called the decision "a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE." It did not say what any of those steps are.

Israel's own airlines are still shut out of Dubai: El Al, Arkia and Israir have been held up by the same security questions, and Etihad, which flies to Abu Dhabi, is now the only carrier linking Israel and the UAE. Emirati authorities halted Israeli airlines' Dubai flights when the US-Israel war with Iran broke out in late February, and those flights never came back.

Before the suspension, flydubai ran 10 daily flights out of Tel Aviv, and Dubai was the main connection for Israelis bound for Thailand, the Philippines, China and Japan. Israel had initially barred the airline through at least Dec. 15.

On Sept. 30, Flight FZ1073 dropped 18,000 feet in 12 minutes after the first officer, Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, turned on Indian Captain Smit Machchhar in the cockpit. The wounded captain got the cockpit door open, and crew and Israeli passengers forced their way in and subdued the co-pilot before the Boeing 737 diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and landed safely.

BREAKING: Passenger footage captures panic aboard a Flydubai flight as the aircraft reportedly plunges 17,000 feet during a violent confrontation between the pilots, with passengers seen running toward the cockpit. pic.twitter.com/2quMsMEuXI

— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) September 30, 2026

UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said investigators found the co-pilot "had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," going at the captain with the cockpit's crash axe and trying to take control of the plane. Israel's Channel 12 reported that al-Hammami told investigators he meant to fly on toward Israel as if nothing were wrong, get cleared to approach Ben Gurion Airport and then crash the jet into a building or another plane at the airport.

Israel has since barred pilots and crew from 31 countries with no formal diplomatic ties to Israel from flying passengers there, and has tightened screening of foreign airlines' crews. Asked a day after the attack whether the co-pilot was linked to Iran, President Trump said, "I would say the answer based on what I'm hearing is yes," and promised that if Iran was behind it, "they'll be hit, very hard."

An al-Qaeda weekly, al-Bayan, hailed the attacker and urged copycat strikes on American and Israeli airliners, and India's National Investigation Agency opened a case under its anti-hijacking and anti-terror laws because the captain is Indian.

When FZ1073's route reopens next week, Israelis connecting through Dubai will be flying the same airline on the same route, while Israel's own carriers still can't land in Dubai at all.

items.title: Is Britain's Left-Wing Establishment About To Shift To The Right?
items.content_text:
Is Britain's Left-Wing Establishment About To Shift To The Right?

Authored by David Goodhart via The Daily Sceptic,

If you are an artist, academic, social worker or a psychologist - or, increasingly, a journalist or doctor or lawyer or civil servant - you are likely to operate in a social milieu in which the range of respectable opinion is strikingly narrow.

Yascha Mounk, The Bourgeoisie Has Switched Sides

The British Establishment is no longer either Conservative or conservative. Consider some of its dominant institutions: Oxbridge and all elite universities, the General Medical Council and almost all health-related institutions, the Bar Standards Board and most of the institutions of the legal profession, the Senior Civil Service, and all the leading regulatory organizations. All now lean Left.

This has been driven by the movement from Right to Left in the political attitudes and political party preferences of the higher professional class in the last decades of the 20th century and first of the 21st. It is one of the most important and least studied aspects of British and European politics.

In this essay - based on a new report I co-authored for the Policy Exchange think tank - I will provide evidence of this shift in the UK, consider some of the reasons for it, show how it has become embedded in our institutions and culture - creating that new progressive Establishment with a distinct worldview - and speculate about whether it might be at least partially reversed in the coming years.

In the 1970 UK General Election nearly two-thirds of those from the higher professional and managerial class voted Conservative, with just 11.3% voting Labour. In the more fragmented field of the 2024 election 43.6% of higher professionals voted Labour and just 15.5% Conservative.

The higher professionals are not an ideologically homogeneous group and there are many exceptions to this shift, most notably in the professions associated with business and finance. And, as one might expect, professions most dependent on public spending, such as teachers and health professionals, have moved further to the Left than most others.

The German terms Bildungsbürgertum and Besitzbürgertum are helpful here: this essay is concerned mainly with the first group, meaning literally the bourgeoisie of the educated (lawyers, doctors, senior civil servants, engineers, academics, architects, accountants), rather than the second group, the bourgeoisie of the owners (today meaning senior corporate managers, business owners and prosperous skilled tradespeople).

The phrase "Right to Left" is shorthand. At the least it needs to be sub-divided into socio-economic attitudes and socio-cultural. The interesting story here is that the most notable shift among the UK higher professional class has come in the socio-economic sphere.

This is partly because higher professionals were already in the 1970s more liberal (progressive is the more appropriate term as modern progressivism is not always liberal) in their socio-cultural attitudes compared to the rest of the population on issues such as immigration, the death penalty and law and order.

On socio-economic attitudes, according to the British Election Study (BES), higher professionals today are now more supportive of public ownership and more opposed to privatization than the wider population. In 1974 the higher professional class was more hostile to the idea of governments redistributing wealth than the rest of the population. Now, according to the BES, the same group is more likely than the rest of the population to agree that ordinary people don't get their fair share of national wealth.

Andy Burnham's recent focus on public control reflects not the radical outsider representing working people in the corridors of power but rather new Establishment priorities (not least the priority given to unwinding Brexit rather than stopping the boats).

The more than quadrupling in higher professional numbers, from one million to 4.7 million - and from 4% of employees to 12% - between the early 1980s and early 2020s is not only a big factor behind their greater influence but also helps to explain the economic shift to the Left. In many cases higher professionals no longer feel themselves members of a privileged caste with a special leadership role, but merely affluent knowledge workers. (The combined higher and lower professional and managerial occupational group is now around 40% of all employees.)

Most higher professionals are in the top 10% of earners, some in the top 1%, but as a group their relative income and wealth has declined. They pay more in tax, are less likely to be privately educated, and younger ones become homeowners later.

On socio-cultural issues the higher professionals have, on average, stayed ahead of the crowd even as the general public has liberalized. The benevolent paternalism of professionals, derived in part from a vocational commitment to the common good, was still a minority view in the middle decades of the 20th century and often pitted against the more hard-headed attitudes of the military and business worlds as well as working-class authoritarianism.

But at elite level the baby-boom professionals came to lead an ideological reaction against the violence and xenophobia of the first half of the 20th century. That reaction came to dominate first education and then the classical professions as the 1960s and 70s university-educated generation arrived at the top of professional hierarchies.

In the past 50 years, in the UK and much of Europe, a politics of social class and material interest has come to be partly eclipsed by a politics of technocratic expertise and benevolent-progressive socio-cultural attitudes, symbolized by one of the first and one of the last acts of the New Labour Government: independence for the Bank of England in 1997 and the Equality Act 2010.

Both actions would have pleased Harold Perkin, the late British historian of - and advocate of - the professional class, who famously pronounced: "The 20th century has become the century not of the common man but of the professional expert."

Progressive, paternalistic professionals

The 'great liberalization' of the past 50 years is one of the professional classes' legacies. New polling by Focaldata, commissioned by Policy Exchange, which compared attitudes among key professional groups with a representative sample of the British public, reinforced by evidence from the British Election Study, shows that higher professionals remain markedly more progressive than the general public.

Higher professionals are five to 10 percentage points more progressive on almost all issues, and on several issues 20 points more, including: certain aspects of immigration, on believing that Muslim immigration is a threat to the British way of life, and on believing that there is an anti-meritocratic appointment and promotion bias against white men.

Meanwhile, the higher professionals remain consistently more paternalistic than the public, believing that the most important decisions about public policy and how people live their lives should be taken by experts rather than individuals themselves or elected politicians. Indeed, 49% of professionals agreed that people should have to pass a civic responsibility test before being allowed to vote, and by 61% to 29% higher professionals believe that courts should be free to overrule decisions made by Parliament.

It is often said that in the 1980s, at the height of the Thatcher-Reagan reaction against post-war social democracy, the Right won the economic argument but the Left won the socio-cultural argument on equality and rights.

But who, in Britain, was this 'Left' that was winning the socio-cultural argument? It was not working class voters whose views remained relatively socially conservative in the 1980s. Neither was it the old public-school elite who continued to dominate the Conservative party, the officer class of the armed forces and the City of London. Rather it was the university educated 'exam-passing' middle and upper middle class professionals who started to grow sharply in number during that decade as higher education also expanded rapidly.

Many higher professionals often embrace views, such as white privilege or transgender self-ID, that are challengingly progressive even in a more tolerant era. This is especially true of the most ideological, activist segment of the higher professionals that often dominate the professional associations, while almost all Whitehall permanent secretaries either literally or metaphorically took the knee during the BLM protests in 2020.

Political scientist Eric Kaufmann traces the origins of professional progressivism back to the 1910-20s in the US and UK and the influence of bohemians like the Bloomsbury group of artists and writers reacting to both the death of God and the horrors of the Great War. He sees the bohemian locomotive then pulling a bigger train of highly educated people, especially a few decades (and another world war) later, after the Civil Rights Act in the US and the student revolt of the late 1960s.

Where academia, education and the arts led the way, law and medicine were soon to follow. In 1979 roughly half of British teachers voted for Margaret Thatcher, in 2024 just 5% voted Conservative. Many educated people, especially in former colonial countries like the UK or France, wanted to challenge tradition and embrace more universalist-egalitarian attitudes.

The end of the Cold War in the early 1990s was a further spur to the progressive worldview, allowing not only a shift in resources from warfare to welfare but also a more subliminal weakening of the need for authority and solidarity.

The great liberalization has been a popular as well as elite-driven phenomenon inspired by the slow evolution of democracy itself, the decline of deference and religious belief, and a shift in relations between the sexes enabled by technology and the modern service economy. Who could be against more democracy and equality for women, minorities and people from lower income backgrounds?

The dominant common-sense of the British public today, a mix of 'you do you' individualism and 'be kind' liberalism, is not the same, and is often far removed from, the progressivism that has come to dominate many national institutions. Opponents of progressivism have often failed to detach the former from the latter. Conservatives have also struggled to find a narrative that embraces what is welcome in the great liberalization while rejecting its excesses and overshoots.

Populism is the nemesis of professional class progressivism, expressed in Conservative politician Michael Gove's famous outburst that "the public have had enough of experts". But where did the experts acquire so much power? The answer is that our politicians gave it to them.

The era of so-called 'club governance' that continued into the post-war decades gave enormous and often unaccountable power to elected politicians, but also to individuals running schools, police forces, businesses and so on. (This was especially true of the UK without a written constitution.)

A new consensus emerged in the 1980s that a modern democracy required more accountability and legal constraint, hence today's regulatory state dominated by the priorities of the higher professionals. Paradoxically, this began to happen as the economy was being de-regulated in the Thatcher years.

Privatization itself required a new layer of regulation. Moreover, to try to make the state more responsive, functions began to be sliced off from central government departments and handed to so-called arms-length bodies (quangos) such as the Environment Agency.

Greater complexity and new technologies have also driven the growth of the higher professionals' regulatory state. A society without social media, drones, online pornography, risky financial instruments, and so on simply needs less regulation.

The New Labour and Cameron era consensus that took root in the 1990s and 2000s meant more regulation but also a more open and liberal society: more immigration, more generous welfare, the pursuit of a cognitive meritocracy through the expansion of higher education, the Human Rights and Equality Acts and greater European integration, thereby deepening rights and shifting more power from elected politicians to lawyers, professional experts and international institutions.

There are some exceptions to this progressive trend. For example, there was no significant reversal of the step-change in income inequality of the late 1980s, and prisons policy became more punitive not less.

Nevertheless, the broad sweep of liberalization follows the script of US writer Christopher Caldwell's theory of the 'two constitutions' in which the second constitution (the courts, the Civil Service, the media, regulators, NGOs etc.) dominated by the higher professional class comes to eclipse the democratic preferences - most notably on immigration and national sovereignty - of the broader public expressed in the first constitution: the basics of elections and democratic representation.

But that doesn't answer the riddle of why a liberal-minded lawyer or doctor was still happy to vote Conservative (or Liberal) in the 1970s but by 1997 had been largely captured by the center-Left. I believe there are five main reasons.

First, there is the decline in relative status and income for all but the most successful higher professionals, largely as a simple function of that big expansion in numbers and the widening differentials within many professional groups. This has been accompanied by the arrival of several new professions in recent decades, such as IT director and project manager, which have provided a status challenge to the older professions.

Second, professional class progressivism has also been driven by the ascendancy - and increased numbers - of public sector professionals in education and the social state, who often have a vested interest in a bigger state. The proportion of public sector higher professionals has grown from 15% of the total to around 25% since the 1980s, driven by big expansions of the NHS and higher education which, together, employ about 500,000 higher professionals.

Third, the greater salience of cultural issues like immigration, national attachment and race and sex equality in recent decades means that people, especially the highly educated, are more likely to form their political identity around such issues rather than the old socio-economic divides.

Fourth, the dramatic expansion in higher education since the 1980s means almost all higher professionals will have been through the normally liberalizing experience of residential higher education. As recently as the early 1980s only about one third of higher professionals were graduates; now almost all of them are.

Fifth, there has been a big change in the gender and social composition of the higher professional class. Today, around half of higher professionals are women - who now lean further to the Left than men - a substantial minority are from ethnic minority backgrounds, and the class is drawn from a broader social base.

Britain has become a socially liberal country. But the last few years has seen an overshoot beyond this decent consensus - sometimes called 'woke' or illiberal progressivism: a regime promoted by progressive higher professionals that includes various forms of compelled speech, unconscious bias training, positive action ('equity' to compensate for past discrimination, not just equality), a belief in white privilege, an assumption that differences in group outcomes must be the result of discrimination, skepticism about the value of national traditions, and a focus on identity politics.

Some of this overshoot is now embedded in public and private sector organizations through codes of conduct, value statements and staff training (and Continuing Professional Development); Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) commitments that are required in job and promotion interviews and public procurement processes; and staff networks based on protected characteristics. One might think of it as a mutation in the traditional 'doctor knows best' paternalism of the professional class, a kind of professional vanguardism often at odds with majority views and promoted by an expanded Human Resources function.

It is enforced by the regulatory bodies, such as the Solicitors Regulation Authority or the Financial Conduct Authority, that have proliferated since the 1980s and much of it is legally underpinned in the Equality Act, including its Public Sector Equality Duty, the Human Rights Act and the European Convention on Human Rights. These laws act as a kind of background written constitution and any decision taken by an elected politician can be overruled by a judge if they have not been sufficiently taken account of.

All establishments have norms and codes, implicit and explicit, and if you want to rise in today's professional establishments in Britain you need to accept the dominant progressive norms or at least pay lip service to them. Even the graduates of many of the top private schools now lean to the Left.

A course correction?

Why does this matter, and can it be reversed in the next few years? It matters not because of the electoral prospects of parties of the Right. It matters because democratic legitimacy is weakened when a large section of the population is alienated by the Establishment. The dominance of higher professional progressivism has helped to marginalize conservative views and the reaction against this is a major factor behind the populist revolt.

It has also interfered with the normal political pendulum swing from Left to Right, so even when the Right wins elections it doesn't really govern. There is something unhealthy about a society in which the Establishment is itself a driving force of progressivism and quasi-counter-cultural activism. Much of the energy in a society, especially in art and culture, comes from having something to push against. But if the mainstream is itself liberal-permissive in outlook the energy dissipates and turns on itself or finds more and more extreme outlets.

Is a course correction possible? The 2016-2024 Conservative governments 'talked Right and governed Left' says Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader. It is only recently in response to Conservative voters drifting to Nigel Farage's populist Reform party that the Conservatives have shifted back to positions more actively offensive to higher professional progressivism on topics such as immigration, asylum and climate action, making a mass return of higher professionals to their former Conservative allegiance unlikely.

It is, however, possible to imagine that at least a minority of higher professionals could openly revolt against the excesses of modern progressivism. Here are four reasons why a limited political course correction by British higher professionals might be possible.

First, there is some evidence that higher professional progressivism is weakly held and discarded when challenged or when it runs up against more fundamental self-interest. Several UK companies happily abandoned their EDI commitments, at least in their US subsidiaries, in the wake of Donald Trump's hostility.

Even the militantly progressive and internationalist British Medical Association, the trade union representing doctors, has recently stressed the importance of giving priority to UK trained doctors over immigrant doctors in its arguments with the Government over reforms to the training system.

Second, we have now had more than two decades to experience some of the failings and unintended consequences of both the Human Rights Act and the Equality Act, such as the idea of indirect discrimination and the debacle over equal pay for work of equal value, as well as the increasingly elastic interpretations of harassment or disability.

Third, the status and influence of higher education institutions, one of the key factors underpinning higher professional progressivism, is now clearly on the wane. The UK will remain a major international center of higher education, but the next few years will likely see a drop in both the number of universities and the proportion of British school leavers attending them.

Moreover, the stranglehold of the Left in academia will matter less for the intellectual life of the country as more influential thinkers, often but not always of the Right, can earn a living through analysis and commentary on social media, podcasts and Substack.

Finally, as noted already, the higher professional class does not feel as economically blessed as it once did. To date this has pushed most higher professionals to the Left in economic attitudes, looking up enviously at the super-rich. But that could reverse, especially if Andy Burnham fails to improve on the economic performance of Keir Starmer. Stifling levels of tax and anxieties about the labor market consequences of AI for even high status professionals and their children could help to de-prioritize progressive concerns.

And with most higher professionals intensely hostile to Reform-style populism, it should be psychologically easier to switch support to a more mainstream Conservative party, partly to avoid a potentially chaotic populist Government.

Rule by largely progressive higher professionals is now being challenged by populists of Left and Right. Some of this is deserved. They have too often pursued their own interests in the name of the general interest. Our societies still need their expertise, but expertise genuinely aligned with the common good. We need a course correction not a revolution.

David Goodhart is a journalist and Head of Demography at the Policy Exchange think tank. His (free) Substack is A Goodhart is Hard to Find. This essay is based on the Policy Exchange report What Britain's New Establishment Thinks... And Why It Matters which can be found on the Policy Exchange website including the detailed Focaldata polling.

items.title: Watch: Ex-Brit Charged In Iran-Linked Plots Shouts Orders To London Arsonist From Iraq
items.content_text:
Watch: Ex-Brit Charged In Iran-Linked Plots Shouts Orders To London Arsonist From Iraq

Footage broadcast for the first time by ITV News on Nov. 26 appears to show Mohammad Ali al-Hassani shouting instructions from Iraq over a video call to someone carrying out an arson attack in London. Al-Hassani is one of three men charged in the US over a string of Iran-linked attacks across Europe and the foiled plot against RAF Fairford, the Gloucestershire base that hosted American bombers.

In the clip, al-Hassani sits behind a laptop in a makeshift office in Iraq, yelling at a man who appears to be acting on his orders. It ends with a voice on the call saying "All right, that's it. Cut, bro," then "Yeah, cut, cut, cut. Well done."

BREAKING: Newly released footage appears to show British-Iraqi man Mohammad al-Hassani directing an attack in London remotely from a warehouse in Iraq. pic.twitter.com/SuYIGbrVdf

— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) November 26, 2026

Al-Hassani was stripped of his British citizenship in October, a relative confirmed to ITV. A letter from the Home Secretary said he was "assessed to be a dual British-Iraqi national" and that it "would be conducive to the public good" to deprive him of his British citizenship. US prosecutors describe him as a 35-year-old Iraqi national.

A relative who has been in touch with him in recent weeks told ITV that al-Hassani intends to keep plotting attacks in the UK until there is no American military presence in Britain. "He was saying 'I like London, I'm in love with London, I love my people, but one thing - they don't have the right, no Americans and no Israelis have the right to attack anyone from the UK,'" the relative said.

The relative cast the campaign against Jewish institutions as revenge for the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, in February: "That was a retaliation for attacking the Ayatollah. You attack our religious leader, we're going to attack your religious places."

Al-Hassani drew on contacts from his years in London's VIP security business to plan some of the attacks, according to ITV. "For a while in London he was dealing with cars and security and all sorts of stuff," the relative said. "And car rentals, he was doing his car rentals as well."

The Justice Department unsealed an eight-count superseding indictment against al-Hassani, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in Manhattan on Nov. 10, as we reported at the time. Prosecutors say the attacks were claimed by a supposedly new group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which the Justice Department calls a front for Kata'ib Hizballah and other terrorist organizations. Of the 18 attacks HAYI claimed in Europe this spring, seven were in the UK, the most of any European country.

According to the indictment, al-Hassani and Mohajeri planned the London campaign in Iraq around April 6 with a map of London on a computer screen, al-Hassani saying "we need to get focused on London." HAYI claimed six attacks in and around the city starting about a week later.

On April 17, prosecutors say, the three men watched one of those attacks live over FaceTime, projected against HAYI's logo, while al-Hassani told the attacker to "light it" and to "throw the fourth one." The next day al-Hassani allegedly joined a video call with a man attacking a London synagogue and told him to "light it up like a Christmas tree", before the attacker lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at the building. Prosecutors have since released video of those calls, as we detailed last week.

From August, al-Hassani allegedly paid associates in Britain to prepare the Fairford attack: one to scout the base's perimeter on Aug. 22, others to buy vans and fuel barrels, research chemical accelerants, buy metal for shrapnel and have decals made so the vans would pass for a "fuel delivery business." On Sept. 26 he allegedly directed drivers taking three vans, some carrying fuel, toward the base. At least two hit a security roadblock and were turned back, and UK authorities recovered the vans and arrested the occupants the next day.

Prime Minister Burnham said in October the plot was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, while Iran's embassy in London denied any involvement. The US pulled its bombers out of Fairford in October.

Prosecutors say al-Hassani and Mohajeri were in Iran at the time of the Fairford plot, and ITV reports al-Hassani's whereabouts are unknown. Al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey and extradited to the US in May, and officials believe the seven-man network ITV identified earlier this month broke up after that.

Officials believe an elite Revolutionary Guard unit led by Rahman Moghaddam has since taken control of parts of the campaign, ITV reports, and the attacks have now reached more than 20 locations across Europe and spread to UK military bases, reportedly funded by Unit 4000, a secretive Iranian intelligence division.

items.title: EU Proposes $55 Billion Tech Fund Amid Quantum Race With US, China
items.content_text:
EU Proposes $55 Billion Tech Fund Amid Quantum Race With US, China

Authored by Owen Evans via The Epoch Times,

The European Commission has proposed a sovereign technology investment fund targeting 50 billion euros ($55 billion) alongside measures to favor European companies and establish Europe as a global leader in quantum technology.

The European proposals come as Washington and Beijing continue to compete for leadership in quantum technologies.

"Major US technology companies are also investing directly in quantum technologies, while large-scale corporate investment remains much more limited in Europe," the Commission said in its Nov. 25 legislative proposal.

The Commission's Nov. 25 proposals include the Quantum Act, a legislative framework aimed at converting European quantum research into commercial products and services, and the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (STEF), an investment vehicle for quantum and other critical technologies such as AI, cybersecurity, biotech, and chips, which it views as "key to European tech sovereignty and economic security."

"Quantum technologies will shape the future of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a profound impact on our societies," said Henna Virkkunen, executive vice president of the European Commission for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, adding that Europe "needs to accelerate now."

"With the Quantum Act, we are putting in place the key elements to turn our world-class quantum research into industrial capacity, strengthen critical supply chains and prepare for the cyber risks linked to quantum computing."

Europe has world-class quantum research and startups.

The proposed #QuantumAct will help turn research into economic value, strengthen our supply chains and pave the way for a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund.https://t.co/LLnYtj50tf pic.twitter.com/SgmzijNZLY

— Henna Virkkunen (@HennaVirkkunen) November 25, 2026

Virkkunen said the targeted scale of the proposed equity fund was 50 billion euros ($55 billion).

Quantum technology uses the behavior of subatomic particles to enable faster computing, and has significant military and commercial applications.

The Commission said the proposal "combines support for quantum innovation with security preparedness" and is needed because "sufficiently powerful quantum computers could break existing cryptographic methods used to protect sensitive communication and data."

According to the Commission, announced public funding for quantum technologies through 2025 amounted to an estimated 8.6 billion euros ($9.4 billion) in the EU, compared with 5.3 billion euros ($5.8 billion) in the United States.

However, U.S. quantum startups attracted around 7 billion euros ($7.6 billion) in private investment in 2025, compared with just 1.1 billion euros ($1.2 billion) in the EU.

In June, U.S. President Donald Trump signed two executive orders aimed at accelerating the development and commercialization of quantum technologies and protecting federal information systems against future quantum-enabled cyberattacks.

The U.S. Department of War announced $350 million in quantum computing initiatives on Oct. 8 intended to strengthen America's leadership in the technology and support national security.

Under the initiatives, the Pentagon will identify potential military applications of quantum computing as the technology becomes available.

The department said it expects applications in physics, chemistry, and materials science to support the development of next-generation weapons and other military capabilities.

In a November 2025 report, the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission concluded that while the United States led the world in most areas of quantum research, China had deployed centralized coordination and industrial-scale funding to "seize dominance" in quantum technology.

The commission found that China had established a lead in quantum communications and was making significant advances in quantum computing and sensing.

In March, China included the development of quantum technologies among the strategic priorities outlined in its 15th Five-Year Plan.
