items.title: 图书作者指控英伟达做种盗版电子书
items.content_text: 图书作者指控英伟达在从影子图书馆如 Anna's Archive 和 LibGen 下载盗版电子书后，通过 BitTorrent 协议进行了做种，做种意味着英伟达与第三方共享并传播了盗版电子书。图书作者在诉状中表示，英伟达采取了部分限制做种的措施，但没有完全禁止做种。图书作者还指出，英伟达通过一个包含 2.5 亿页内容的 PDF Extraction Project 项目与包括 Adobe 在内的商业合作伙伴共享盗版书籍。这些内容部分来自影子图书馆。英伟达此举是为了从 PDF 文件中提取 token 去构建差异化模型，它还将 PDF 提取功能整合进 NeMo 管线让客户能利用其 PDF 内容。作为交换，Adobe 承诺在其部分产品中使用英伟达的大模型。诉状指控英伟达不仅自行分发了盗版书籍，还协助他人实施侵权行为，它既直接侵权还协助侵权。

items.title: 前沿 AI 实验室可能找到了 RSA 的弱点
items.content_text: 多位计算机科学家称，前沿 AI 实验室如 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 可能发现了能破坏互联网通信安全的算法。德州奥斯丁的计算机科学家 Scott Aaronson 称他从多个可信来源确认 AI 实验室拥有一个或多个颠覆性的重大发现。AI 实验室的目标与 RSA 等公钥加密系统相关。研究人员称，他们听说前沿 AI 实验室发现了能在多项式时间内破解公钥加密的算法。公钥加密是互联网应用安全的基础，它所依赖的数学问题对传统计算机而言几乎不可能在合理的时间内解决。如果一种算法能在多项式时间内解决这些问题，情况将会彻底改变，互联网所依赖的安全基础可能随之动摇。最坏的情况将是 P = NP 被证明。

items.title: 能在PC上启动的 Lisp machine 仅 7KB 还带个打方块
items.content_text: Nala Ginrut 写道： 周末闲来无事，我让claude把我的AnimulaVM移植到PC上，Animula是目前唯一产品级能运行在10KB内存MCU里的lisp machine。 结果claude花了20分钟用汇编写了个微缩版本，可以在PC上直接启动并且进入打方块游戏，游戏是用Scheme写的，用我的Laco编译器编译的。理论上如果bios支持legacy CSM的话，是可以直接把这7KB镜像烧入软盘或者U盘直接启动的，否则只能在qemu上启动。 我认为这是AI试图挑战old-school hacker的一次例证，如果再这么搞下去，感觉人类快要完蛋了。 总之各位少年，在人类完蛋之前不打算来一局打方块吗？

items.title: 科学家用海鸟监视关闭 AIS 信号的船只
items.content_text: 并非所有渔船和货船都以透明方式运营。由于它们规避监测，其对海洋野生动物的影响无法量化。一项新研究提出了一种发现未被监测船只的策略：将录音设备绑在海鸟身上。船只可通过关闭自动识别系统（AIS）追踪技术来隐匿其活动。研究人员将轻型录音设备安装在三种海鸟（北方塘鹅、韦斯特兰海燕和巴利阿里鹱，它们各自生活在不同的海洋环境中）身上。他们通过 GPS 绘制了些海鸟的活动轨迹，分析了记录各种独特船只声音的音频记录。他们发现，记录到的船只声音中有相当大一部分与 AIS 报告的活动并不重合。例如北方塘鹅平均每天在船只附近停留 68 分钟，其中至少有 22 分钟是在未被监测到的船只周围。换言之，在塘鹅捕捉到的船只音频中至少有 32% 来自未开启 AIS 的船只。研究人员指出这只是一个保守估计，实际比例可能接近 57%。

items.title: Kimi 向科学家提供最高 2 万美元 API 免费额度
items.content_text: Kimi 大模型开发商月之暗面宣布了 Kimi for Science 项目，欢迎自然科学、工程学及相关交叉学科领域的研究人员加入。月之暗面表示，“科学始终源于人类的好奇心、严谨的探索精神，以及对未知世界的不懈追求。一个有价值的科学假设，往往需要经过大量的文献调研、数据分析和反复验证。而一次意料之外的发现，也可能成为下一项重大突破的起点。然而受限于时间、算力与人力资源，许多值得深入探索的想法，始终未能获得应有的关注与投入。我们相信 AI 能加速科学研究，拓展探索与发现的边界，帮助研究者突破时间、资源与研究方法的局限，让更多大胆而富有想象力的科学构想从可能走向现实。”月之暗面将向入选的研究人员提供最高 20,000 美元的 Kimi API 额度（约 70 亿 token），具体金额将根据研究需求及评估结果确定。

items.title: Take-Two 无法阻止用户利用 AI 将 GTA 6 移植到 PC 上
items.content_text: GTA 6 开发商 Rockstar 的母公司 Take-Two 与微软和索尼签署了独占协议，这款备受瞩目的大作目前只有主机版本，PC 版本发布时间未知。但在 AI 工具的帮助下 PC 玩家正以惊人的速度将 GTA 6 移植到 PC 上。Take-Two 已采取行动，试图遏制这一行为：他们通过 DMCA 通知从 GitHub 上删除了逾 3000 个相关库。但这并没有放缓 PC 版本的移植速度。移植者们已经能利用 AMD 中端显卡 9070XT 和 FSR 超分辨率技术在 Linux 上实现稳定运行 30+ FPS。

items.title: 文明的历史是小麦的历史
items.content_text: 根据苏美尔神话，世界之初即无耕种也无畜牧和纺织，原神们生活窘迫，为此他们创造了谷之女神 Ashnan 和羊之神 Lahar，将他们派去帮助人类。Ashnan 和 Lahar 合作为神祇们提供了面包、酒、奶和兽皮。但众神们又争执起了谁的贡献更大。智慧之神 Enki 裁定谷之女神 Ashnan 贡献更大，理由是无谷物就没有面包和酒。推而广之，也就不会有城市，更不会有苏美尔文明。古苏美尔人的认识至今仍然正确：人类的历史是小麦的历史。人类食用小麦的历史比城市、文字乃至车轮的出现都要久远。现存最古老的文字记录并非史诗或宗教典籍，而是关于谷物储存与税收的行政记录。虽然世界其它地区的主导粮作物不同，比如东亚是水稻，美洲是玉米，但是小麦支撑起了罗马帝国与工业革命。

items.title: 欧盟委员会称浏览器竞争是 DMA 优先事项
items.content_text: 欧盟委员会回应了 Open Web Advocacy 的公开信，认可浏览器是互联网的入口，是内容出版商触达读者的主要方式，而浏览器竞争是 DMA（Digital Markets Act）的优先事项。欧盟委员会表示，目前正就相关事宜进行磋商，确保竞争对手的浏览器能在 iPhone 和 iPad 上与 Safari 展开有效竞争。苹果公司此前被指控通过合规的要求阻止竞争对手的浏览器使用自己的引擎，违反了 DMA 相关规定。

items.title: 一人户二人户占全国家庭构成的近六成
items.content_text: 一个时代的家庭模板，正在悄悄退场。曾经被视作社会基本单元的三口之家，如今占比不足两成；一人户、二人户相加，已经接近全部家庭的六成。最新的家庭结构抽样数据，展现了一个很直观的变化：一人户占比 26.4%，二人户占比 33.2%，两者相加，已经接近六成。而曾经代表主流的三口之家，占比仅 19%。四人户 12.1%，五人及以上大家庭只剩下 9.3%。家庭这个最小单元，正在变得越来越小。很多人会把一人户、二人户简单等同于单身和丁克，但现实比标签复杂。一人户里面，既有主动选择独居的年轻人，也有子女离开后独自生活的老人；二人户里，有还没生育的年轻夫妻，也有相伴养老的老年夫妇。它不是某一类人的选择，而是一整个社会结构变迁的结果。

items.title: IBM 停止签证担保，让 H-1B 持有者选择离职或离开美国
items.content_text: 蓝色巨人决定停止为其咨询部门员工提供美国工作签证及绿卡担保。该公司咨询部门有逾 15 万员工，受影响员工可选择到其他国家工作，或在 2026 年 12 月 31 日前离职。IBM 未披露具体有多少员工会受到影响，也未说明其中有多少人身处美国。员工有三周时间决定是否接受外派。对于不愿接受海外职位的员工，公司将提供相当于三个月的离职补偿金，将 2026 年 12 月 31 日定为他们的最后工作日。在匿名员工论坛 Blind 上，一位 IBM 员工说到印度工作可能意味着减薪 80%。 HireMe CEO George Carrillo 指出，调动工作岗位可能意味着举家搬迁。它会影响配偶的工作、子女的教育、医疗保健以及多年的规划。人力资源部门应提供明确的选择、截止日期和协调一致的支持。

items.title: 旅行者 1 号发回无法解读的信息
items.content_text: 北京时间 11 月 18 日 18 时 16 分 07 秒，旅行者 1 号与地球的距离达到约 259 亿公里，相当于光在真空中传播 24 小时的距离，也就是一光日。但与此同时旅行者 1 号出现了技术故障，给这一里程碑时刻蒙上了一层阴影。11 月 14 日旅行者 1 号发回的信号缺乏帧同步信息，意味着 NASA 无法解读接收到的科学数据或工程数据。遥测数据的缺乏让任务控制人员无法监测其运行状态，也无法获取其在星际空间收集到的测量结果。导致此次故障的确切原因尚不明确。

items.title: 物理学家使用重力发送无法屏蔽的信息
items.content_text: 昆士兰大学研究人员利用重力、电梯和一台高灵敏度重力仪成功穿墙传递信息。实验在大学的 Parnell 楼进行，研究人员让电梯在两个楼层之间往返移动，其中 1.8 公吨配重在 0 和 1 之间切换，相邻卫生间里的重力仪探测到了重力场的变化，将信号翻译为单词 Gravity（重力）。Charles Woffinden 博士表示，不同于电磁信号，重力信号无法通过在传播路径上放置普通物质屏蔽。虽然目前的系统还远未达到实用阶段，但它证明利用一种普通物理屏障无法阻挡的方式进行通信是可行的。研究人员利用的电梯来自 1950 年代，运行速度很慢，每分钟仅能传输 1 比特数据，发送一个单词需要整整一个小时。研究人员称，如果利用量子传感器，重力通信距离能提高到 500 米，数据传输速率能达到每分钟 15 比特。

items.title: 极端高温引发地表淡水急剧下降
items.content_text: 根据发表在《科学》期刊上的一项研究，2023 年和 2024 年的全球极端高温导致地球地表淡水资源出现前所未有的下降，河流流量以及湖泊和水库蓄水量急剧减少，即使在湿润地区也是如此。中科院研究人员分析了 1991 年至 2025 年间全球河流流量以及湖泊和水库蓄水量的变化，发现了三个截然不同的阶段：1991 年至 2006 年间的显著波动、2007 年至 2022 年间的相对稳定期，以及 2023 年至 2024 年间的突发性中断——在此期间，河流流量和地表水蓄水量均急剧下降。与 1991 年至 2020 年的平均水平相比，全球河流流量下降了约 5.7%，湖泊和水库的有效蓄水量则下降了 9.5%。尽管河流流量自 2025 年起开始回升，但作者发现，在他们考察的历史记录中，2023–2024 年的下降幅度是前所未有的。南美洲受到的冲击尤为严重：河流流量下降了 17.8%，地表水蓄水量减少了 16.5%，而与此同时，部分地区却遭遇了极端降雨和洪涝灾害。研究人员将这些下降归因于太平洋厄尔尼诺现象与热带北大西洋同时变暖之间的一种不同寻常的相互作用。虽然厄尔尼诺现象通常会抑制亚马逊地区的降雨，但异常温暖的大西洋放大了其效应，导致大气中的水汽偏离南美洲北部，从而加速了河流流量和地表水蓄水量的下降。

items.title: 今天的老年人相比上一代人记忆力衰退放缓
items.content_text: 今天的老年人相比上一代人认知衰退更慢记忆更好。一项针对 1910-1964 年间出生的 21.9 万人的研究发现，出生年份每向后推移十年，60 岁时的记忆力得分便会提高 10%。全世界很多国家的人口正在老龄化，患有痴呆症的人数也在上升。但过去四十年美国人任何年龄患痴呆症的个人风险下降了三分之二。研究人员推测，记忆力的提升可能得益于童年时期更好的教育、医疗保健和营养状况；而认知功能衰退速度的放缓，则可能受到人生后期多种因素的影响，例如心血管疾病和代谢性疾病治疗水平的改善。

items.title: 英国人性生活频率大幅下降
items.content_text: 根据发表在《柳叶刀》期刊上的一项研究，英国人性生活频率大幅下降，从 1990 年每月四次降至如今的每月两次；三分之一的 16–24 岁年轻人表示从未有过性行为，而 1990-2010 年间这一比例是五分之一；过去十年同性性行为的报告在增加；观看网络色情非常流行，一半年轻女性和近九成年轻男性表示过去一年曾看过色情；无子女女性明确表示不打算生育的比例过去十年间翻了一番；等等。

items.title: 已故网络工程师 Dave Täht 获得 Jonathan B. Postel 服务奖
items.content_text: 2025 年 4 月 1 日去世的网络工程师 Dave Täht 获得了互联网协会颁发的 Jonathan B. Postel 服务奖。今年初路由器发行版 OpenWrt 曾为纪念他而以他的名字命名 v25.12.0。互联网协会称：在 Täht 看来，视频通话中断、网页加载缓慢、进度条冻结——这些现象统称为缓冲区膨胀（bufferbloat）——都是阻碍互联网连接的障碍。所谓缓冲区膨胀是指数据在负责转发流量的硬件设备中滞留的时间。Täht 致力于寻找并推广解决网络拥塞的方案，旨在让人们真正享受到互联网的全部潜能。

items.title: 基因编辑猪肾在人体内正常工作一年
items.content_text: 基因编辑猪肾在人体内正常工作一年。58 岁的美国新罕布什尔州居民 Molly Falco 迎来了接受猪肾移植一周年的重要时刻。去年 11 月 22 日，她在麻省总医院接受了基因编辑猪肾移植手术。过去一年里，猪肾持续承担清除体内毒素、产生尿液及调节体液平衡等功能，让长期饱受肾病困扰的她逐渐恢复正常生活。如今她重新开起了汽车，能够为家人做饭，甚至计划恢复滑雪。美国约 9 万人正在等待肾脏移植，而 2025 年实际完成的肾移植手术不足 2.6 万例。由于猪器官在大小和部分生理功能上与人体器官相近，猪成为异种器官移植的重要供体来源。 人体免疫系统会识别猪细胞表面的特定分子，并攻击移植器官。研究人员通过基因编辑，去除猪体内部分容易引起排斥的基因，同时引入有助于提高人体兼容性的人类基因，以减轻免疫系统对移植器官的攻击。Falco 接受的猪肾来自生物技术公司 eGenesis 培育的基因编辑猪，共经过 69 处基因编辑。其中 3 处用于去除容易引发免疫排斥的猪抗原，7 处用于引入提高人体兼容性的人类基因，另外 59 处用于使猪内源性逆转录病毒失活，降低潜在的跨物种感染风险。

items.title: 中国发现新古人类支系
items.content_text: 中科院研究人员针对在南宁隆安穿山洞和柳州鹿寨龙船洞两处地点获得的 4 颗人类牙齿化石（分别距今至少 10.1 万年和 10.5 万年—4.3 万年）开展了古蛋白质组学和形态学综合分析。研究人员将穿山洞和龙船洞发现的牙齿，与其他人属标本进行比较。结果显示，两个组合呈现出截然不同的表型特征。研究人员对龙船洞以及穿山洞样本进行了古蛋白质提取，发现龙船洞样本可能代表华南地区一支具有丹尼索瓦亲缘关系的谱系，而穿山洞牙齿可能属于华南地区一支不同于丹尼索瓦人的独立谱系。研究提示华南可能是古老型人类的地理避难所与演化熔炉，为理解东亚古人类种群结构、区域变异与可能的基因交流提供了重要基准，代表了重建亚洲古人类种群演化历史的重要一步。

items.title: 地球连续六天气温比工业化前水平高 2C
items.content_text: 根据欧盟哥白尼气候变化服务中心(C3S)的数据，全球气温已连续六天比工业化前水平高 2C。本周一全球日地表气温比工业化前水平高 2.24C 创历史新高，预计未来至少几天内气温仍将维持这一高位。此前只有两次日气温升幅超过 2C 的记录，分别出现在 2023 年 11 月和 2024 年 2 月，那两次持续时间较短，升温幅度都不及这次。科学界担心全球暖化可能在加速。目前地球正处以一次超强厄尔尼诺事件中。上一次如此强度的厄尔尼诺现象发生在 1870 年代，曾引发大规模饥荒，导致 5000 万人丧生。最新的厄尔尼诺现象将在未来几个月内达到峰值，其全面影响可能要到数月后才会显现。

items.title: 艾滋病疫苗终于触手可及
items.content_text: 本世纪初，南非 KwaZulu-Natal 省的一名年轻女性感染了 HIV。她本可能成为统计数字的一部分，但通过参与 HIV 研究她却给数百万人带来了希望。她被发现能对 HIV 病毒产生极其强烈的免疫反应。她需要在药物的帮助下才能控制病毒，但她体内的抗体被认为至今发现的最强效 HIV 抗体之一。在科学文献里她被称为 CAP256。科学家现在认为，通过模拟她感染 HIV 过程中的部分关键元素，能训练其他人的免疫系统产生同样强效的抗体去阻断多种不同的 HIV 毒株，最终研发出一种能彻底阻断 HIV 感染疫苗。CAP256 体内广谱中和抗体的存在给科学家研发疫苗带来了希望。

items.title: The Generation X Christmas pudding
items.content_text:
In further Worcestershire news: A woman preparing to tuck into her late grandmother's 52-year-old Christmas pudding with her family says if they get E. coli from the traditional dessert "so be it". Daphne Townsend, who lived near Tetbury, made her family the steamed pudding in September 1974, something she did each year to give the festive treat three months to mature ahead of the big day. She died in 1975 but her family kept the pudding and have decided to make Sunday the day they enjoy her culinary skills one last time ...

... Wallington, who has been feeding the pudding after it spent "40 to 50 years sat in a cupboard" ... said: "We're just going to go for it." "It's dehydrated a bit so I've been chopping it up with a little drop of stout and a little drop of brandy. "Grandmother would have put stout and barley wine into hers but I can't come across barley wine." Dutson, who is hosting the gathering at her house in Stoke Prior, Worcestershire, said relatives are coming from Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire, Wiltshire, Somerset, and North Wales to sample the long-standing Christmas pudding.

items.title: Is the Mimbres School a Lefty Cult—or the Future of Higher Education?
items.content_text:
The university as we know it is only a few hundred years old. Robes and lectures have been around since the Middle Ages, but it was only in the seventeenth century that German professors and ministers dreamed up written exams, promotion with tenure, and all the rest. It wasn’t until the nineteenth that the model encircled the world and came to seem inevitable. William Clark tells the story in his 2005 book, Academic Charisma and the Origins of the Research University. Over more than 650 surprisingly hilarious pages, he recounts the perverse paperwork and fragile egos that have come to define the modern university: Celebrities like Leibniz and Kant show up, but only for their backhanded letters of recommendation, obsequious funding requests, and other administrative tedium.

In March 2025, ten people, seemingly all leftist millennials and Gen-Zers, gathered on Zoom to discuss Clark’s book. The event was hosted by an unaccredited institution called the Mimbres School for the Humanities. Joy Shokeir, a teaching fellow at the school, brought up Charles Darwin. When the English naturalist was a young man, she said, he dropped out of medical school. Then he tried seminary school at Cambridge but gave up on that too. Clark’s book explains that life sciences like zoology weren’t absorbed into the university until the nineteenth century—which, Shokeir pointed out, explains why Darwin never indulged his obsession with bugs in academia. Instead, he leveraged his wealthy family’s connections to get onto a military surveying ship, the HMS Beagle, where his work began in earnest. The students at the reading group had come to Mimbres to make like Darwin: leave the university and find somewhere to study on their own terms.

The school’s leader and founder, Colin Drumm, logged on too. He wore a lichen-green Baja hoodie, hood up, red beard and hair protruding. Professors often blame administrators for their problems, he said, but the bigger issue is the professors themselves. “One theme in this book is that it’s been difficult for a long time to get the professors to do their jobs,” he said. “They are taking public pay, and they are not taking their responsibility seriously.” He portrayed the administrators’ mentality: “Well, if we can’t get the professors to do their jobs, we can fill up all their time doing surveillance stuff so at least they’re working for their money, right?” Drumm’s tone was halfway between humor and outrage. “That’s the institution we have!”

In copious posts on X, Drumm makes his case against professors in detail. They are “vain and pretentious and afraid of their own shadows.” They have every incentive to do bad work both as teachers and writers. They rush to publish the first idea that comes to mind. They are unduly deferent to the tastes and preferences of undergraduate students. Far from the radical ideologues imagined by the right, they “are cynical institutional careerists who believe in nothing.” “Part of the reason that the professors have become so stupid,” he wrote in April, “is that they are only really accountable to children and to one another. If they had to interact more regularly with thinking adults they would be less silly and useless, generally.” 

I’m a university professor myself, teaching in the tiny philosophy program at the University of South Dakota in Vermillion. Is Drumm right that I haven’t been doing my job? Like my colleagues, I work hard. But even before I stumbled across the Mimbres School, I had started to worry that something was going sideways. It wasn’t just the usual suspects: the Trump administration’s never-ending assaults, the demographic cliff that is predicted to decimate enrollment, the race between students and professors to see who could use AI to shirk more of their responsibilities.

The scarier problem was that I couldn’t tell any more when I was adjusting to a new reality and when I was capitulating to it. I had developed an elaborate spiel about how philosophy classes would train my students to process complex information in a way that would gratify their future employers. I spent a lot of time guiding them on how they should and should not use AI. I started phasing out formal written assignments and adopting goofy, for-profit apps to spice up lessons. Meanwhile, I found myself spending less and less time on what a colleague calls “Doing the Thing”: slowly and carefully reading a lot of difficult books, discussing them, and then doing it again, thinking hard without knowing where it would lead. Humanities professors had been finding a variety of ways to sing the praises of Doing the Thing, but no one had a good plan to keep it alive.

When a student heard about my research, he told me about an online provocateur whose Ph.D. dissertation on a related topic had gone viral and who was making himself notorious on X. It was Drumm. Soon I tracked him down on leftist podcasts, where I found him arguing about Marxism and Modern Monetary Theory. I followed him to the Mimbres website, where I bought a subscription through the crowdfunding website Patreon, which for $30 a month gave me access to videos of classes and reading groups like the one on the seventeenth-century German university. I ended up visiting Drumm twice, first in 2025 as a “visiting scholar” and again this August, when I participated in the school’s first in-person symposium. In the mountain desert, near what Drumm calls the “physical campus” of the online school, I Did the Thing more than I had in a long time, learning about Greek economic history at the same time that I wondered whether my university job, whose contours had taken shape in the seventeenth century, might just dissolve in the twenty-first.


The Mimbres School’s growth has been steady, but by no means stratospheric. Drumm put together his first online seminar—applying the field of complexity theory to global history—around 2019, looking for ways to monetize his Facebook following. More ad hoc seminars followed in the feverish days of the Covid lockdown. The first course in Mimbres’s official archive, “Race and Finance From the Money View,” had 15 students. The school incorporated as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in 2023, and last year Drumm declared $126,371 in academic revenue, up 44 percent from the year before. With around 360 paying subscribers—there are five tiers of participation—Mimbres remains a small player in a sprawling industry of unaccredited “alt-ed” or “para-academic” universities.

That industry reflects Americans’ dramatically falling confidence in higher education. In July, Gallup released a poll reporting that after a brief uptick, the share of Americans who say they have “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in the university has fallen to 38 percent, near the lowest since Gallup started asking in 2015. Most of the press on academia’s dismal public image reflects the ascendant arguments of conservatives, free-speech crusaders, and the Trumpian right. Even self-flagellating internal discussions among academics often circle around the supposed dominance of leftist groupthink. If you’ve heard of the para-academic schools at all, you’ve probably heard about the conservative ones. In the media blitz announcing the opening of the University of Austin, co-founder Niall Ferguson wrote that “academic freedom dies in wokeness.” The school, whose co-founders also include journalist Bari Weiss and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale, immediately collected an enormous pot of donations from billionaires, which it used to offer free courses on Western great books and Christian-inflected science. Psychology professor turned self-help celebrity Jordan Peterson has a more down-market, fully online school of his own. Judging from the trailers, its video lectures are given by highly credentialed professors but also enhanced with AI-generated images: Plato with a cloudlike beard, a sad young man on the steps of a crumbling apartment building, the word “nihilism” floating in space, everything fine-tuned for students conditioned on algorithmic video.

Leftists have either been more reluctant to criticize the university or their voices haven’t been amplified as much. But they have stepped into the alt-academic arena too. The Brooklyn Institute for Social Research started in 2012 as a passion project by Columbia Ph.D.s, with classes in bars and church basements fueled by box wine and corn chips. Now BISR, as it’s known, offers dozens of online courses with titles like “The Palestinian Intellectual Tradition” and “Late Capitalist Architecture.” A 2023 article noted that the clientele, who pay $355 per four-week course, “skews white collar and college educated.” The school’s online boutique suggests the same, with its erudite but corny T-shirts and Valentine’s Day–card gift subscriptions.

Many if not most of the instructors at BISR, judging from their online bios, are from a less well-heeled demographic than their students. Though they mostly have Ph.D.s, they are part of a new precariat that cuts across the educational divide. They pick up gigs one at a time to supplement a patchwork of adjunct contracts and service jobs. The BISR website boasts that “as a labor-forward organization, 70 percent of all tuition fees go to supporting BISR faculty in their teaching and research endeavors.” As I learned from Xafsa Ciise, who has taught both at BISR and Mimbres, the catch at BISR is that instructors are paid per student enrolled (70 percent of course tuition). On this “eat what you kill” model, instructors only make real money when they recruit their own students—that is, they do much better when they are internet celebrities with an established following. (Ciise will be leaving Mimbres School this December, after finishing her current course.) 

The students at Mimbres hail from at least 25 countries, but most are Americans. They are almost all in their twenties and thirties. The school is home for the sort of disaffected young people who abandoned the Democratic Party in droves in 2024. Many of Mimbres’s instructors have Ph.D.s, but more than a few abandoned grad school. They’re hustling for gigs just like their counterparts at BISR. Everyone seems to have flirted with Marxism or the Occupy movement. But they have cast that all aside as the exhausted politics of their parents and their professors.

Deborah Wang, an analytics engineer in Cincinnati, is one of four students to complete Mimbres’s most onerous offering, a Foundations Program that offers one-on-one feedback and culminates in an intensive final research paper. Wang ruefully recalls supporting Hillary Clinton in the Democratic primary in 2016. She had completed a degree in Asian studies at Berkeley, where one professor took for granted what she calls a “State Department–inflected view on China.” The main question back then, she told me, was how and when China would finally adopt the perfected, American form of democracy. By the time Trump was in office, Wang had landed and then quit a job as a development coordinator fundraising at NPR. She then got a second degree, this one in engineering, in 2020. As she and her partner entered their thirties, they were politically adrift. “He would be YouTubing a lot of alt stuff, and I remember reacting not so great to some of it because it was quasi–Alex Jones curious,” she said. They were galvanized by protests against the oil pipeline being built at the Standing Rock Reservation in North Dakota. “Obama’s indifference at best was really, really disillusioning,” Wang said. Her online gaze turned to criticism of the Democratic Party from the left, and soon enough she encountered Drumm online.

Wang was drawn to Drumm’s persona—he was “very snarky and kind of mean,” she said affectionately—and in 2023, she signed up for a class at Mimbres, an introduction to Black studies and Afropessimism titled “What is Blackness?” At first, Wang was put off by the canonical authors circulating in the class and at the school: “All the fucking Aristotle, Plato, Schmitt, Hegel … I was in my naïveté very surprised how many Black scholars were into this stuff.… And then to my delight, what the Black scholars do is they completely decimate it.” One of Mimbres’s best rules, she said, “is that we do not respect books, and we do not love books—we read them adversarially.” This irreverent, even hostile style of study makes it easier to think openly. “We’re not a political party,” she told me. Of course, there are connections between politics and scholarship, but “you should not mistake yourself for doing politics when you write an essay.”


The Mimbres School is named after the valley in southwest New Mexico where Drumm is planning its physical campus. Before I left for my first visit, I uploaded a draft research paper on commerce and politics in ancient Greece; six faculty and five students gave excellent feedback over two hours on Zoom. Soon after I arrived, though, I found myself alone in the desert.

The campus, such as it was, consisted of two small houses on a 52-acre property. I stayed in one. My second day there, a brush fire spread over the hills a few miles away. I retreated to Drumm’s small house 15 minutes away while the local fire brigade casually got things under control. The rest of the time, the country was very still. I occasionally spotted a deer, perhaps one of the “grey ghosts” peculiar to the region, barely visible as it passed through tufts of grass. When Drumm first showed me around, he pointed to the spaces where he envisioned the bustling campus of the Mimbres School of the future. The first new building would be for conferences and seminars, with a big table, a kitchen, and dorm rooms. Later there would be an art room, a gym, a music studio. Eventually there would be touch screens everywhere, providing constant access to the school’s online offerings.

Every day, Ciise and Drumm met up with me to work. They brought their two dogs, former strays they rescued from around Silver City. Drumm read constantly and rapaciously, flipping back and forth on his laptop between PDFs of academic books, the Mimbres server, and X. I looked up from my own, slow progress and watched him squirm and scowl through seven hundred pages of philosophy that he hated. His feed populated with barbs and bon mots about the Stoic authors he would be covering for his course “Philosophy: Friend or Foe” (of course, the verdict was “foe”). Periodically, he disappeared into another room to teach a course or attend one by a colleague. Through the wall, I heard him come alive on Zoom for a session on a recent work of political philosophy, “an early contender for the worst book of the year.” He held forth, cracked wise, and invited questions, generous and even warm, perhaps in spite of himself. 

I opened my books with the zeal of the born again. Over the past year, something awful had dawned on me. I was suffering from the professor’s version of an affliction that has sparked a lot of think pieces about our “post-literate era” and the “end of reading.” I still looked at written words for hours every day, but hardly any of it was reading anymore. I ran my eyes over the philosophical chestnuts I had assigned students for the week. I “kept up with the literature” in my field, honing rebuttals to anyone who might disagree with whatever ideas I hoped to publish soon. But I rarely turned a page without knowing in advance what I’d find and what I’d think of it.

The young people at Mimbres seemed to be immune to that. They introduced themselves on the school’s discussion board as software engineers, baristas, and graduate students. Some wrote about being trans, or about having autism or ADHD. They replied with the school’s favorite emoji, 🌱, the seedling, symbolizing growth and new ideas. Then, with remarkable seriousness of purpose, they showed up at six-week courses on Kant, early hominins, and the formation of Islam. They read hundreds of pages a week and then ponied up more money to upgrade their subscriptions and take on more readings. Mimbres impresses me in many ways, but the best thing about it is invisible: the unknowable hours of solemn study it generates, by students who have never experienced anything like it, who have despaired of finding it elsewhere, or who, like me, might otherwise have been on the cusp of forgetting that it matters.


In a faux-rustic bar on the outskirts of Silver City, Drumm and Ciise told me about the school’s roots in the prestigious and quirky Ph.D. program in history of consciousness at UC Santa Cruz. Before their arrival, a group of celebrity professors retired, including the biologist-philosopher Donna Haraway and the activist-intellectual Angela Davis. Not much later, another was fired for sexual harassment and assault. Over one Bloody Mary and then another, Drumm described the remaining faculty’s bitter fights about who would replace them, and how intra-left tensions of their hiring committee meetings seeped into the graduate seminars, turning students against each other. (The worst of modern academia’s inheritance from the German provinces was on full display.) Drumm recalls that almost all his professors disappointed him. “What happened in American academia in the twentieth century,” he told me later, was that boomer humanists read thoroughly and broadly and then fell under the influence of post-structuralism. “They destroyed the canon in their own minds and then didn’t teach it to their students. And what you then got was a succession of Gen X professors who had learned from their boomer professors that the canon had been destroyed, but who hadn’t read any of it.” When students protested an introductory course on the humanities at his undergraduate alma mater, Reed College, Drumm went online with a modest proposal: “to punish everybody” by making them read both the Western canon and the forgotten, suppressed literature of the global south.

Meanwhile, he and his classmates were peering over an economic and existential precipice. After the global financial crisis of 2008, it had become clear that few millennials would accede to anything like the homes, careers, and families their parents assumed as a birthright. Drumm’s initial reaction to the crisis was (“naturally enough,” he recalls in his dissertation) to form a reading group on Marx’s Capital. But gradually he gave up on Marxism too. He found a way forward, and the seed for his eventual school’s curriculum, in the work of his dissertation supervisor, the political philosopher Robert Meister. Meister’s research at the time focused on financial options: the contracts that give their holders the right but not the obligation to buy or sell something at a fixed price into the future. After economists developed mathematical tools to assess their value, options became popular for retail investors and essential to elites’ portfolios. They are strange assets, valuable even (or especially) when they are never exercised.

Meister argued that financial options were a key instrument for transmitting injustice across the generations, so that the dynasties of the rich persisted even as everything else changed rapidly. Not only were the world’s most powerful people buying market-traded options to hedge against risk; they also availed themselves of hidden, unofficial options like the Troubled Asset Relief Program created by Congress in 2008 to bail out banks during the Great Recession. Meister argued that the transformation extended far beyond Wall Street. Since the 1970s, he wrote, financial ways of thinking have saturated our lives. It’s not just that we have come to think in terms of “investing” in education, a career, or a vacation. More than that, people around the globe, from the most powerful to the most destitute, get to the end of the month by refinancing and by hedging one debt against another. Our very selves have in the past 50 years become “essentially, a strategy for creating and rehedging options in a world of ever-changing risk.” Like contemporary dancers, most of us are “never not falling down.”

For all the damage financialization had done, Meister argued, it needn’t be wholly negative. Scholars and activists on the left must, he argued, abandon yesterday’s platitudes about justice in favor of a newer approach informed by the strange logic of finance. They should fight to protect their ability to liquidate their investments and flee in the face of crisis. And they should find ways to exact a premium from the elite in exchange for the tacit protections afforded them by the system. In a Discord chat, a historian from the Mimbres community pointed out to me how distant this approach is from the mainstream left’s. While everyone else was “crying and vomiting about how bad ‘financialization’ is,” he wrote, Meister was saying, “No, you need to financialize metaphysics too to keep up.”

In his dissertation, Drumm applied this approach back to Shakespearian England, then further to the workings of the earliest medieval mints, and ultimately to the first coins minted out of electrum in Lydia in the eighth century BCE. He learned that the economy of the American South was fueled by mortgages; enslaved people, not land, were often the collateral. His educational project, as realized at Mimbres, became broad enough to unify what might otherwise seem a hopelessly scattered curriculum, from the history of double-entry bookkeeping to the anthropology of Papua New Guinea, from Roman monetary crises to agricultural strategies in the face of the Little Ice Age.


As the 2016 Democratic primaries came and went, Drumm’s Facebook posts about academia and Bernie Sanders started to attract a following. Meanwhile in Alabama, an anthropology student named Jules Delisle got pregnant, dropped out of her M.A. program, and moved to Alberta. Over the next few years, she found herself without Canadian work authorization or family except for her two young children. Even before the Covid-19 quarantines hit, she was isolated. “I was completely deprived of all human interaction other than my children for years,” she said. “I was tandem breastfeeding, right?” Posting under a series of pseudonyms, she encountered Drumm through online drift, like many of his other colleagues and students. Soon he suggested she lead an online seminar. And soon after that, she was co-founding a school with him and they were bickering over pedagogy. As the organization grew, they brought two new co-organizers on board. Both had freshly defended Ph.D. dissertations—one on African material culture, the other on medieval usury.

The Mimbres organizers joke frequently about the idea that Mimbres is a cult (a thought that also occurred unprompted to some of my colleagues when I told them in 2025 about the trip I was planning to New Mexico). But they’re trying hard to design an institution free not only from the pathologies of the university but also from pathological communities everywhere. “Colin and I don’t talk a lot about ourselves on purpose, so that we don’t drive parasocial attachment,” Delisle told me. “We are friends, and we are friendly, but I also want to cultivate in people a suspicion of strangers on the internet.”

I’m 47 years old. When I got my job, the adjunctification of the university was underway and the job market was contracting, but I managed to dodge both the financial crisis and the deeper collapse of job opportunities that would soon follow. The signature transformation of my life was more subtle: the disappearance of the ragged books and magazines from the coffee tables of my childhood and the colonization of everything by algorithmic fragments. The latter cast their spell on me, but incompletely.

To me the strangest thing about the Mimbres School, charming and off-putting by turns, is how it combines serious-minded scholarship with the foolishness of social media. In July 2025, Drumm struck gold with a viral post on X. In a since-deleted post, a toy store owner had recommended giving young people graphic novels to get them interested in reading: “A good bridge to real literature!” she wrote. “The best way to turn a student off of books forever is to try to trick them into thinking that reading is fun,” Drumm responded. “Reading is not fun, and if the only reason they are reading is for fun they will stop when they realize the truth.”

The post got 1.7 million views. Hundreds of people earnestly told him that he was missing out on one of life’s treasures, that he just needed to find the right book. At least five, less earnest, called him a “retard.” Drumm responded to many of them. Deep in the replies, he said what he really meant: that students would only make progress if they kept turning pages even when putting down the book would be easier; that studying history properly means looking squarely at such topics as genocide and slavery. But mostly he chummed the water, calling the commentators “infantile” and telling them to do their homework.

Back on the Mimbres server, Drumm was cheerful. “People do NOT care when you post about reading books online,” he wrote—there was “only a trickle of interest” in his many posts about economic history. “But post about how books are bad, and you’ll get a million views and two percent growth for the month.… Nobody in here is going to be shocked or disillusioned because I said reading wasn’t fun and then clowned on people, so there is only upside risk.… That is just how you build this business.”


In a history book on the Mediterranean beloved at the Mimbres School, there is an interesting point about pirates. Piracy and commerce, the authors write, “flourish in profound symbiosis.” On the one hand, Mediterranean pirates have always depended on the legal market. If it disappeared, whose ships would they raid? But on the other hand, the flourishing of piracy also opened up opportunities for aboveboard businesses. For example, inland merchants sometimes prospered when piracy scared customers away from the sea. And some pirates used the capital from their raids to become legitimate entrepreneurs.

Increasingly, the world of higher education embodies similar dynamics. On the one hand, it will be a long time before the para-academic schools can get anywhere without the flows of books, scholars, and disaffected young people cast off from old-fashioned universities. On the other hand, even at their most hostile, the alt-ed schools give a welcome option to some of our best students and to young, precarious scholars graduating from our classes. They also give traditional universities a new incentive. Drumm is right that countless forces are conspiring to make university classrooms worse. In my more hopeful moments, I wonder if competition with the para-academic schools could give us a reason to tack in a better direction.

But the lessons of their institution are not easily translatable to mine. A course I proposed recently was turned down by a committee of colleagues; among the reasons given was that it was “too reading-focused.” On the first day of a new semester, I told students a line I had cribbed from the Mimbres organizer Alirío Karina. You can assume that every book is trying to manipulate you, I said. Your job is to figure out how and for what reason. There was a glimmer of recognition and surprise—and perhaps gratitude—in some students’ eyes. But there was also some confusion. There is no question of leading freshmen in an undergraduate general education course through the sorts of intellectual byways that appeal to Mimbres’s community. What works for the idiosyncratic 25-year-olds in Drumm’s Zoom seminar room obviously won’t work for the 18-year-olds in mine.

Survival for the Mimbres School, meanwhile, depends on finance. Drumm told me he’d need $700,000 for a main building with a conference room. “We have half a mil,” he said, “and if we get to a mil we could really get started.” (“Who’s ‘we’?” I asked him. He replied, “My parents and me.”) For now, the Mimbres campus is also Drumm’s parents’ vacation home. There are colorful metal lizards on the walls and a family photograph from the 1990s showing a 10-year-old Colin smiling in a grassy field with his sister and parents. Drumm describes his mother and father as “Texas Democrats” and dodges direct questions about them. But they are in cheerful attendance at his lectures and events, and it is they who have the capital to invest in renovations. Drumm isn’t lying when he says that he has staked everything on Mimbres. He is fiercely committed to curricular independence and runs all his online operations on academic revenue, but in the background he has a hedge: the mom-and-dad put. Like the university—and like just about any institution or community that manages to persist—Mimbres depends on stores of wealth and power, on who has the option to do what. “My background gave me security against risk,” he told me. “I want to enable other people to take risks in ways I have been able to.” 

This August, Mimbres held its first-ever in-person event, a symposium on slavery that Drumm scheduled in New Mexico’s monsoon season, when the country is at its most beautiful. In the call for submissions, he and the other organizers wrote that scholars of slavery have been misled by the idea—common to Marxists and mainstream economists alike—that slavery is exclusively about labor and production. The symposium would complicate the picture, showing how households “consolidate assets, manage reproduction and inheritance, secure political influence, and transmit wealth and authority across generations.” Rather than bringing finished papers, Drumm and the other organizers asked each “facilitator” to put 200 pages of reading on the table, intended for extensive collective discussion. Everyone who planned on showing up was instructed to read as much as they could, “and then a bit more.” I applied to lead a session on Plato.

Drumm and his fellow organizers had rented a New Mexico ranch for the symposium. There were 24 of us. The topic was desperately serious, and the national political climate was threatening (many of the participants taught courses in Black studies, a discipline now in free fall). But it was the best intellectual gathering I’ve attended. We stepped out into the desert to goggle at a tarantula that ambled past. We jumped and then laughed when a dust devil shattered a glass table outside. We ate excellent Afghan food prepared in the ranch’s kitchen. But mostly, surrounded by taxidermized deer heads, we Did the Thing. Drum did sneak online, of course, if only to describe the atmosphere on Discord: “everyone sitting in silence reading, quieter than the library.”

There was another, older professor in attendance: Susan Mattern, a classicist from the University of Georgia and the author of major books on Galen and the history of menopause, brand new to Mimbres. On her return home, she wrote, that “if civilization lasts another hundred years there’s a decent chance textbooks on intellectual history will have a chapter on this event.” Drumm was thinking in different terms. On the first day of the event, my flight had been delayed and I was the last to arrive. I walked into the ranch as he was wrapping up his opening remarks. We might as well admit it, he said: “This school is fake. No one in legitimate academia will be impressed that you were here. So let’s forget about the nonsense they do over there and get to work.”

items.title: The U.N. Climate Talks Were a Disaster. But There’s a Silver Lining.
items.content_text:
“Breakdown.” “Collapse.” “Failure.” Those were some of the words that media coverage used to describe last week’s COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. The talks ended in acrimony and finger-pointing after the nearly 200 participating nations could not reach consensus on how to advance the official mission of these annual summits: to protect humanity from “dangerous” amounts of man-made global warming.

Most news coverage also identified the main reason for the lack of consensus. As Reuters reported, Saudi Arabia “was at the forefront of resisting language on reducing reliance on fossil fuels,” even as “the European Union, several small island states, and other nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the oil, gas, and coal that scientists say drive global warming.”

Coming on the heels of a summer that featured 50,000 excess heat deaths across Europe and a glacial collapse in Nepal that killed at least 7,000 people and wiped out 10 percent of the country’s gross national product in minutes, the failure to highlight fossil fuels’ role in the climate emergency unleashed both derision and dismay. “A climate deal that leaves out fossil fuels is like a plan to quit smoking that never mentions cigarettes,” commented Katharine Hayhoe, the chief scientist at the Nature Conservancy.

Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and COP31 co-president, opened the final day of talks by declaring that “a historic decision” was in the offing. What followed was historic all right, though not in the way Kurum hoped. This COP marked only the second time in the 31-year history of these summits that no final agreement (known in COP parlance as a “cover decision”) was published.

Yet a strong case can be made that COP31 was not a total failure, but a much-needed turning point toward more effective climate diplomacy going forward. “No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure,” said Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser and global engagement director for the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. Bill Hare, chief executive at Climate Analytics, wrote in The Guardian that “the failure of COP31 in Antalya was a line-in-the-sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no.”

COP31 vividly demonstrated what has been evident for years: Petrostates—including the U.S., which boycotted these talks for the second year in a row—will never willingly agree to leave fossil fuels behind. And they will exploit the COP tradition of consensus decision-making to delay action as long as possible.

By refusing at COP31 to keep playing along, the vast majority of the world’s countries were, to borrow from Beckett, no longer “waiting for Godot”—no longer waiting for petrostates to help rather than hinder the fight against climate breakdown. Instead, many of these countries are moving ahead on their own to do what both science and justice call for.

One of the few bright spots at COP31 was further growth of the Santa Marta coalition of countries that is committed to a global phaseout of fossil fuels. The coalition first took shape at COP30, where 87 countries wanted the final agreement to endorse developing a global “roadmap” to phase out oil, gas, and coal. But when Saudi Arabia and Russia led a handful of petrostates in refusing to consent, consensus decision-making meant that the endorsement of a roadmap was excluded from the agreement.

Undaunted, many of those countries met in April 2026 in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin developing a roadmap themselves. Collectively, the countries that met in Santa Marta—a group that included Germany, the world’s third-largest economy; France, the sixth-largest; the United Kingdom, the seventh-largest; Brazil, the tenth-largest; and the Netherlands, the eighteenth-largest—amount to the biggest economic superpower on earth. Combine their GNPs and the total is larger than that of the U.S. Include California—whose governor, Gavin Newsom, said at COP31 that he backed the Santa Marta effort “100 percent”—and the coalition’s GNP is nearly as large as that of the U.S. and China put together.

If these countries can implement credible plans for transitioning away from fossil fuels to solar, wind, batteries, and other forms of clean energy, it would put governments and financial markets on notice that staying invested in fossil fuels will be a risky proposition that could leave them with trillions of dollars of stranded assets. This scenario became more plausible at COP31, as the coalition expanded to include not only California, the world’s fourth-largest economy, but also Spain, Ireland, Belgium, Finland, Denmark, Norway, Luxembourg, and Pacific island nations.

Petrostates’ obstructionism at COP31 also led to renewed calls to reform the decision-making process at future COPs. “COPs are designed to fail,” Juan Carlos Navarro, the minister of the environment for Panama, said in an interview with Covering Climate Now. Minutes earlier, Navarro had delivered the summit’s most piercing sound bite, telling a press conference that “we are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.” In the interview, he explained that consensus decision-making means that “all it takes is one idiot to torpedo the entire process. If we don’t change direction, by the time we have COP61, the world will be five degrees [Celsius, or 9 degrees Fahrenheit] warmer.”

Panama plans to press this issue at the U.N. General Assembly, Navarro said. “Decisions at the COP should be made by simple majority, just like at the General Assembly,” he said, adding that “more and more countries” are coming around to this view. An effort within the U.N. to update the operating rules for COPs is another potential avenue for reform.

Such reform is not as unlikely as some observers seem to think. Chris Bowen, the climate minister of Australia and the co-president of COP31, acknowledged after the talks ended that consensus decision-making was partly to blame for the outcome. But Bowen misstated the relevant history when he asserted that “when COPs were created … [decision-making] was made consensus only.”

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research, walked through the history in a LinkedIn post during COP31. How COPs would make decisions was initially discussed at the very first COP, held in 1995. A proposal was made to reach decisions by consensus if possible, but if “all efforts have been exhausted and no consensus reached,” then a two-thirds majority vote would serve as a last resort. “But oil producing countries opposed this, with support from U.S. oil lobbyists,” Rockström wrote.

The issue was left unresolved. Nevertheless, Rockström said at a CCNow Press Briefing, in subsequent years “a culture took hold … to operate under consensus,” though in fact “there is nothing hindering … the COP process to have majority voting today.”

How the various efforts to reform decision-making at U.N. climate summits unfold is a story worth watching—and covering. There would seem to be enough time to fix the process before COP32 takes place next November in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Doing so could make a world of difference.

items.title: John Berger’s Radical Appreciation of Art
items.content_text:
Beloved prolific writers take a long time to catch up with; their legacies form slowly, through waves of collected works, citations, and reissues. So it is with John Berger: art critic, television and radio host, novelist, filmmaker, playwright, essayist, activist, who died in 2017 at the age of 90. His was a “long life of short books,” writes Tom Overton in his new biography, John Berger: From Life. Even before his death, regular new collections and evangelizing by younger writers made him quietly ubiquitous. His influence reaches beyond the work he is most famous for: the 1972 BBC television series Ways of Seeing, which became a paperback classic and art school staple.

A casual reader could merely sample the bonanza of recent Berger publications marking the centennial of his birth. NYRB Classics has new editions of the novel G., which, for all its cringey sex, is still fantastic, as well as the essay-poem-epistle And Our Faces, My Heart, Brief as Photos, and the essay collection About Looking, with the canonical “Why Look at Animals?” and “Uses of Photography.” Verso, which is publishing From Life, has recently reissued more than a dozen of his books, including Hold Everything Dear, a late work that collects writing on Palestine and post-9/11 politics, and A Seventh Man, a collaboration with the photographer Jean Mohr about the experience of migrant workers in Europe in the 1970s.

The wonderful thing about Berger is you can open him almost at random and find lines that land regardless of your familiarity with the subject matter. Some of my favorite pieces can be found in Portraits, a 2015 collection of essays on artists. The cover of one edition features a fragment of a “Fayum portrait” of an Egyptian woman of the third century BCE—a likeness painted in tempera and attached to a mummy. Berger finds the Fayum portraits remarkable for their intimacy and immediacy; “they gaze on us,” he writes, “like the missing of our own century.” The piece is typical of his writing in its ability to “drill holes in time,” as Overton puts it, between the creation of an artwork and our reception of it.

The accessibility of his criticism is arresting. (The Success and Failure of Picasso opens simply, “Picasso is now wealthier and more famous than any other artist who has ever lived.”) Elsewhere, as Overton notes, “things tip to the enigmatic.” As with Walter Benjamin, another long-lived star in a similar firmament, Berger’s “Marxist, materialist view of history had space for a spiritual, mystical dimension.” Ben Lerner, in a lovely new introduction to G., describes Berger as “a butterfly catcher one second and a stoneworker the next.” In all of it, one finds what Geoff Dyer defined as the two concerns of Berger’s life: “the enduring mystery of great art and the lived experience of the oppressed.”

But to dip in and out of his work without context is somehow anathema to Berger’s way of seeing, which was all about context. As he writes in an essay about photographic portraits: “I am includes all that has made me so.”


Overton got to know Berger after he donated his papers to the British Library in 2009. Then in his twenties, Overton would call Berger to ask for context about something, and would get a story in return. They became close, and Overton edited Portraits and a companion book, Landscapes, contributing helpful scholarly introductions. After Berger died, Overton discovered a cache of more personal material from the 1960s and ’70s, stored in a bomb shelter in Geneva. With access to reams of intimate material, Overton does not pass quickly over the more embarrassing parts of the life and work. This is a book for Berger devotees, who will perhaps not be surprised to find in it a man much like his writing: generous, romantic, marked by tremendous intelligence and “utter, intense sincerity,” politically unswerving, occasionally obtuse, and very male.

Born in London in 1926, Berger grew up in the shadow World War I cast over his father’s generation—the source, Overton argues, of Berger’s later preoccupation with the relationship between the living and the dead. Like many upper-middle-class boys of that era, at a young age—nine years old, in his case—he was packed off to boarding school and made to feel the family’s sacrifice for his education. The school was a “totalitarian system” and “an absolutely monstrous place,” Berger later said. Overton says it helped to form his “hatred of the British establishment and its culture.” In secondary school, he became a Marxist, reading the Stalinist Labour Monthly and pinning a hammer-and-sickle to his lapel.

He started studying painting in London in 1942, when he was 16, and still too young to be called up to fight in World War II. He lived there with a girlfriend, “by our wits and with the Old Masters”; the National Gallery, at the time, was exhibiting one “Picture of the Month,” keeping the rest stored in Welsh caves for safety. “As an apprenticeship in looking,” Overton writes, “it encouraged a close focus, and a habit of return. It also took the distinction between oil paintings and their reproductions and added in the emotional weight of a literal sense of exile and yearning.” Berger rejected an officer’s commission and spent his military service in a training camp in Northern Ireland. He would later present this experience as part of his formation as a “storyteller,” claiming that he wrote letters for illiterate working-class conscripts, though Overton can’t turn up evidence of his having done so. After V-E Day, he got “psycho’d out”—declared psychologically unfit—by some combination of acting and an actual breakdown.

In the 1950s, Berger stopped painting. “There were too many political urgencies,” he later said. He became an anti-nuclear activist and cold warrior on the side of communism, though never a party member. The vehicle for his politics was art writing, chiefly for The New Statesman. Rather than “Socialist Realism, he argued for Social Realism,” Overton writes, by which he meant regionally specific art with everyday themes. “‘I’m not pleading for anything ‘folksy,’” he once told students. “But there is a difference between ‘folksiness’ and the present situation where artists in Oslo, Buenos Aires, Tokyo and Toronto all paint as though they lived in Paris.” His support for social realism led him to champion some second-rate artists and dismiss some great ones. He was, for example, vocally critical of U.S. abstract expressionism. And though he did eventually soften that position, he remained, as he put it in a 1968 essay, “intransigent” in his opposition to the commodification of art. In a small act of protest, which he maintained throughout his career, he had the images in all his books printed in low-quality black-and-white, so that they might function like technical illustrations and avoid any association with advertising or coffee-table consumerism.

In a small act of protest, which he maintained throughout his career, he had the images in all his books printed in low-quality black-and-white, to avoid any association with advertising or coffee-table consumerism.

In 1962, Berger settled in Geneva with the Russian émigré Anya Bostock, who was working as a translator for the United Nations. The move marked what Joshua Sperling, in A Writer of Our Time (2020)—a more straightforward, intellectual biography—calls Berger’s “prolific, peripatetic middle period.” He made popular TV and radio series, wrote several novels, a trio of biographies, and developed, with Jean Mohr, the documentary format of some of his best-loved books: A Fortunate Man, which follows a country doctor (a friend of Berger’s) on his rounds, interspersing Mohr’s photos with Berger’s reflections on his vocation, and The Seventh Man, which takes a similar approach to migrant workers. He rallied students at Oxford against the Vietnam War and experienced the fervor of 1968 in France and Prague. He collaborated with Alain Tanner on several films. Nineteen seventy-two was a watershed, Overton writes: Ways of Seeing debuted on BBC, and G. won the Booker Prize.

Ways of Seeing was markedly less lavish than other popular art history shows. (Kenneth Clarke’s 1969 series, Civilization, took the audience on a kind of grand tour of Europe with footage that was exceptionally visually rich for the time; the BBC even hoped the show would encourage viewers to rent new color TVs, Overton writes.) Ways of Seeing was stripped back, partly due to budget but also because the whole point of the show was that its viewers were not on a grand tour. Instead of encouraging viewers to consume works of art, he wanted to think about them and the worlds that shaped them. When the audience saw an Old Master, it was being reframed by the angle of the camera and what it captured, by the music, by Berger himself, who, in the famous first scene, cuts into a reproduction of a Botticelli with a knife. The material facts of art—who it was made by and for, and how; how it was accessed—mattered. Berger’s direct address to his viewers and over-the-shoulder shots of the cameraman, his collaborator Mike Dibb, were part of dispelling the mirage.

Jo Livingstone described Ways of Seeing in this magazine as “a basic primer on the complicity of the European art tradition from 1500 to 1900 with the politics of the same period.” Hans Holbein’s The Ambassadors is related to colonialism; Gainsborough’s Mr. and Mrs. Andrews to enclosure; the Renaissance nude to the male gaze. Overton emphasizes the role of Berger’s collaborators—researcher Chris Fox brought in “Merleau-Ponty-influenced thinking on the nature of sight”; the rostrum photographer Ken Morse provided “persuasive visual energy.” But Berger was face of the series and, by the end of the year, of the Booker Prize, too.

The prize was funded by Booker McConnell (now the Booker Group), a company founded in the nineteenth century that made money from enslaved workers in the Caribbean and British Guyana. Even though Berger enjoyed royalties from his BBC program, the prize represented a lot of money to him at the time—5,000 pounds. Yet at the prize ceremony, Berger announced that half the money would fund his next project, on migrant workers, and he would donate to other half to the British Black Panthers, revolutionaries who were, as Overton puts it, “in London now because the Bookers had been in the Caribbean.” Berger had learned about their work through his friendship with C.L.R. James. Rebecca West heckled him; the diners started banging on the table to interrupt. The fame that ensued for Berger was “permanently destabilizing,” Overton writes.


Overton credits Bostock as an unnamed collaborator on Ways of Seeing. She appears in the second episode, “Women and Art,” one of a group of women invited to discuss the program’s arguments. The nudes in the paintings Berger shows “are what is called idealized, and therefore they are, to me, very unreal in connection with any deep-down image I might have of myself,” Bostock says (the women participants are listed in the credits but go unnamed on-screen). At the end of the episode, Bostock provides an alternate image from the early Renaissance, of a woman in a loose, comfortable dress: “she is at ease, she is relaxed, she is not playing any part at all, she is able to combine pleasure with thought, and with dreaming, and she might spring into action at any moment.”

Bostock translated from German and Russian to English—Marx, Trotsky, Lenin, and Brecht, as well as texts key to Berger’s work, including Georg Lukács’s The Theory of the Novel and Ernst Fischer’s The Necessity of Art. She was also active in the women’s liberation movement. She held consciousness-raising meetings in her flat, and she made her own BBC radio program in 1972, called “Women’s Liberation.” But while Berger was in London, Bostock was usually back in Geneva, taking care of their two young children and providing for their family with a steady salary.

Bostock was the third of Berger’s four wives; he had left his second, Rosemary Guest, because he fell in love with Bostock, and had left his first, Pat Marriott, to be with Guest. The dedication of G. reads, “For Anya and her sisters in women’s liberation” without a smidge of irony. Bostock felt that its Don Juan plot was “at least partly John’s attempt to understand his own behaviour through fiction,” according to Overton. Berger was, while writing it, involved with another woman he knew in Geneva, named Annar Cassam. He slept with Cassam on a trip to Prague to see “the last embers of European socialism,” and to Bostock, Overton writes, “it seemed a betrayal of the reasons John traveled there, as well as her. They tried, for a time, to understand it as an alternative living arrangement: a sidestepping of anything so conventional as a bourgeois marriage. Anya spoke of respecting John’s ‘convictions.’” He did the same thing to his last wife, the American Beverly Bancroft, for whom he left Anya in 1973. By 1980, he was splitting his time three weeks with Beverly and their son, Yves, and one week with the French Ukrainian writer and actor Nella Bielski.

Overton gives Berger’s wives and lovers their due as intellectual influences and as people in their own right. He also gamely tracks down archival evidence, more or less subtle, of many other overlapping affairs. Bostock is the most present—Overton knew her and uses her diaries as a guide to Berger’s papers—and the effect of Berger’s decisions on her life is keenly felt. When he left her with the children, she had to give up translating. She wrote to a friend in 1973 about “the damned recklessness” of talent and “the privileges of weakness.” Many people noted Berger’s generosity, as well as the intensity of his attention when he was with them; some of those same people later were startled at how he could cut them out of his life. His son Jacob called it his “human turnover.”


Bostock, according to Overton, did not buy Berger’s idea of himself as “a storyteller.” She thought it was false modesty, an abdication of his moral role. Overton and others agree with her. “­Storytellers lose their identities and are open to the lives of other people,” Berger once said. Berger was certainly open to the lives of others, but you do not, reading him, forget who he is. In the mid-1970s he moved to the Haute-Savoie, in the French Alps, where he worked alongside his peasant neighbors. Their vanishing culture became the subject of his fictional trilogy Into Their Labours, published between 1979 and 1990. Some found his new focus affected—a friend he had fallen out with mocked him “milking his peasants.” Some found it a betrayal. The left was in defeat, and Berger had influence. There was a generation of artists and radicals growing up on Ways of Seeing, and he wasn’t speaking to their moment.

Berger was certainly a romantic. His 1984 book, And Our Faces, My Heart, Brief as Photos, theorizes alienation and the figure of the migrant rather too poetically at times; when Edward Said cautioned that exile was “compelling to think about but terrible to experience,” he may have been thinking of Berger’s high-flown meditations. Berger’s exile from his own culture was a choice, and the respite he found in rural life was a function of his relative privilege. Even at his most sentimental, however, he isn’t advocating a nostalgic restoration of the past but rather a deep respect for its embedded knowledge and struggle against the forces that would eradicate it. (In this, he is much like Wendell Berry, the American agrarian poet and thinker who died this summer.) His approach in much of his later work calls back to his argument for social realism—art that is grounded in its place of origin even as it fights the inequities that define that place.

In an afterword to Into Their Labours, Berger wrote that the role of capitalism is to “sever every link with the past and to orientate all effort and imagination to that which is about to occur,” because the system’s “present reality is dependent upon its future fulfilment.” What better description of the financialized economy, of the looming AI bubble? Against this, he admired the peasant “conservatism not of power but of meaning. It represents a depository (a granary) of meaning preserved from lives and generations threatened by continual and exorable change.”

You can see this kind of depository in To the Wedding (1995), a beautiful novel he wrote after his daughter-in-law died of AIDS. The protagonist’s similar fate is juxtaposed with that of soldiers who died in a railway accident in the same valley in which she lives—she knows their story well. As Berger writes in Pig Earth, part of the peasant trilogy: There will be justice “when the living know what the dead suffered.” This is the message we may take from Berger into our era of livestreamed genocide.

Berger hardly traveled beyond Europe, only once to the United States and several times to Palestine. But he never stopped engaging with militant global politics. He was an early convert to Third Worldism and enacted his solidarity in the 1990s and 2000s through exchanges with Subcomandante Marcos of the Zapatistas (the basis of his 2008 novel, From A to X), and with his excoriation of the war on terrorism and advocacy for Palestine.

There is a through line of political clarity reaching from those writings back to his work against nuclear weapons and the Vietnam War. The things about which he remained intransigent are the correct ones. In our era of public declarations of allyship, it’s striking to read his Booker speech. The decision to give the money to the Black Panthers was not a question of guilt or conscience or philanthropy but one of shared struggle. “The issue is between me and the culture which has formed me,” he says. I am includes all that has made me so.

items.title: How to Bat Down Your Uncle Frank’s Stupid MAGA Thanksgiving Arguments
items.content_text:
Well, it’s Thanksgiving again, which, in addition to all the usual excess, brings for some of you the now-decade-old tradition of having to sit there and endure your MAGA uncle bleating on about immigrants and wokery and Sleepy Joe. Thankfully, I’m spared this at my sister’s table, where I’ll probably be somewhere in the ideological median of the 10 assembled. But if you are not so lucky, I feel for you. As a public service, I herewith suggest some strategies and offer up a little ammunition for you once old Uncle Frank gets a bit in his cups and is on a roll. Below are a few thrusts he might make, and how to parry them.

1a. “This holiday wouldn’t even exist if it were up to you people.”

Actually, virtually no one wants to “cancel Thanksgiving,” in the words of the instantly infamous 2020 Twitter post from Wisconsin Democrat Francesca Hong that surfaced earlier this year during her gubernatorial run. Hong expressed a view that is probably held by a small number of lefty academics and grad students but is hardly representative of anything.

That said, Uncle Frank, would you like to take a stab at guessing the Indigenous populations of North America in 1500 and 1900? In or around 1500, when Europeans began arriving on our shores, there were around 10 million Native Americans. By 1900, there were 300,000. No, they weren’t all slaughtered. Most died from disease. But the near extinction wasn’t always so passive, either. Mass forced displacement of people didn’t help. And in some cases, white settlers distributed blankets contaminated with smallpox to make sure more Indigenous people died. So, you know, if Native Americans aren’t exactly in the mood to celebrate meeting up with us, can you really blame them?

1b. “Yeah, but what about this thing I heard on Fox about Loudoun County forcing third graders to think of Thanksgiving as a ‘Day of Mourning’?”

Not true. Loudoun County did have, among its instruction materials, one slideshow for grade-schoolers that said teachers could teach kids that for Native Americans, “Thanksgiving marks the beginning of a long period of violence and discrimination.” But it was optional. All of one teacher is known to have used it.

2a. “Maybe, but the economy is still so much better under Donald Trump than Joe Biden.”

That’s true only with respect to the worst of the inflation rates, which peaked at 9.1 percent under Biden and 4.2 percent under Trump. However …

GDP growth was stronger under Biden: 3.2 percent to 2.3 percent in Trump’s first term; so far in his second, it’s around 2 percent. Job creation? Trump’s first term was negative 2.7 million because of the pandemic; so far in the second, it’s around 950,000 jobs. That’s super-lame for two years of an administration. Under Biden, the number for his four years was close to 15 million. Even if you don’t count the pandemic against Trump, his pre-pandemic job creation was around 6.6 million—good, but not 15 million. Or, by the way, the 11.5 million netted under Barack Obama.

2b. “OK, but … in general, Republicans are way better for the economy.”

Actually, that’s complete bullshit. The list of statistics showing the economy to do better under Democratic presidents is longer than Tacko Fall’s arm. But suffice it to say, Uncle—on GDP, median household income, stock market performance, even deficit reduction—the numbers of the last few Democratic presidents are light-years better than the Republican numbers. And here’s a great fact: We’ve had 11 recessions in this country since World War II. Ten have come under Republican presidents. Ten of 11. That, dear uncle, ain’t no coincidence.

3. “But Trump’s been great on immigration. Anybody who came here illegally deserves what they get.”

OK, let’s grant that people who crossed the border illegally did technically break the law. However: About 75 percent of those people work. The labor force participation rate between foreign- and native-born populations is about the same, at 78 percent. Also, Uncle, the people you like to call “illegal” pay taxes—at least $90 billion a year. Sometimes, they pay Social Security and Medicare taxes, even though they’re not even entitled to those things. Also (and I assume, dear Uncle, that you’re pretty worked up about the deficit), it’s worth pointing out that undocumented immigrants in recent years have paid about $3 trillion in taxes while using just $1.3 trillion in various benefits, meaning they’re net deficit reducers by $1.7 trillion! (And this stat comes from a conservative-libertarian outfit!)

4. “Well, you people are still so obsessed with letting men play women’s sports.”

Nobody’s “obsessed” with that except JD Vance. Out of 510,000 scholarship NCAA athletes, fewer than 10 are transgender. In the Olympics, the number is lower. For sure, there are people and groups who don’t want to see 1 percent of the population picked on, but there’s no one out there actively plotting to recruit trans athletes to take over women’s sports.

5. “Maybe so, but thank God for Sophie Cunningham!”

Actually, while I’m certainly not here to defend her, that whole thing is mostly being pushed by people on X who are making money by stoking hatred and divisions. They may not give a crap one way or the other. But that’s the free market, Uncle Frank, so you should be all for that!

6. “Well, by God, we’re beating China!”

Are we? You can buy Nvidia chips like candy in China! These, by the way, are the same chips Sleepy Joe banned from being sold in China for national security reasons. But they’re on the market now, available not only to the Chinese military but to anyone with the money to snap ’em up.

7. “But he’s keeping Iran from getting a nuclear bomb.”

The only reason Iran got close to having nuclear capability is Trump tearing up the agreement Obama negotiated. Ever hear of Nick Burns? He said back when Trump tore up the deal that it would make Iran a nuclear threat again and maybe lead to a war.

8. “Well, he settled eight wars.”

Some of those countries weren’t really at war; others still are. On balance, one of the eight seems like it’s a legit claim.

9. “All right. But he caught those cheating Somalis up there in Minnesota.”

The Biden Justice Department started that investigation. Merrick Garland, no less!

10. “Pass the whipped cream.”

Actually, that’s not whipped cream. It’s nondairy, nut-free, oat-based—

11. “Gladys, get your coat!”

items.title: Water Bear
They Voted to Get Rid of Flock Cameras. Now Comes the Hard Part.
items.content_text:
In mid-August, dozens gathered outside of Wilmington, North Carolina’s New Hanover County Courthouse to protest the more than three dozen Flock Safety Automated License Plate Reader cameras that had been installed in their communities the previous year. The crowd carried signs comparing Flock Safety tech to George Orwell’s “Big Brother,” claiming that the company was “conditioning” Americans to view their “privacy as selfish.”

It was just a snapshot of what had been taking place across America. The company markets its sleek, egg-shaped devices to police departments as a covert tool for scanning, identifying, and monitoring vehicles on the road. Typically mounted on poles or posts along roads and parking lots, the cameras photograph passing vehicles and record identifying details, including their license plate number and their make, color, and certain distinguishing features like roof racks and bumper stickers. Law enforcement agencies can also tap into a national network fueled by the devices, accessing traffic data from across the country, wherever the cameras were installed.

The backlash in New Hanover County had been brewing for months. In August, anti-Flock community members spoke before the rural county’s Board of Commissioners for an hour and a half, decrying the surveillance technology’s likeness to a digital panopticon, its ties to billionaire technocrat Peter Thiel, its various privacy breaches, and the lack of public oversight of the devices, which have been used by police officers to stalk exes and current partners, among other inappropriate abuses.

During the meeting, several board members claimed they were unaware of the details of the contract inked between the sheriff and Flock Safety. The officials then reassembled in a private conference room on a hot day in early September and ultimately decided to take a step back.

“Our public is being used as a test case as the Flock company itself shifts its position to address the overwhelming pushback, and that makes me feel uncomfortable, as if they have unleashed something they were not aware of, the power behind it,” County Commissioner Rob Zapple said at the special meeting. “I think the chances for abuse are clearly there, and we see them continue to happen across the country.”

On September 8, the board arrived at a unanimous decision: It was time to get rid of the Flock cameras. The board opted by a 4–0 vote to prematurely end the two-year, $219,000 arrangement, asking the company for a $53,500 refund to cover the nine months remaining on the contract. The sheriff’s office unplugged its devices from the national Flock network and powered down the cameras themselves, waiting for the company to collect them per the terms of the contract.

By all accounts, the local anti-surveillance movement appeared to be a success: Residents had risen up in opposition to devices they believed violated their privacy and, perhaps, their constitutional rights and convinced government representatives to act. New Hanover County is far from alone—across the country, the backlash to Flock has been growing. Not only that, but it’s surprisingly bipartisan; the demand to remove these cameras has been building in red and blue counties around the nation.

It’s also, in many cases, just the start of another set of problems. Voting to get rid of the cameras is fairly easy. Actually getting rid of the surveillance network they develop is another matter altogether.


Flock Safety was founded in 2017 and in April was valued at $8.4 billion. Its name has become synonymous with the increasingly controversial use of automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, by law enforcement.

Flock frames its high-tech cameras as indispensable tools for law enforcement, and promises that its round-the-clock recordings can help law enforcement agencies locate missing people and capture criminals with its national vehicle lookup. Flock advertises on its website that 20 percent of the cases cleared in 2025 were assisted by its technology (an enormous figure that some scholars have patently rejected). The company has even expanded beyond traditional law enforcement arrangements and currently has contracts with homeowner associations; hospitals; universities; and commercial retailers, including Lowe’s and Home Depot, where its cameras monitor parking lots.

The company has pitched its cameras as an essential component of modern-day crime-fighting, but in reality its core product is its expansive national database. Many experts argue that it has actually created a dangerous new avenue for potential abuse.

There is already a pile of evidence demonstrating such abuses. A 2025 report by the Electronic Frontier Foundation found that police officers across the country have tapped Flock’s database to track protesters, target people of color, and surveil women seeking reproductive care. An August report from the Institute for Justice recorded at least 200 cases of ALPR abuse. These included a Texas sheriff’s deputy who used 83,000 Flock-licensed cameras to hunt down a woman who allegedly received an abortion and a Georgia police chief who used the database roughly 600 times to track the movements of his ex-girlfriend and her child. Even retired members of police forces have been caught logging in to the software to pursue their own personal crusades and vendettas.

The problem is even bigger than the individual bad actors who might be using Flock’s data network, as the software’s development appears to be outpacing the government’s ability to curtail abuses.

The problem is even bigger than the individual bad actors who might be using Flock’s data network, as the software’s development appears to be outpacing the government’s ability to curtail abuses. When a participating law enforcement agency conducts a search on Flock’s database, the program returns “hits” that include specific license plates, vehicle makes, car model, color, and cosmetic details, all with time-stamped GPS images. But the cameras are likely capable of tracking much more than that. Despite Flock executives’ repeat promises that the company’s tech is not designed to track individuals, a hacker collective that broke into a Flock-licensed ALPR camera reported to Wired in September that the cameras do detect the drivers of the cars.

Flock’s database, moreover, encourages nationwide tracking that many states and municipalities are attempting to regulate. One possible solution could involve introducing warrant requirements that would force a law enforcement agency to seek out a judge’s approval and require it to justify searches before tapping into a broad national surveillance network. It would also have the benefit of slowing the entire process down, turning a lightning-speed digital query into multiday, real-life oversight.

That could prove to be a more effective solution to preventing potential abuses than state regulation, which fails to account for the national nature of Flock Safety’s data sharing network. For instance, when law enforcement officers from thousands of miles away access data collected in, say, New Hanover County, their out-of-state searches have the potential to bypass local safeguards, effectively making regional regulations obsolete.

This kind of surveillance overreach isn’t hypothetical. Audit logs obtained by Mark Williams, a Wilmington-based attorney and founder of DeFlockILM, revealed that nearly 3.9 million searches had accessed North Carolina’s regional database between March and May alone. Those searches were conducted by 3,904 agencies, and the vast majority of them (approximately 90 percent) came from outside the state.
