These products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.”

items.title: Is Trump Flip-Flopping on Congestion Pricing?
items.content_text:
After years of trying to destroy New York City’s congestion pricing system, the Trump administration is now offering grants to take similar policies nationwide.

The Federal Highway Administration announced Thursday that it would invest $100 million to target and eliminate congestion, including funds to implement “HOV toll lanes, as well as congestion, cordon and parking pricing programs,” Gothamist reported.

Just hours after the announcement was made, that specific language was removed from the official online press release, according to Streetsblog NYC. Similar language describing congestion pricing can still be found in the description of the federal Congestion Relief Program.

Trump first announced that he would challenge New York City’s new congestion pricing program in February 2025 by declaring himself king. In March, a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration did not have the authority to revoke the city’s pricing policy. The Department of Transportation appealed that decision in June, arguing that it was the judge who had overstepped the bounds of their authority, and that the FHWA officials could revoke policies whenever it pleased them. The appeals court has yet to rule on the matter.

In August 2026, Trump again mocked congestion pricing, claiming that the program was being run by “Radical Left Jihadists,” referring to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was elected after the policy was already in place.

In a statement to Gothamist, DOT spokesperson Danna Almeida denied that the grants would possibly fund congestion pricing programs like the one in Manhattan.

“As the statute is written, the grant program is nothing like New York City’s illegal cordon pricing program, nor does it impact the ongoing litigation,” Almeida said. “The Secretary has been clear, dollars collected from tolling should be reinvested back into roads and drivers should have access to free alternative routes.”

Since the city first began charging drivers $9 during peak periods to drive south of 60th Street in Manhattan, New York’s Metropolitan Transportation Authority reports that traffic is down 15 percent.

items.title: Trump’s January 6 Slush Fund Is Still Alive
items.content_text:
Thought that President Donald Trump’s so-called “Anti-Weaponization” slush fund was dead? Not quite.

Trump administration officials intervened to secure a $2.5 million payout for five plaintiffs in a class-action lawsuit against the IRS, with each plaintiff getting half a million, ProPublica reported Thursday.

The Department of Justice initially sought to dismiss the case, but in August it intervened before the final fact-finding period with a proposal that would pay 250 times the legal limit of $1,000 for such cases.

The five plaintiffs included Shelby Lowman, a golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley, as well as Safe Harbor, a company connected to the president’s media business without a website or public presence. These plaintiffs alleged that the IRS and government contractor Booz Allen Hamilton had failed to securely safeguard their financial information—the same charges that Trump had levied against the IRS in his own $10 million lawsuit.

That lawsuit had resulted in the creation of the president’s $1.776 billion slush fund, paving the way for government payouts to anyone the administration saw fit. The fund was supposed to have been killed by court order months ago.

After these latest settlements, two more people connected to Trump businesses came forward to continue the litigation. Critics are concerned that even more plaintiffs could join in a backdoor attempt for Trump allies to receive massive payouts from the government.

items.title: “I Don’t Know”: Trump Nominee Has Horrifying Answer on January 6
items.content_text:
The president’s latest nominees aren’t even willing to describe what happened on January 6, 2021.

Michael LoSapio, who currently heads security for the software company Palantir, has been tapped to run the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. He shocked lawmakers during his confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill Thursday when he refused to answer a straightfoward question about the MAGA-stoked insurrection.

“Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021?” asked Connecticut Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.

“I—I don’t know,” LoSapio said.

“You don’t know?” Blumenthal repeated, apparently stunned by LoSapio’s response.

“I don’t know how you would classify—” LoSapio stuttered, when Blumenthal interjected to press him.

“Really?” the senator asked.

But by that point, LoSapio had decided to double down.

“No, I don’t believe it was an attack, no,” he said.

There was a long silence, and then Blumenthal—who was one of the many lawmakers in the Senate chamber when Donald Trump’s sycophantic followers attempted to break in that day—asked: “You’re giving us that answer?”

“I wasn’t involved in politics,” LoSapio deflected.

“You weren’t involved in politics? Were you alive on the planet?” asked Blumenthal.

“I was,” LoSapio said.

“Let me ask you again. I’ll give you another chance. January 6, 2021, was the Capitol attack—” Blumenthal said, to which LoSapio simply responded: “No, sir.”

Then Blumenthal decided to ask the man seated beside LoSapio: Trump’s nominee for director of the Office of Government Ethics, Michael Chamberlain.

“Mr. Chamberlain, January 6, was the Capitol attacked?” asked Blumenthal.

“There were certainly some people who engaged in behavior they shouldn’t have,” Chamberlain said.

“How do you expect to be the chief arbiter and adjudicator of ethics in the U.S. government when you cannot answer a simple, factual question? Do you really want this job?” asked the senator.

But Chamberlain could barely muster a response about fairness and impartiality, ignoring the enormous political leverage that his and LoSapio’s revisionary answers had afforded the president.

It has been nearly six years since Trump supporters rioted on the U.S. Capitol in an attempt to block the certification of what Trump claimed was a “stolen” election. In the time since, Trump has invariably tried to brush the events of the day under the rug or rewrite them entirely. Hours after his second inauguration, he granted clemency to nearly 1,600 individuals who faced criminal charges for storming the Capitol, and later tried to create a $1.776 billion slush fund to reward them for their participation.

items.title: Elon Musk Tries to Split From Trump After Midterms Humiliation
items.content_text:
After Republicans’ resounding defeat in the midterm elections, Elon Musk suddenly sees “positives and negatives in both parties.”

“I’m not MAGA,” he said at The New York Times’ Dealbook Summit on Wednesday. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think I’m like—if that means a sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

This is a dramatic reversal for the world’s richest man, who proudly proclaimed himself “dark MAGA” shortly before the 2024 presidential election. In the most recent election cycle, Musk threw away nearly $500 million trying to help Republican candidates at the ballot box in November. In Texas alone—where Musk relocated his massive Tesla and SpaceX operations from California in an attempt to avoid Democratic oversight—the tech CEO burned at least $212 million in support of Ken Paxton’s doomed bid for the Senate and another $12.3 million in funds for conservative political groups.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said via Zoom at the Dealbook Summit. “Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

Now that Texas has gone blue, the new Democratic Attorney General Nathan Johnson, Senator-elect James Talarico, and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (who campaigned directly against Musk and his artificial intelligence data centers) may make the billionaire’s life a whole lot tougher.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk posted on X in the early hours after the election.

He also quietly deleted posts he’d made before the election in support of the Republican Party.

On Wednesday, Musk had changed his tune further. “The new governor, actually, I think, is going to be quite moderate,” he said. “I don’t think she’s sort of a far-left governor. And based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor.”

Musk has clearly seen the writing on the wall, according to CNN data analyst Harry Enten. “The Democratic brand is, simply put at this point, in a much better position than the Republican brand,” Enten said Thursday morning. “Elon Musk is reading the tea leaves. He’s no fool. He sees what’s going on. He saw the results just a few weeks ago. He sees the polling now.… That is why, all of a sudden, he wants to make friends with Democrats.”

Musk can try to get cozy with the new Democratic majority in Congress all he likes, but the House is already gearing up to launch investigations into him and his businesses, starting with his role in the Department of Government Efficiency fiasco, his government contracts, and his AI chatbot Grok.

“Lawyer up,” Representative Robert Garcia, soon-to-be chairman of the House Oversight Committee, wrote on election night.

items.title: House Democrats Love Hakeem Jeffries. But Does the Rank and File?
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.

Inside Washington

What did we learn from Tuesday’s vote among House Democrats to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker, clearing the path to his ascension to that position next January 3? Mostly, we learned that Jeffries and his team did a bang-up job of tamping down any opposition to his rise. It was impressive work, which Chuck Schumer hasn’t been able to match in his own leadership drama. But Jeffries’s decisive win can’t erase one nettlesome fact that no one was in the mood to talk about yesterday: A decent chunk of the party rank and file wanted someone else; there’s something of a disconnect between Jeffries’s support within his caucus and his support from Democrats out there across the country.

The vote, conducted by recorded-but-secret ballot, was overwhelming: 251 for to 11 against with two abstaining. Before the vote, some House watchers were saying 40 “no” votes could signal trouble, and 11 is obviously far short of that. The “no” votes came from incoming members whose criticisms of Jeffries mainly focus on Israel policy: Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania. 

Even without the hard work from Jeffries’s team, this outcome was practically guaranteed. Democrats were never going to turn down the opportunity to elevate the first Black speaker ever. Voto Latino president Maria Teresa Kumar was quick out of the gate Wednesday morning to make the point: “The framers of the Constitution did not have people who look like Hakeem Jeffries in mind.” 

That doesn’t mean there weren’t rumblings of opposition. Massachusetts Representative Ayanna Pressley was the subject of a petition urging her to run. She seemed to be considering it for a few days publicly. But Axios reported that she was never actually serious about running and that her public Hamletting had actually miffed some fellow Progressive Caucus members. “She’s only playing coy with people online,” one CPC member told Axios. “The rest of us know she’s not running. But that’s generating additional calls and making people … even more pissed off in the end.”

That online petition was one of many trying to push for a Jeffries alternative. At least one person was paid to gather names. Still, hundreds of thousands of people did sign these things. It’s hard to know whether grassroots opposition to Jeffries—over his ties to some corporate donors and AIPAC—is truly widespread or is one of those “Remember, Bluesky isn’t the real world” phenomena. In a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll of Democrats only, Jeffries’s approval numbers were 40–29. That was a lot better than Schumer’s (34–43), but 40 percent isn’t exactly unreserved love.

For now, both moderate and progressive activists in Washington are making positive noises about the presumptive speaker. Adam Green of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee is a big backer of Chris Van Hollen in the Senate leadership contest, but he said Wednesday morning that he was encouraged by Jeffries’s recent embrace of a vast Medicare expansion. Jeffries indicated he might support lowering the eligibility age (to exactly what, he didn’t say) and adding dental, vision, and hearing. “A lot of people in Congress are gradually realizing they don’t need to live in a lowest-common-denominator environment that is needed with a slim majority,” Green told The TNR Blue Book. “Jeffries coming out for lowering the Medicare age is an example of economic populists raising the floor and ceiling of what’s possible.”

Likewise, Jim Kessler of the centrist group Third Way said that moderates trusted Jeffries, albeit for very different reasons. “Jeffries knows and publicly acknowledges that he only holds the gavel if Democrats can win in the difficult districts that many Dem moderates represent,” Kessler said, pointing to at least 57 districts won by Donald Trump in 2024 that next year will be represented by Democrats. “Every one of those seats is precarious, and moderates feel they’ll have a speaker who believes that in his bones. In addition, they’ve seen how Jeffries has been a target of the extreme left faction within the Democratic coalition, and that is an experience that many moderates share with him.”

So for now, and presumably through next January, Jeffries will bask in the glow of history and unity. Then he’ll take the gavel (on January 3, he’ll need only 218 votes to become speaker, so he can endure many more defections than he did yesterday). And then the work will begin. 

Jeffries will start with a unified and energized caucus—but also with at least a dose of skepticism from rank-and-file Democrats. Those skeptics won’t just be lefties upset about Israel, but also more mainstream voters who aren’t convinced he’s the political pugilist they think the party needs in these final two years of Trumpism.

Speaking of Trump, it’s worth remembering that Jeffries won’t just be facing challenges from his own caucus or base. “Congress will not only face an executive that is both deeply hostile and contemptuous of the rule of law and the role of Congress,” longtime Congress-watcher Norman Ornstein told The TNR Blue Book. “It is also likely to have the Elon Musks and Peter Thiels of the world willing to spend hundreds of millions to blame everything that goes wrong on Congress, and a media and social media dominated by oligarchs tilting toward Trump. Changing the way Congress does its business and communicates, with much more focus and internal discipline in messaging, along with balancing key legislative initiatives with the accountability agenda, are key. Business as usual won’t work.”

Ornstein’s last sentiment is one Jeffries might want to print out and tape to his bathroom mirror.

—Michael Tomasky


Outside Washington

Stateline’s Shalina Chatlani reports on states’ issues applying the new Medicaid work rules enacted in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Last week, the administration pushed the deadline for instituting the changes back by six months, but that may not do much to limit the chaos. “Every state is dealing with its own set of circumstances, and so are enrollees,” Chatlani explains, noting that differences in minimum wages from state to state can affect the number of hours people need to work. And documentation presents a further challenge: In the first four months of Nebraska instituting the new rules, Chatlani reports, “at least 956 people lost their Medicaid because of paperwork.” Democrats including Representative Hakeem Jeffries—set to become speaker of the House—have indicated they want to try to repeal these work requirements when they take control of Congress in January.

Amid news that the United States has officially lost its measles-elimination status, The Guardian’s Michelle R. Smith reports this week that the anti-vax group previously led by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is back on Facebook and Instagram, “four years after Meta removed the group for repeatedly violating its misinformation policies.” Innocuously titled the “Children’s Health Defense Fund,” the group has “reopened or opened six accounts on Facebook and Instagram from May through September this year” and is using these accounts to tell parents that their kids could die if they are vaccinated, while denying that recent deaths related to the current measles outbreaks had anything to do with measles.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

Public Citizen published a new report alleging “alarming conflicts of interest” among “a dozen” high-ranking Trump administration Securities and Exchange Commission officials. “The grift is a feature, not a bug,” Public Citizen co-president Lisa Gilbert says in the organization’s press release. Some examples cited in the press release: “SEC enforcement actions against several of SEC Chairman Paul Atkins’ previous clients were dropped soon after he came to the SEC,” and “the SEC’s new Crypto Task Force has at least two officials with close ties to the crypto industry, including a former crypto industry lobbyist.”

The Roosevelt Institute Book Club meets at 1 p.m. Thursday on Zoom for a discussion of Daniel Driscoll’s Why Carbon Taxes Failed. “Drawing from archival documents, statistical data, and in-depth interviews with policymakers and activists,” the event website teases, “Driscoll argues that carbon taxes can work—but they have to be smartly sequenced behind public investment and planning.”

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Here’s Why That’s B.S.

Watch TNR’s Edith Olmsted tackle Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s bizarre set of statements about the recent FAA ground stop—and why he took a government jet to Louisiana when everyone else was grounded.


Political Trivia Question of the Day  

During the 1950s, when nuclear paranoia and fear of nuclear Armageddon reigned over the land, American schoolchildren received instruction via a three-word catchphrase about what they should do in the event of a nuclear attack while they were in school (yes, for real). What was this phrase? Hint: Two of the words were verbs. 

(Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Rubio’s and Hegseth’s “Swords” Comments Should Sicken Sane People
items.content_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently warned the International Criminal Court, or ICC, against trying to claim jurisdiction over American citizens by saying, “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth used this same quote on X to signal his own defiance of the ICC, and, given how he has treated the courts during his tenure, his defiance of the law in general.

The warning against quoting laws to men with swords is attributed to the Roman general and statesman Pompey the Great, known to his enemies as “Pompey the Teenage Butcher.” Interestingly, after Pompey said this, he attempted to overthrow the Roman government and was subsequently assassinated and beheaded for his part in the Roman Civil War—something that Hegseth and Rubio seem to have missed when choosing to use the phrase as a sign of disdain and resistance against attempts to constrain their “America First” policies.

The fact that the U.S. secretaries of state and defense ascribe to this “might makes right” stance should set off alarms both domestically and internationally. Their amoral and sophomoric attitude of “Good. Bad. I’m the guy with the gun” also runs contrary to the most basic tenets of their jobs.

Let’s start with Rubio and the State Department. His role is to administer the soft-power arm of the U.S. government, with the use of military force intended to be the last resort. His diplomacy is expected to be a tad more subtle than “Do what we tell you, or we’ll kill you and your family,” and his moral authority is supposed to come from ideals like democracy, freedom, and human rights rather than the barrel of a gun or the pointy end of a Tomahawk cruise missile.

American voters demonstrated their exceptionally short memories by forgetting what a chaotic dumpster fire Trump’s first term was and voting him back into office. The rest of the world, however, remembers. The reputational damage Trump’s reelection inflicted on America is probably worse than when the United States waded into Iraq in 2003 on its own, without the backing of international consensus (the “Coalition of the Willing” barely counts, but it’s still more than we have today with Iran).

I have seen much of the classified intelligence shown to the president before Iraq. When I worked at the Navy’s Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, I was in charge of Long Range Plans and Policy in 2005 to 2006. Part of my portfolio of information was the 2003 intelligence that laid out why the United States believed Iraq had weapons of mass destruction. The Bush administration genuinely believed there were hidden chemical weapons.

They may have been looking for an excuse, but from everything I saw, the people who put together the intelligence briefings, and Colin Powell, genuinely believed these assessments. Up until the last moment, Saddam Hussein was more afraid of Iran than of the United States. He was deliberately acting shifty to give the impression that he still had weapons of mass destruction to deter an invasion by either country. In reality, most of the missing munitions had simply been lost in the chaotic final days of the Iran-Iraq War, and it never occurred to American analysts that someone could simply lose hundreds of artillery shells full of mustard gas and nerve agents.  

The Department of State attempted to convince the world that the intelligence was correct; who could forget Colin Powell holding up that little vial during his trip to the United Nations? It was ham-handed, it was wrong, but the administration was at least trying (or pretending) to play the game and follow the rules, building consensus and a coalition. When Saddam Hussein was toppled, the United States tried to put in place a democratic government.

Contrast that with Rubio’s State Department. There’s no attempt to bring about some sort of consensus. The approach of the United States toward diplomacy has reached true rogue state status. We have nukes and a vast military, and we don’t give a damn about international law. Countries that refuse to accede to our threats either have their leadership kidnapped and replaced with new dictators willing to openly bribe Trump or have their leaders killed outright. Delcy Rodríguez in Venezuela handed over her country’s natural resources to Trump in exchange for his putting her in power and leaving her there as a vassal. In the latter case, Trump killed the previous Ayatollah Khamenei in Iran and wounded his son, who became the new Supreme Leader. The United States does not diplomatically operate on moral principles; the current defining motivation is the gaining of benefit for Trump and his family. Refusal to go along with Trump’s demands results in devastation, either at his hands or those of  fellow dictators (like Putin in Ukraine).

Even when Trump and Rubio are gone, the international community will remember what has happened, and what sort of people Americans are willing to not just tolerate but elect, repeatedly. This is why Canadians now see China and Xi Jinping as far more reliable partners than the United Sates, even though many assume Trump will be gone in two years. It’s the difference between lawful evil and chaotic evil: At least one will honor their contracts.

Hegseth’s echo of Rubio’s attitude is also a giant red flag. Since the turn of the nineteenth century and Theodore Roosevelt, the military has understood its role in America’s “Speak softly and carry a big stick” diplomacy-first posture. The U.S. military has also long accepted the supremacy of civilian control, as well as the Posse Comitatus Act, which restricts using federal military forces to execute domestic civilian laws.

The idea of a U.S. military that is told “no” by the courts and then decides to go ahead and do something anyway because there is no military force that will stop it should send chills down the spine of any sane person. People who believe that power equals power and might makes right, and that they are the only rightful rulers of a country, make for the most ruthless of dictators.

This is doubly true now that Hegseth and Trump have spent years weeding out flag officers who might not be personally loyal to the administration first, along with all the judge advocate general officers who would try to circumscribe their power by adhering to the law.

It is not hard to imagine a scenario in 2028 where Democrats win the election, the courts block Republican attempts to steal it, and Rubio or Hegseth applies this logic to U.S. courts, as well: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.” Indeed, both have been dropping big hints that they intend to run for president in 2028. Rubio has been trying to position himself as the moderate and sane option compared to others in Trump’s orbit, but this quote clearly says otherwise.

Democracy in the United States depends on respect for the law and the concept of institutional forbearance, which is voluntary self-restraint by rulers from using their powers to the absolute limit, even when it is technically permissible to do so. Rubio and Hegseth have clearly illustrated, through their endorsement of might makes right, that they have no intention of following the rule of law, even to the extreme detriment of the United States and the world.

items.title: Stephen Miller Benches Markwayne Mullin After Disastrous Press Run
items.content_text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin can’t handle the heat.

Mullin’s calamitous communication flubs earlier this week frustrated other Trump administration officials, to the point that White House chief of staff Stephen Miller intervened to yank Mullin off-air, according to White House insiders who spoke with Politico Thursday. Miller was across the Pacific Ocean with Donald Trump in Manila when he stepped in.

“Despite the mixed messaging from Mullin, the administration was able to take the reins—even overseas—and put together a coordinated response to inform the American people,” a White House official told Playbook.

Miller replaced Mullin with National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who are now jointly handling the White House’s messaging on immigration and Friday’s FAA ground stop.

“This is a perfect example of why Stephen was put in the role as chief of staff—he knows all the different components, every member of the Cabinet trusts him, and he can quickly get them coordinated to deliver on a unified goal,” the official added.

The issues began last week, when Mullin effectively reopened the doors to the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program by telling reporters at the National Harbor in Maryland that he would be open to a policy that offered permanent legal status to immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children.

Days later, Mullin broke from the administration’s rhetoric on the emergency FAA ground stop during an appearance on Fox News, indicating that the nationwide disruption was potentially related to the recent implementation of AI systems. Making matters even worse for the White House, Mullin cited “one guy who is very smart with tech,” though he explicitly added that it was not Elon Musk.

That interview sparked “WTF” reactions from White House aides, and moved Miller to strip Mullin of his communication duties.

“We need to speak with one voice and the right voice, and the decision was made to put Jay out there,” a person close to the White House told Politico.

items.title: Trump Forces Reporters to Go Dark on Air Force One, Raising Red Flags
items.content_text:
Reporters traveling to Washington with President Donald Trump on Air Force One were told to surrender their phones to administration officials before takeoff on Thursday.

The plane was on its way back to the United States following the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where Trump met with both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“At 6:45 pm consider this your wheels up,” the White House pool report said. “Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons.”

“Pool reporters traveling with the President say that on departure, they were asked to hand over their phones (to US officials) for security reasons. This is very unusual,” wrote NBC News chief White House correspondent Garrett Haake in a post on X.

The “security reasons” for seizing the devices are still unclear.

Fox News’s Jaqui Heinrich suggested on X that the plane might be making an unscheduled stop. “Phones were not taken after Beijing departure in May,” she wrote. Others are speculating about a flight restriction over Alaska or a potential detour to nearby North Korea.

It is abnormal for reporters to surrender their phones on Air Force One unless the president is traveling to a war zone, Andrew Feinberg of The Independent wrote, for instance when Trump flew to Iraq’s Al Asad Air Base in 2018 and to Bagram Air Field in Afghanistan in 2019.

Members of the press covering the president have been forced to jump through a series of hoops in recent months, following Trump’s attempt to ban MS NOW, CNN, and Politico from the White House in September for what he deemed unfavorable coverage. That ban led to several lawsuits, including one from Columbia University’s Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School’s Freedom & Information Access Clinic.

“The Policy violates the First Amendment. The White House has long maintained a protected forum for certain members of the press to engage in the First Amendment activities of newsgathering and reporting,” the lawsuit reads.

items.title: Donald Trump Cancels Second Mainstream Interview in Days
items.content_text:
Donald Trump pulled out of another mainstream interview Thursday–this time nixing a sit-down with NBC News.

The interview, CNN reported, would be in Philadelphia with NBC News' senior business correspondent, Christine Romans. CNN’s Brian Stelter said one source suggested that it had only been “postponed.”

It was the second time in a week that he had canceled a scheduled appearance outside the conservative news sphere, CNN’s Reliable Sources reported Thursday. He had canceled an in-studio appearance on the CNBC flagship show, Squawk Box, which was due on Friday.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Mitch McConnell Called Donald Trump a ‘Stupid’ and ‘Despicable Human Being’
items.content_text:
Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell called his party’s presidential nominee, Donald Trump, a “stupid,” “ill-tempered,” and “despicable human being,” according to his own records.

McConnell made the withering assessments in a series of private “personal oral histories” that he gave to Michael Tackett, the deputy Washington bureau chief of the Associated Press, who has a forthcoming biography about the Kentucky senator called The Price of Power. The AP conveniently reported the book’s juicy details.

McConnell’s remarks were made after the 2020 election that Trump lost, and the senator was apparently elated to see the backside of the former president, musing, “it’s not just the Democrats who are counting the days” until he leaves office.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Witnesses Say Would-Be Organ Donor Started ‘Thrashing’ on the Table
items.content_text:
Disaster was averted at a Kentucky hospital when an ostensibly deceased organ donor began “thrashing” around in the operating theater, a preservationist tells NPR.

“He was moving around,” Natasha Miller recalled of the patient, whom NPR identified as Anthony Thomas “TJ” Hoover II. “He was crying visibly.”

The two surgeons assigned to the transplant naturally refused to go through with the procedure, which was reportedly scheduled to take place at Baptist Health Richmond Hospital in October 2021. But when her colleague called Kentucky Organ Donor Affiliates, which coordinated the harvest, Miller said the supervisor told them they “were going to do the case” and needed to “find another doctor.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Menendez Family Members: We Had ‘Gut-Level’ Fears Erik and Lyle Were Sexually Abused
items.content_text:
Relatives of Lyle and Erik Menendez spoke in an interview Wednesday about their long-running fears that the brothers had been abused for years before they killed their parents.

After a press conference in which they’d called for the imprisoned siblings’ freedom, the family members told Chris Cuomo on NewsNation about how their suspicions only deepened as time passed.

“Over the years we really did know that there was abuse at gut-level. But as time goes on and we all talked to each other more and more, it validates the fears and the gut-level reactions that we had,” the brothers’ cousin Karen VanderMolen-Copley told Cuomo. “That solidified the knowledge that the sexual abuse actually did occur, because that’s not something you want to believe, and then once you talk to each other it becomes more and more obvious.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Liam Payne 911 Caller Said One Direction Star’s Life Could Be in Danger Minutes Before Death
items.content_text:
A hotel worker called 911 to request urgent assistance before musician Liam Payne fell to his death from the third floor of the building in Buenos Aires on Wednesday.

The 31-year-old British singer and former member of the boy band One Direction died after he “jumped from the balcony of his room,” Buenos Aires Security Ministry Communications Director Pablo Policicchio told the Associated Press. He added that police had been called to the Casa Sur Hotel in the Argentine capital after receiving an emergency call shortly after 5 p.m. local time about an “aggressive man who could be under the influence of drugs or alcohol.”

A transcript of a 911 call published by the BBC shows a worker at the hotel telling the operator that they have “a guest who is high on drugs and who is trashing the room” and the staff therefore “need someone to come.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Stormy Daniels Says Trump Is Trying to Silence Her Again
items.content_text:
It appears Donald Trump is once again attempting to silence Stormy Daniels, despite his recent convictions in that category.

MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow reports that Trump’s lawyers tried to “get another hush money deal” with the adult film star, to keep her from making any “public or private statements related to any alleged past interactions” with the former president. In exchange for her written agreement, Trump’s team reportedly offered to adjust the debt she owes Trump for the unsuccessful defamation case her lawyer brought against him in 2018.

Daniels still needs to pay “hundreds of thousands of dollars” in legal fees, Maddow explained, and in hammering out the exact amount, Trump’s lawyers allegedly offered to “pretend” she owed their client “less than they actually believed” she did. Whereas they first estimated Daniels’ debt at $650,000, Maddow reported, they said they would settle her tab for $620,000, if she promised not to make any “defamatory or disparaging statements about him, his business, and/or any affiliates, or his suitability as a candidate for president.” They then adjusted the fee, asking $635,000 if she refused to sign a non-disclosure agreement. Daniels reportedly turned them down, paying $627,500 and declining to sign the NDA.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.content_text:
Former President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Jan. 6, 2021— the day his supporters occupied Congress in a failed insurrection to try to stop lawmakers from certifying Joe Biden’s election victory—was a “day of love.”

Trump made the baffling claim during a televised election town hall hosted by Univision.

Ramiro González, a construction worker from Tampa, told the meeting he deregistered as a Republican because he found Trump’s “inaction” during both Jan. 6 and the COVID-19 pandemic “disturbing.” He asked Trump to square his controversial behavior during the attack on the U.S. Capitol—and the fact that many of his own former administration officials don’t support him any longer—with why he should be re-elected.

items.title: Tegan and Sara: The Pop-Rock Twins Driven Mad by a Wild Catfishing Scheme
items.content_text:
Online interactions are based on trust, since there are few definitive ways to certify the identity of the person with whom one is communicating. Naturally, this situation can lead to deception and manipulation, as it has—to tormenting effect—for Tegan and Sara, the popular indie rock duo whose lives have been turned upside down by a mysterious bad faith actor who, for more than a decade, has impersonated Tegan with fans, friends, and business partners.

Fanatical: The Catfishing of Tegan and Sara is an investigation into the myriad means by which the internet can be wielded to nefarious ends. More than that, though, it’s an anatomy of a crime and the complicated wreckage wrought by it, not just for the famous artists but also for the innocent admirers who were tricked into believing that fiction was reality.

Premiering on Hulu on Oct. 18, following its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, Erin Lee Carr’s documentary is a chilling snapshot of the unholy marriage of corrosive fandom and online duplicity. At its center are Tegan and Sara, the identical twin songstresses who began making a name for themselves in the early 2000s both for their talent and for being openly gay. This earned them a loyal fanbase of queer women and men who saw themselves reflected in Tegan and Sara, and that bond was strengthened by the siblings’ active interest in interacting with fans in person—Tegan would chat with show attendees in line and at the merch table—and on LiveJournal and other budding message-board platforms that afforded a previously unavailable degree of contact.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: ‘Anora’: The Screwball Stripper Odyssey That Should Win All the Oscars
items.content_text:
Movies can’t, by definition, be all things to all people, and yet Anora—winner of the Cannes Film Festival’s highest honor, the Palme d’Or—manages to vacillate between assorted registers with stunning, and ultimately affecting, aplomb.

Another of The Florida Project and Red Rocket writer/director Sean Baker’s tales of marginalized individuals struggling to survive and find themselves in an often-unforgiving world, the film is a character study, romance, crime saga, screwball comedy, and vérité drama all wrapped into one unique and dexterous package. More impressive than its nimbleness, however, is its poise and empathy, the latter of which is chiefly bestowed upon its protagonist, whose life is thrown for a rollercoaster-grade loop-di-loop thanks to a chance introduction.

Ani (Mikey Madison, in a star-making turn) is a Brighton Beach 23-year-old who lives with her sister and earns a living stripping at a local club. Anora, which hits theaters Oct. 18, introduces her at the end of a long pan along a bench where men are receiving lap dances from erotic professionals. Fixating on Ani’s face as she flashes the fake smile that her customers crave and her superiors demand, Baker’s camera creates immediate, intimate engagement with the young woman, and that continues as it presents snapshots of her daily (or, rather, nightly) routine at her place of employment.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Jimmy Kimmel Mocks Fox News’ Post-Harris Interview ‘Orgy’

Kimmel responded, “Alright, save it for the post-show orgy, everybody! Come on now.”

The late night host was skeptical that the Fox News pundits’ praise came from a genuine place of journalistic integrity. “They all sit there in fear, imagining Donald Trump on the toilet watching them,” he said.

items.title: Trump Gushes Over ‘Fair’ Bret Baier After Fox News Kamala Harris Interview
items.content_text:
Donald Trump praised Fox News chief political anchor Bret Baier for a “great job” in his interview with Democratic 2024 presidential hopeful Kamala Harris on Wednesday night, claiming Baier had “showed how totally incompetent Kamala is” while himself demanding she undergo a cognitive ability test.

Trump joined his campaign in calling the interview a total disaster for Harris. During the interview, Harris and Baier engaged in multiple back-and-forths; at one point, on the topic of immigration, Harris clapped back at Baier as he interrupted her: “May I finish responding to you?”

Immediately after the interview aired, the campaign—notably advisers Stephen Miller and Steven Cheung—took to X to decry Harris’ responses.

items.title: Anderson Cooper Literally Calls Bulls*** on Surrogate’s Trump Defense
items.content_text:
CNN anchor Anderson Cooper was flabbergasted Wednesday by a surrogate’s defense of Donald Trump, calling his explanation for the former president’s bombastic statements literal “bulls---.”

On AC360, former California Lieutenant Gov. Abel Maldonado, a Republican, said that Trump’s recent comments calling for the military to “handle” Democrats were simply his way of expressing his inner New Yorker. “He’s a fighter,” Maldonado added.

The conversation began when Cooper brought up Trump’s former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Mark Milley, who, alongside other military leaders, have begun to warn of the dangers of re-electing the former president. Milley has called Trump a “fascist to his core.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Liam Payne’s Snapchat Story Seemingly Sheds Light on Singer’s Final Hours
items.content_text:
Liam Payne was seemingly having a “lovely day in Argentina” just hours before his death on Wednesday, according to what appear to be a series of final posts made to his Snapchat account.

The former One Direction member was found dead in the courtyard of a Buenos Aires hotel, having apparently plunged 13 to 14 meters from his balcony, according to local police. A cause of death has not officially been determined, and it was unclear whether the fall was accidental or intentional.

On his Snapchat Story, however, it would have appeared to any fan that Payne was having a relaxing vacation. In since-deleted posts in the hours before his death, he posted a front-facing video in which he told followers, “It’s a lovely day here in Argentina. This is the breakfast table. Just enjoying coffee and breakfast even though it’s 1 p.m.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Chris Hayes Furious With Fox Over ‘Edited’ Soundbite in Harris Interview
items.content_text:
MSNBC’s Chris Hayes called out Fox News for not showing the full context of Donald Trump’s “enemy within” comments during Vice President Kamala Harris’ interview on the network earlier Wednesday.

The anchor of All In opened his broadcast by calling attention to something that Harris herself did in the sit-down with Fox’s Bret Baier. The clip that the right-wing network showed to Harris as part of Baier’s question was of Trump during his all-female town hall event in Georgia—the one where Trump bizarrely argued he was the “father of IVF.”

In the clip that Fox aired directly to Harris during her interview, Trump wasn’t heard talking about how former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi or Rep. Adam Schiff are the “enemy within.” Instead, Fox made it so Harris had to react to him talking more mildly about “phony investigations.” The network omitted Trump’s line about “the enemy within.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: ‘Real Housewives of Salt Lake City’: Is Heather Gay a Hypocrite for Taking Ozempic?
items.content_text:
The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City is TV’s best soap opera, week after week offering twists more shocking than secret twins and characters returning from the dead. That’s because it’s all real, happening in the most haunted suburb in the continental United States.

Where else do two women connect over knowing the long-lost birth father of one’s child? Is there another city where women squabble over body positivity in a parking lot off the side of a snowy mountain? Surely, there’s no other place on Earth where Lisa Barlow could come across anywhere near a voice of reason.

But that all happens here in Salt Lake City. Five episodes in, Season 5 has continued to evolve into the most captivating season in modern Real Housewives history, carried by the ever-changing bonds between our OGs and a team of wonderfully bizarre newbies.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Review: Will Adam Driver Explode in ‘Hold on to Me Darling’?
items.content_text:
It doesn’t matter how long a play is: sometimes 75 minutes can feel like 3 hours if the play is bad, while a three-hour play may first elicit an inner groan, then flow pleasurably by if the writing and performances are in well-oiled tandem.

Kenneth Lonergan’s Hold on to Me Darling (Lucille Lortel Theatre, to Dec. 22) belongs, mostly, to the latter category: it is long, and it feels long, but that’s OK; not gold-standard wow, but far more than pleasant. This is down to Lonergan’s engaging writing and a collection of differently distinctive, carefully drawn performances, led by Adam Driver as a famous country star called Strings (real name Clarence), wondering if he could/should give up all the trappings of fame for a simpler life after his mother’s death.

It is an off-Broadway treat to see Driver, most recently seen on the big screen as the star of Francis Ford Coppola’s polarizing epic Megalopolis, here bestriding—he is so tall, he is really bestriding—the compact Lucille Lortel stage. Theater fans last saw him on Broadway in Burn This, for which he was nominated for the Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play. He is renowned for playing powder-keg personas. With characters like Adam in Girls, Charlie in Marriage Story, and Pale in Burn This, the question, the bubbling menace, was when will Adam Driver go off? Those characters memorably combusted—thrashing, shouting, snarling and occupying spaces that could barely contain them—and Driver made it so that you recoiled from their crackling fury.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Fox News’ Bret Baier Whines About Harris After Bad-Tempered Interview
items.content_text:
Fox News host Bret Baier recapped his Wednesday night interview with Vice President Kamala Harris, telling his colleagues that he got a sense early on that Harris “was going to be tough to redirect without me trying to interrupt.”

The interview, Harris’ first on the right-wing network since becoming the Democratic nominee, was broadcast on Special Report after being filmed in the previous hour. According to Baier, the interview had been scheduled for 5 p.m., but Harris showed up 15 minutes late. This, he complained, was like “icing the kicker” in football.

“We were supposed to start at 5 p.m. This was the time they gave us. Originally, we were going to do 25 or 30 minutes. They came in and said, ‘Well, maybe 20.’ So, it’s already getting whittled down. And then the vice president showed up at about 5:15 p.m. We were pushing the envelope to be able to turn it around for the top of the 6 p.m.. So that’s how it started,” Baier said.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Defiant JD Vance Says ‘No,’ Trump Did Not Lose 2020 Election
items.content_text:
Republican vice presidential candidate JD Vance boldly said “no,” Donald Trump did not lose the 2020 election, when pressed on the issue at a campaign event Wednesday in Williamsport, Pennsylvania.

The Ohio senator has avoided directly denying the results over the past few weeks.

When quizzed by The New York Times about the results over the weekend, for example, he refused multiple times to answer the question, on one occasion claiming he was “focused on the future”—echoing an answer he gave to Democratic opponent Tim Walz at the vice presidential debate.

items.title: Liam Payne Was Embroiled in Bitter Legal Fight With Ex When He Died
items.content_text:
Prior to his untimely death in Argentina on Wednesday, One Direction’s Liam Payne, 31, was in the middle of a legal spat with his ex-fiancée Maya Henry.

On Monday, The Sun reported that Henry, 23, had lawyered up in an attempt to stop Payne from constantly messaging her family and friends.

“Maya Henry issued a cease and desist last week to Liam Payne following the emergence of new and concerning information…She has retained attorneys Marco Crawford and Daniel Cerna to represent her. At this time, that is her only comment on the matter,” a spokesperson for Henry told the tabloid.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Harris Shuts Down Bret Baier as He Plays the MAGA Hits
items.content_text:
In a contentious interview with Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris, Fox News host Bret Baier spent no time going after the vice president with a laundry list of the subjects often highlighted by former President Donald Trump on the campaign trail.

Immediately after the interview kicked off, Baier opened by asking: “How many illegal immigrants would you estimate your administration has released into the country over the last three and a half years?”

Harris began a carefully worded answer, but Baier consistently interrupted her before she could finish a sentence.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Watch Liam Payne’s Phenomenal ‘X-Factor’ Audition That Made Him a Star
items.content_text:
A collective gasp echoed like a thunderclap in a valley in our Daily Beast newsroom late Wednesday afternoon at the news that singer Liam Payne, who became famous as a member of the group One Direction, died at age 31.

TMZ reports that Payne fell from a hotel balcony in Argentina, where he had reunited with bandmates at 1D-er Niall Horan’s concert. He had, according to the site, been behaving “erratically,” earlier in the day, and was spotted smashing a laptop in the hotel lobby and having to be carried back to his room. He had been in headlines on gossip blogs over tension with his ex-fiancée Maya Henry, who, TMZ says, alleged “he'd left her after asking her to get an abortion.”

In the shock of his death, fans couldn’t ignore the eerie nature that Payne had just connected with his One Direction bandmates. Dark questions emerge when a celebrity dies so young: What role did the often horrific toll of fame have on a person like Payne, who has been open about addiction and suicidal ideation? But there’s also an impulse to go back to the roots of a person’s talent, to revisit what it was that we all fell in love with—and was their passion—in the first place.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Billionaire Bill Ackman Admits Debate Conspiracy He Pushed Is Fake
items.content_text:
Billionaire Bill Ackman spent days after the ABC presidential debate promoting false claims that a network “whistleblower” had allegedly uncovered collusion between ABC and Kamala Harris’ campaign. Now, a month and multiple denials later, he sees the claims differently.

“It seems pretty clear that the alleged @abc whistleblower debate story claiming that @KamalaHarris was given questions in advance and other advantages was a fake,” Ackman posted on X alongside a blog post by Megyn Kelly discussing the dubious claims.

What Ackman, CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management, did not acknowledge, however, is that he was one of falsehood’s early boosters. After an X account named “Black Insurrectionist” claimed it had been in touch with a whistleblower who alleged the Harris campaign had been given debate topics ahead of the showdown with Donald Trump and had demanded Trump—and Trump alone—be fact-checked.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: CNN’s Stars Get Massive Salaries Frozen as Bosses Sharpen Ax
items.content_text:
Journalists at CNN, including some of the network’s biggest personalities, are living in fear of “inevitable” layoffs and pay cuts as its new CEO looks to shore up finances amid declining ratings.

That’s according to The Ankler, which reported Wednesday that 77-year-old Chris Wallace—whose already been relegated to a weekend program—is among the network’s most well-known names whose future is in limbo.

Wallace’s $8.5 million contract, signed by the ex-CNN boss Jeff Zucker to recruit him away from Fox News three years ago, is reportedly up and he was spotted in CEO Mark Thompson’s office on Tuesday.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: One Direction Star Liam Payne Dead After Fall in Argentina
items.content_text:
Liam Payne, a former member of the boy band One Direction, was found dead in a hotel courtyard in Buenos Aires, Argentina on Wednesday evening, according to CNN and La Nacion, both of which cited local police.

The singer died after an apparent fall from the balcony of his third-floor hotel room. Argentinian authorities told Good Morning America that Payne had been staying at the hotel CasaSur in the upscale neighborhood of Palermo.

He was 31.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Kamala’s GOP Posse Predicts ‘Hidden Harris’ Victory
items.content_text:
WASHINGTON CROSSING, Pennsylvania—At a campaign rally in the most important swing state in the country, anti-Trump activist George Conway told the Daily Beast why he thinks Kamala Harris can win over Republicans.

“She’s kind of done it already,” he said. “Look at all those people who voted for [Nikki] Haley when she was already done. I actually think there’s kind of a hidden Harris vote for Republicans who are just exhausted by Donald Trump.”

Turnout is another factor that plays to Democrat’s advantage, Conway predicted. “I also think that even the people who are still for Trump and won’t vote for Harris, I don’t think the turnout’s going to be great for him.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: HomeKit Weekly: Meross’s new presence sensor splits a room into three zones for Apple Home
items.content_text:
Presence sensors tell Apple Home when someone is in a particular room, which is awesome for running automations based on that. They don’t tell it where in the room you are, though. That’s why these types of automations end up being all-or-nothing type things: you walk into a room, and every light comes on at full brightness, whether you came in to read at your desk or to grab something off the counter. The Meross MS605 splits its detection range into three distance zones, and each of them shows up in Apple Home as its own presence sensor so you can build automations around them.

朋友一边结婚当新娘，一边叫了感冒药送到了我手里；\
